This tiny inkwell contains an alphabetic inscription in ancient Etruscan, a language that has never been fully decoded.

According to recent reports, when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell.

Industry observers note that this small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

Recent findings suggest that the vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in Upcoming York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

Recent findings suggest that according to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet demonstrates that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Recent findings suggest that thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#303. The 7 Best 3D Printers for Latest Makers, No Matter What You’re Making

📅 26 Jun 2017 • ⏱️ 31 min read (6214 words)
General 🌐 Popularmechanics

The 7 Best 3D Printers for Latest Makers, No Matter What You’re Making

📅 26 Jun 2017 | ⏱️ 31 min read | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you’re printing parts, toys, tools, or making art, a 3D Printer is an incredible tool for crafting and creating.
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that here’s an example of why I love 3D printers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re printing parts, toys, tools, or making art, a 3D Printer is an incredible tool for crafting and creating.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that here’s an example of why I love 3D printers. Over the holidays, the drain in my bathroom sink broke. Part of the pop-up assembly snapped, and the stopper was stuck in the down position. I didn’t have time to run to the hardware store, so I searched for an at-home solution. I checked online and found that someone had created a 3D-printable version of the exact part I needed. And 30 minutes later, part in hand, I repaired my sink.

It has been revealed that 3D printers can replicate virtually any part or product through a process called additive manufacturing, which assembles physical objects by layering a pliable filament or building material. Most consumer 3D printers work with various plastics, but there are printers that work with a wide range of materials including metals, ceramics, composites, wood, and more.

In a recent development, in the decade since 3D printers first exploded onto the consumer tech scene, these tools have become much easier to use. It used to be that you’d spend more time fiddling with the printer than using the product that you just printed. While they are still hobby-grade (read: expensive) tools, modern printers make it easy to set up a print, and you don’t have to babysit your project to make sure everything comes out okay.

Sources indicate that buying a 3D printer today isn’t too different from buying a table saw—you’ll need to do some research to find one that fits your space and can print what you want to print. Once you have it, you can focus on designing and printing everything from toys to tools to tech.

Industry observers note that I’ve taken the time to test some of the most highly rated and popular 3D printers to highlight the best for new customers. These are some of the easiest printers to use, and should allow technically minded newcomers to get up and printing as promptly as possible.

Industry observers note that I’ve been a maker and tinkerer for decades, and have used 3D printers both professionally and as a hobby, printing everything from board game pieces to replacement parts for appliances. I’ve seen first-hand how diverse the 3D printing community is, and that we have a wide range of needs.

Industry observers note that A tabletop gamer needs a different type of printer than a print farm operator, or an artist, or a maker. On top of that, there are a ton of nuances to consider when comparing 3D printers from size and speed to print quality and affordability. For this guide, I specifically prioritized printers that are easy to use. I imagine that, if you’ve come to Popular Mechanics for advice, rather than a deep message board or 3D printing influencer, there’s a good chance that you’re just starting out and haven’t put down roots in the community. That’s okay! Welcome! I’m here to help you get started.

Recent findings suggest that nearly all of these printers are new models, released in the last year. There’s one exception, the Creality Ender 3 V3 SE, which is our “Easiest to Use” pick. It was tested, though, by contributor Sascha Brodsky to see how well it holds up against newer models.

It has been revealed that I tested each of the printers we recommend by printing all kinds of things, from detailed busts and decorative lithopanes to peg board organizers, table saw rails, and shop vacuum accessories. I sent a core group of models through all the printers, and pushed the boundaries of individual printers with a range of sizes, styles, and filament types. All told, I stacked up more than 100 hours of print time per printer.

Sources indicate that I focused on printing with common filaments that a fresh user would most likely use, such as polylactide (PLA), polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG), and thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU). During testing I used the manufacturer’s slicer and – when possible – their branded filament as well. I printed models taken off the manufacturer’s online services, as well as third-party sites. I selected a variety of models, from functional to decorative, and from large to miniature. I tried to push all the printers in terms of consistency, performance, and precision.

Industry observers note that I also recorded how long it took to set up each printer, from opening the box to producing a completed 3DBenchy benchmark model. (Or “box to Benchy” time, as I like to call it.) I also had more subjective measurements, such as how intuitive the printer interface and slicer are. I made note of anything I found confusing in their UI, and I tracked whether they needed babysitting to complete a print. I also tracked any failed prints, to see if the printer had an error detection system, or if it continued to run through the failed print.

And through it all, I identified which printers made the process easiest, from set up to printing and troubleshooting. Once I got them through all that, I was able to see which ones stood out from the rest in terms of price, performance, and features.

Released in the U.S. last November, the Bambu P2S is Bambu’s mid-line printer, falling between the entry-level A1 and their premium H-Series models. This is hands-down the most user-friendly 3D printer I’ve ever operated. From setup and basic operations to remote printing, it’s so easy to use it almost feels like running on autopilot.

In the last few years, Bambu has revolutionized the 3D printer industry by bringing more intuitive, beginner-friendly features to the market. Their business is based on creating a full ecosystem for owners to explore. Bambu provides their own filament with RFID chips on the spools, so the printer can change its settings to match that specific filament’s needs. And their Maker World website is full of models and tools, including one-click projects (such as RC cars), that start a 3D print and simultaneously ship out any hardware or electronics needed to complete it.

According to recent reports, bambu encourages—some critics would argue “pressures”—consumers to use all of these integrated services. The situation is not unlike the “walled garden” of Apple’s iOS App Store, which curates a library of beautifully designed products that are accessible and easy to use, at the expense of some creative freedom for both users and developers.

Recent findings suggest that regardless of how you feel about this kind of manufacturer ecosystem, though, the P2S is an impressive machine. It’s an intuitive system that’s easy to use, and works right out of the box. Of all the printers I tested, the Bambu P2S was the only one that never gave me a single connection glitch, and any failed prints were identified and paused to allow me to address the issue.

That ease of use even extends to the Bambu mobile app. Most 3D printers have a mobile app that allows you to track progress or view your print progress in real time through a camera, but Bambu’s Handy app is on another level: It connects directly Bambu’s Maker World, allowing you to set up prints remotely from your phone, automatically handling slicing. To be honest, I didn’t think I’d use the app, but I rapidly found myself breaking out my phone while watching TV and sending a quick print to the P2S. It was so easy to use, it just became second nature.

Industry observers note that for new customers, I loved Bambu’s tutorial library, including tutorials in both text and video. This is even true for the “experimental” services in their Creator’s Maker Lab, where users can create their own models using a range of manual and AI tools. I tried a few of these with moderate success. (It struggled with photos of people wearing glasses, and it tended to generate disturbing results, including a 3D model that combined two of my dogs into a single nightmare creature that would be at home in a Cronenberg film.).

No printer is perfect, of course. The P2S uses a single nozzle to print multiple colors, which means the machine needs to reset, purging the old color and cutting some filament for the change, before resuming the print. Doing that once isn't a substantial deal, but complex prints may have hundreds or even thousands of color changes.

This takes its toll on both efficiency and print time: In a couple of complicated prints, I found that the printer discards three to four times as much filament as it used for the actual print. Likewise, I printed a single-color mask piece in 2 hours and 4 minutes, but a 3-color version of the design took an astronomical 19 hours and 30 minutes.

One other minor glitch: it struggled with any filament that wasn’t well-wound. I buy a fair amount of this stuff, and some manufacturers ship filament that’s loosely wound. I can get away with using it on a single-color printer or even a multi-toolhead machine. But with filament changing designs like the P2S, the filament gets bound up. I never had this issue with Bambu filament, or with well-wound 3rd party filament.

The Bambu P2S exemplifies how 3D printers have improved over the past few years. While other printers may have a specific task where they perform better, but the P2S is so incredibly easy to use, which makes it a great all-around option for beginners who may or may not know what they plan to print most. It’s the closest thing to a “set it and forget it” experience that you can get with a 3D printer.

Sources indicate that the Centauri Carbon is fast, affordable, and fun to use. It’s also a rare find for entry-level printers looking to enter the hobby with a low investment, with print quality and features that are typically seen in more expensive models. It doesn’t have many of the bells and whistles that I love from my other picks, but it delivers great value for its price, and it’s a perfect starting point for general use printing.

It has a strong sense of fun in its design. For example, the included waste-bin model that clips to the back of the printer isn’t just a bland box, it’s a tiny model of the Centauri Carbon. I felt the slightly playful nature of the design reflected a desire to make things enjoyable for the user, something that included keeping setup simple, with a box to Benchy time of one hour, 11 minutes, the fastest time I’ve found to date.

Elegoo seems to want to balance a streamlined UI with robust options. Their custom version of the Orca slicer tucks away some features in the name of streamlining, but they’re still there if you go digging. (That may be a good thing or bad thing, depending on how much you like to tinker with settings.) A recent software patch added an integration for Nexprint, Elegoo’s 3D model site, which makes it much easier to download projects straight into the slicer.

One simple UI choice that I appreciated is that the mobile app has a clear pause button, so if something looks wrong, you can stop the print before it completely goes off the rails. It’s a weird bit of psychology, but just being able to clearly see it made me more comfortable during long print jobs.

It has been revealed that the Centauri Carbon was noisier during operation than the other printers I tested, but silent at rest. (It has relatively hard feet, which seemed to cause more vibration in the bench than other printers.) That left me more inclined to leave it on, which opened the door for me to queue up projects more spontaneously.

One issue worth noting: When the Centauri Carbon debuted, Elegoo announced that it would have a multi-color option sometime in 2025. Now, finally, a multifilament printing option is slated for Fall 2026 availability with the $55 Canvas upgrade.

Out now is the full-blown second iteration of the Centauri, the Centauri Carbon 2 Combo (which comes with the Canvas upgrade) and will run you $450, while the original Carbon costs about $415—$360 for the printer, plus $55 for the Canvas upgrade.

Read the Full Review of the Elegoo Centauri Carbon 3D Printer Here.

Sources indicate that the QIDI Q2 can print with more durable materials that can withstand abuse from high heat and prolonged sun exposure. It lacks some of the added conveniences found on Bambu’s P2S or Snapmaker’s U1, but it’s priced accordingly. That makes it a standout if you’re looking for a fully enclosed, single-color printer that can print more robust materials.

There are two specific areas where the Q2 excels: First, it’s a great choice if you want to print materials that require a higher nozzle temperature and/or could produce a higher volume of fumes. Second, it keeps most of the customization options readily apparent, making it a good printer if you know you like to tinker with settings and dial-in custom quality and performance.

The Q2 was easy to unpack and to set up, with a box to Benchy time of 1 hour and 20 minutes. (The unit I tested did not include the QIDI Box multi-color kit, which meant I only had to set up a single filament feed.) That said, setup may pose a couple challenges for first-timers: The quick-start guide was light on details, and occasionally skipped steps. For example, there’s no mention of the cover in the setup instructions. It’s not a dealbreaker—chances are that you’ll realize you can put the cover on top—but I found myself wondering more than once if I’d accidentally missed something. Once the Q2 takes over the process and begins to calibrate, though, setup is a breeze.

It has been revealed that I found almost everything about the Q2 worked right out of the gate. If you find that you need to make tweaks, though, there is a library of helpful tuning tutorials with photos. (I wish someone handed me these back when I started 3D printing).

It has single-band, 2.4 Ghz WiFi, which allows you to send files directly to the printer, and an interior camera so you can monitor prints remotely. The Q2 is relatively smooth and quiet while printing, though it keeps a fan running even when idle, ironically making it both among the quietest and loudest printers I tested.

Recent findings suggest that it has an AI error detection that can potentially spot the “spaghetti” strands of filament caused by a failed print. Mine went off twice, alerting me in time so I could make adjustments before the print went off the rails.

I did run into an problem with a clogged nozzle after about 60 hours of printing. When I took off the cover, I pressed on the nozzle fan and found it had snapped its support struts. I’m not sure if the fan went bad and caused the clog, or if I damaged the fan when I pressed on it. Regardless, QIDI sent a replacement fan and hot end, and I was up and running with relative ease.

While my tests focused on basic filaments such as PLA, PETG, and TPU, the QIDI Q2 has a higher-temperature nozzle (370 degrees Celsius) and an interior box temperature of up to 65 degrees Celsius. This allows it to print with more robust materials, like polycarbonate (PC) and acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS). It also ships with a hardened steel nozzle, allowing it to print materials like carbon fiber (CF) or glow-in-the-dark filaments, which would damage softer brass nozzles. If your long-term printing goals include using your printer to make automotive parts, or other, more durable items that need to withstand high temperatures and forces, I think the Q2 can help you learn the ropes, and get where you want to go once you know what you’re doing.

I have a lot of affection for the Creality Ender-3 V3 SE. My colleague Sascha Brodsky recommended it as our “easiest to use” pick when it introduced in 2023, and for good reason. It was one of the first 3D printers to come mostly assembled, with clear instructions and enough user support to get you up and running, as well as features like automatic bed leveling that made the printer far easier to use than other models available at the time.

Today, the V3 SE is older than most of my recommendations, but it’s still an attractive (and very affordable) option. In its heyday, it was an outstanding selection for those new to 3D printing, and helped bring features like auto-leveling and partial assembly to market at an affordable price. Three years later, it still compares favorably with newer models in terms of setup time, with about an hour and a half from box to Benchy, putting it only a little behind the single-color enclosed printers on our list.

It's worth noting that even a few years in, I use this printer fairly regularly, especially when printing TPU or other flexible filaments. Softer plastics are generally susceptible to print issues, especially in enclosed printers that tend to run hot. If you’re not careful, you can end up with a sticky, stringy mess of a print, or even a clogged nozzle. Luckily, the Ender-3 V3 SE’s open frame and durability manages heat well, and gets the job done with ease. I’ve never had a problem, and that's what keeps me coming back.

In a recent development, that remarked, the design has started to show its age. It doesn’t have WiFi, so you’ll either have to set up a controller (such as a Raspberry Pi) or shuttle an SD card back and forth. With a max toolhead speed of 250 millimeters per second, it’s far slower than modern printers like the QIDI Q2 which can run at up to 600 mm/s. It also has a smaller print bed, no camera for remote monitoring, and no error detection.

Recent findings suggest that the Ender-3 V3 SE is capable of producing attractive prints, but the quality you’ll get is dependent on your ability to dial in the settings. It doesn’t automate settings or provide a seamless integration with online models. It also doesn’t have advanced calibration features like input shaping, which updates the printer’s settings to account for environmental vibration. Instead, you’ll need to hand-calibrate all those settings. On the plus side, it’s wide open to tweaking and adjustments, making it a great choice if you like to tinker and optimize performance.

The Ender-3 V3 SE is a venerable printer, and still has a lot to offer. Its user-friendly design was ahead of its time and, while it’s no longer our pick for Easiest to Use, the V3 SE remains a great choice for consumers who want to use flexible filament or are working with a tighter budget. It’s often available on sale, bringing its cost below $200, and if you’re willing to be patient, Creality sells factory-refurbished models for even less.

According to recent reports, the Snapmaker U1 set crowdfunding records when it rolled out on Kickstarter, thanks to its clever multi-head system that keeps four nozzles preheated and loaded with filament. It can change tool heads on the fly, rather than changing filament fed through a single nozzle. With no need to purge older filament, the U1’s design cuts print time and dramatically reduces waste. Seeing this printer go head-to-head with a filament changer, the choice is clear: I'll take the Snapmaker every time.

The U1’s setup kit is top-notch. It has an extensive, step-by-step assembly document, with full color images of each step, and a QR code that links to a video walkthrough. I loved that it shipped with extra parts, so a broken part doesn’t bring you to a complete standstill until you order a replacement.

Recent findings suggest that assembly and calibration took longer than other printers, because with four print heads, there’s essentially four times the work. It had a box to Benchy time of 2 hours and 49 minutes, more than double single-color printers like the QIDI 2 or Elegoo Centauri Carbon. (For an apples-to-apples comparison, I printed an actual Benchy model; the full-color test model that comes with the U1 adds a few hours of time, though the result is an adorable baby dragon, which immediately scored me points when I gifted it to my wife.) Even with the longer setup time, it never felt onerous.

Industry observers note that I was pleasantly surprised to see that the U1 comes with a generous amount of starter filament. It ships with four colors, each with 500 grams of filament, compared to most printers which ship with only a few grams, just enough to print a test Benchy. Snapmaker filament rolls also have RFID, so that you don’t need to manually enter the filament details.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, it does not ship with a lid for the enclosure, or any kind of filter in the case. This can become a problem when you print with materials that require higher nozzle temperatures. Snapmaker doessell a lid, along with a HEPA/activated carbon air filter, for $150. With the lid attached, the internal chamber can reach up to 50 °C, allowing the U1 to print higher-temperature materials like ABS and PC. Obviously, though, it’s annoying to pay extra for a feature that you might see as a core component of the printer. (If you’re open to a DIY solution, though, the U1 forums have a discussion thread where owners are sharing their own custom tops. This is why I love the 3D printing community!).

Industry observers note that overall, printing was a breeze, whether using Snapmaker or third-party filament. The U1’s AI error detection worked well, pausing prints if any debris was detected, and allowing me to fix it or cancel the job without wasting more filament. In fact, I had no problems with the U1's hardware at any point during testing. Where I did run into headaches was with the software. As it stands, Snapmaker's version of Orca is sluggish to load, and I had to reconnect the slicer to the printer every time I opened the software. The software is still in beta, and I expect this will be improved before release. Hardware this polished deserves a quality app to go with it.

Read the Full Review of the Snapmaker Here.

Industry observers note that testing the Elegoo Mars 5 Ultra was an exercise in both delight and frustration. There’s no disputing its print quality, especially when I produced beautifully detailed game miniatures. But I ran into regular obstacles on the path to those beautiful prints, in the form of poor or even confusing documentation. In a review focusing on ease of use, those pain points really stood out.

Resin printers like the Mars 5 Ultra are especially popular with gamers, who print miniatures for tabletop games. These small figures tend to be packed with details, and printers like the Mars 5 Ultra can generate layers as thin as 0.01 mm, 10 to 20 times thinner than a typical FDM printer. If you want sharp visual details, resin printing is the way to go. The Mars 5 Ultra is an especially good way to learn about printing with resin, thanks to a pair of features that make it more user-friendly than its peers.

Sources indicate that first and foremost, it has a tilt-release resin vat that reduces the suction forces between the build plate and the vat. When the build plate bed lifts up after each layer is complete, the vat tilts, creating an angle that makes it easier to separate. (Think of it like pulling off a sticker or a bandage -- it takes far less force if you start on one corner.) Since the tilt-release makes separation easier, your settings don't have to be dialed in quite so precisely in order to get a clean separation from the vat, and support points can be slightly smaller. As a result, you spend less time adjusting settings or removing support marks, and more time enjoying your finished prints.

According to recent reports, it also has a very helpful error detection feature, which is great for new printers. If the Mars 5 Ultra detects foreign objects in the vat—usually chunks of supports or models that have fallen off the print plate—it will pause operation and send a notification. That can minimize damage to the model you’re printing, and prevents debris from getting trapped, which could also crack the vat itself. (In general, I think any feature that keeps toxic resin where it belongs is a substantial value-add.) Both the vat and error detection save time and reduce the frustration of a failed print. They’re also more commonly found on printers that cost twice as much as the Mars 5 Ultra.

In a recent development, unfortunately, the standout design is somewhat undercut by Elegoo’s confusing and contradictory support documentation. The instructions told me to install Chitubox (an industry-standard slicer) from the included USB stick. But the only slicer on the USB was Elegoo’s SatelLite slicer. Now, I actually like SatelLite, but it’s not what they told me to expect. What’s especially frustrating is that Elegoo actually has a fantastic unboxing video with a clear, easy to follow walkthrough. But there’s no mention of it in the manual and no QR code linking to it on the packaging. So I only saw it when I stumbled across it online.

Industry observers note that setup aside, this is an excellent printer. It’s well designed and easy to use, and produces quality prints with minimal fuss. (Or at least minimal fuss for resin.) The touchscreen is easy to read and well laid out, with an easy to understand user interface. It is a little small, but it’s sensitive enough that I didn’t need to tap twice, even while wearing gloves.

I also love Elegoo’s optional in-box heater. I picked one up when the temperatures plummeted. Since I’d set up the printer in my garage, I thought I’d fall behind on testing. But the heater installed easily and worked spectacularly well. Before I knew it, I was churning out prints even though the weather was well below freezing. But that heater was the reason I was able to get a full test run on the printer, even during a polar vortex.

The Bambu X2D costs about $100 more than the P2S, and for that additional cost it delivers active heating, better venting, and a dual-nozzle design, letting you print more demanding materials faster and with less waste.

Most enclosed printers depend on passive heating, maintaining the internal temperature simply with the captured heat from the nozzle and print bed. By contrast, the X2D has a built-in heater allowing the internal chamber to reach temperatures up to 149 degrees Fahrenheit (65 degrees Celsius). The X2D’s active heating also allows this temperature to be consistent, making it much easier to reliably print materials like Nylon and ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene).

If you want to print material that can withstand the heat of an engine bay or exposure to the elements, the X2D is a fantastic choice. In addition to the active heating, it has an external carbon and HEPA filter to reduce fumes and airborne particles. It also has a dual-nozzle design that reduces waste when printing two-color models, and allows for easy support printing and removal.

The downside to the X2D is that I found it’s surprisingly prone to minor issues and inconveniences. I ran into a weird error when printing the Benchy model that shipped on the internal memory, and had to do additional tweaking to align models and the prime tower on the print bed. None of these would be unusual from another manufacturer, but Bambu has made a name for themselves by delivering the smoothest possible user experience. The X2D doesn’t quite live up to that standard.

It’s a very good printer for both standard and high-temperature filaments. And for the relatively small step up in price, it compares favorably to the P2S if you want to move beyond decorative items and start creating durable objects that can withstand a real-world environment.

Read the Full Review of the Bambu X2D 3D Printer Here.

There are two types of 3D printer built with home customers in mind: FDM and resin. (While other types of 3D printers are available, they’re intended for industrial use, with a learning curve and price tag to match.) As a rule of thumb, FDM printers are faster and produce more rugged prints than resin, while resin printers excel at fine detail.

Fused deposition modeling printers (FDM) are like a hot glue gun for plastic. They feed a strand of plastic filament through a heated metal nozzle, laying out the print onto a heated metal bed. They’re cleaner and easier to use than resin, and require less safety precautions. They tend to have larger print volumes, but they don’t produce prints that are as highly detailed as resin.

It has been revealed that resin printers, on the other hand, create layers of material by dipping a flat bed into a vat of liquid resin, then curing a layer of material with UV light. (It’s similar to the process of making candles, where you dip a wick into wax repeatedly.) They are typically more complicated to use, as the models have to be washed and cured after printing is complete. Printer resins are toxic until cured, and using resin printers requires significant safety precautions. Resin printers produce highly detailed prints, prized by users ranging from tabletop gamers making miniatures to the dental offices, creating surgical implants and guides.

Both types of printing have their pros and cons, depending on your space, your style, and what items you want to print. Generally speaking, FMD printers are good for larger items, items that need to be more durable, or when you need to turn around prints quickly. They are also a good choice if you’ll be printing in areas with less ventilation or if you’ll have children or pets around while printing. Resin printers are a better choice if you want outstanding detail, and have room to set up a cleaning station for your prints.

In a recent development, FDM printers are usually described by the head movement (either CoreXY or bed-slinger) and whether or not it’s enclosed or open frame. CoreXY printers move the head left to right, and front to back. On a bed-slinger, the head moves left to right, but front to back adjustments are made by moving (“slinging”) the bed itself.

According to recent reports, enclosed printers are just that–enclosed on all sides. These are typically CoreXY printers, and allow for higher temperatures and provide filtered vents for filaments that produce more fumes. They also usually cost more than open-bed printers.

Sources indicate that to start printing, you’ll need some 3D models and software (called a slicer) to send them to your printer. Luckily, some of the best options are free.

Recent findings suggest that every 3D Printer uses some type of slicer software, which allows your printer to analyze objects and create a blueprint for making a 3D printed copy. True to its name, it creates a digital model and “slices” it into anywhere from one to a few thousand printable layers, creating the building blocks of a 3D print design. The result is a detailed set of instructions for printing, called G-code. When you load a design, your printer follows the G-code to assemble the design, layer by pre-sliced layer.

Industry observers note that printer manufacturers provide a proprietary slicer or an open-source slicer customized for their specific machines. For testing purposes, I used the slicer provided by the manufacturer. Honestly, once you get used to one slicer, they’ll all feel pretty similar.

Creating your own print designs isn’t necessary, though, if you don’t feel compelled. There’s no shortage of sites with free or paid 3D print designs that you can download and print. Once you have a little bit of experience printing, there’s a whole world of printable tools and products to explore within the 3D printing community.

When a plastic part breaks, there’s a good chance someone else has run into the same issue and created a 3D version of that part to download and print. Many printer manufacturers support some kind of community site, where customers can upload, remix, and review 3D models.

Yes, when used properly. Both FDM and resin printers pose safety risks during operation. FDM printer risks include the hot end of an FDM nozzle and fumes from melted plastic. Resin printers pose more risks, as resin itself is toxic, and should not be allowed to touch unprotected skin, and should only be used in an area where the fumes can be safely vented outdoors. Resin printers also use UV light to cure the prints, which can damage your eyes if not properly filtered.

Industry observers note that FDM safety precautions are fairly straightforward. First, don’t stick your hand in the print area while the printer is running. This may sound obvious, but it’s surprisingly tempting to do, since sooner or later you’ll spot a bit of loose filament or some other bit of debris laying on the bed in the middle of a print. It’s very easy to reach in and grab that debris without pausing the print -- but the print head moves very fast and without warning. That nozzle is probably around 300 degrees celsius / 580 Fahrenheit, and having it slam into your knuckle can leave a puncture and a burn.

Recent findings suggest that second, make sure the room where you operate the printer is well ventilated. Proper ventilation is especially key when using high VOC filaments. These include acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) and acrylonitrile styrene acrylate (ASA), but the fumes will vary by manufacturer, so err on the side of caution.

Resin requires more extensive safety precautions. You’ll need to invest in PPE such as nitrile gloves, a respirator (use filters rated for VOCs and not just dust debris), and possibly UV safety glasses. When resin printing, venting is even more notable. In most cases it’s easy to safely vent your 3D printer, but if you’re concerned, consider getting an air quality monitor to ensure that you’re working in a safe environment.

Recent findings suggest that your primary expense using a 3D printer is your printing material, which will be plastic filament for these printers, but could be other materials with more advanced models. You can buy a one-kilogram reel of PLA filament for about $12 to $19. If you need a specialty filament, you’ll likely pay double that amount, and prices can go much higher for premium materials.

Then there’s the hit to your electric bill. FDM printers typically use about 50 to 100 watts to operate, depending on what material you’re printing and the ambient temperature. If your electricity is 20 cents per kilowatt-hour, your printers will likely cost less than 2 cents per hour to operate.

It has been revealed that lastly, there will be other costs over time: You may need replacement bed plates for FDM printers, or post-processing supplies for resin printers. Other parts may break and need replacing, as well.

Once you have a print and some compatible printing material, all you need to do is figure out what and how to print. I recommend new printer owners pick up some calipers ($30 or so, but you can get away with a $10 set). You can actually 3D print most of the other tools you’ll use. In fact, printing storage bins and organizers for your printing tools is a great way to learn the ropes while making useful prints.

In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

It has been revealed that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a fresh study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

According to recent reports, however, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

In a recent development, of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at Upcoming York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus noted.

Industry observers note that it's notable to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

According to recent reports, the "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus remarked. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, remarked in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, noted in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites.".

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes.".

Recent findings suggest that weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an key question for future research.".

#301. Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1625 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported.
  • Now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread.
  • A upcoming study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported. Nearly 500,000 Americans are diagnosed each year. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick. Antibiotics can treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may affect the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

Now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread. For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, Upcoming York, have tracked the complicated relationships among ticks, mice, oak trees, predators, and weather. Their research has uncovered unexpected patterns that could help predict when people face greater exposure to infected ticks.

A upcoming study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries. The findings show how decades of observations can reveal connections that shorter studies might miss.

"On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk," said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the extensive data collected over the years have been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from coincidences and statistical fluctuations.

Industry observers note that "Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare," stated LaDeau. "This research has followed an ecological community -- including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms -- examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study.".

Deer May Play a Smaller Role in Lyme Disease Risk Than Expected.

Recent findings suggest that when Lyme disease first gained recognition in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely driver of rising tick populations. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying numerous adult ticks, suggesting that areas with more deer might also produce more ticks.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. Although deer cannot pass the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks. Scientists suspected that larger deer populations would allow more female ticks to reproduce, eventually increasing the number of young ticks capable of spreading the infection.

In a recent development, but decades of monitoring have produced a different picture. On the Cary Institute's 2,000-acre forested research property in Dutchess County, Upcoming York, researchers found no statistically significant connection between deer numbers and the abundance of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks responsible for much of the Lyme disease transmission to humans.

"We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data," remarked Ostfeld, "but the whole data set in its entirety indicates no such thing.".

Mice Are a Much Stronger Predictor of Tick Surges.

While deer populations failed to predict the abundance of nymphal ticks, mouse populations showed a much clearer relationship.

Recent findings suggest that years with especially large mouse populations were followed by approximately 40% more nymphal ticks the next year. White-footed mice are particularly crucial because they provide excellent blood meals for tick larvae and are highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to those feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can retain the bacteria as they develop into nymphs. When these nymphs take another blood meal, they can pass the infection to humans.

The findings suggest that tracking mouse populations could provide a valuable early warning of unusually high tick numbers.

How Acorns Can Predict Tick Populations Two Years Ahead.

One of the most unexpected discoveries involves something that might seem entirely unrelated to Lyme disease: acorns.

It has been revealed that oak trees periodically produce exceptionally large crops of acorns in synchronized events known as acorn masting. These unusually productive years provide an abundance of food for forest rodents, allowing mouse populations to expand during the following year.

That increase in mice then supports larger numbers of young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly heavy acorn crop can reliably predict an increase in nymphal ticks two years later.

In a recent development, the relationship reveals a remarkable sequence of events in which the reproductive cycle of forest trees helps determine future tick abundance. It also offers researchers another potential tool for anticipating periods of greater Lyme disease exposure.

Why More Mice Don't Always Mean More Infected Ticks.

Although mouse abundance helps predict how many nymphal ticks will appear, the researchers discovered that it does not consistently predict what percentage of those ticks will carry Lyme disease bacteria.

Initially, scientists expected both measures to rise together. Because mice are efficient transmitters of B. burgdorferi, an increase in mice seemed likely to produce not only more ticks but also a greater proportion of infected ticks.

According to recent reports, early observations appeared to support that idea. However, as additional years of data accumulated, the apparent relationship gradually disappeared.

"It kept me up at night," noted Ostfeld, "because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.".

According to recent reports, the explanation appears to involve the other animals that share the forest with mice. Skunks, squirrels, and opossums also serve as hosts for feeding ticks, but most are much less effective at passing the Lyme disease bacterium to them.

In a recent development, when these animals are abundant, more larval ticks may feed on hosts that are unlikely to infect them. This can reduce the percentage of nymphal ticks carrying the bacteria, even when mouse populations are high.

"So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts," explained Ostfeld. "It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case.".

Industry observers note that this finding highlights an important distinction between the total number of ticks in an environment and the proportion carrying the pathogen. Predicting the risk of infection requires understanding the broader community of animals that ticks feed on, not simply counting mice.

Extreme Heat and Cold May Not Kill Ticks in the Wild.

Weather has also produced some unexpected results.

Earlier laboratory experiments suggested that exposure to intense heat or severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that ticks are surprisingly capable of surviving these conditions.

Researchers believe ticks protect themselves from temperature extremes by retreating into deeper soil layers or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less severe than at the surface.

However, the long-term data also revealed a more complicated relationship with temperature. Years that are warmer overall tend to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual, despite the ability of individual ticks to withstand short periods of extreme heat.

At the same time, warmer conditions generally favor mouse populations, which can lead to more ticks. These opposing effects make it difficult to predict how changing temperatures will ultimately influence Lyme disease risk.

What 35 Years of Research Mean for Lyme Disease Prevention.

Taken together, the discoveries show that Lyme disease risk depends on a network of ecological interactions that is complicated but not entirely unpredictable.

Sources indicate that mouse abundance, for example, provides a stronger indicator of future nymphal tick numbers than deer abundance at the study site. Similarly, unusually harsh winters may not reduce tick populations as dramatically as previously expected.

By understanding these patterns, public health officials may be better equipped to anticipate periods of increased tick exposure and develop more effective prevention strategies.

Still, important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will affect ticks, the animals they feed on, and the oak trees that influence rodent populations.

"You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far," said Ostfeld. "We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it's very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production.".

According to recent reports, the research site in Dutchess County has undergone significant environmental changes since monitoring began in 1991. Climate shifts, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species have all altered the conditions in which the forest's plants and animals live.

Researchers intend to continue following these changes to determine how ticks and their hosts respond over time. Their work could provide increasingly valuable insights into how future environmental changes will influence human exposure to Lyme disease and other infections carried by ticks.

An astronaut from Pakistan is set to launch on China's Shenzhou 24 mission in the coming weeks and become the first-ever international visitor to the Tiangong space station.

A pair of astronaut candidates from Pakistan have been training at the Astronaut Centre of China in Beijing, following an agreement reached between China and Pakistan in Islamabad in February 2025 and a subsequent selection process.

Recent findings suggest that china's human spaceflight agency confirmed in a Nov. 7 press statement that the upcoming Shenzhou 24 mission will carry one of the astronauts. The agency also released a mission patch.

Recent findings suggest that "China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun mentioned Nov. 9. "Having the Pakistani astronaut on board China's spaceships will mark the first-ever joint mission of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.".

According to recent reports, it is not yet known which of the two candidates will fly on Shenzhou 24. They were named in Pakistani press reports as Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, both pilots from the country's military forces. The pair were chosen from a wider pool of around 20 finalists.

In a recent development, the chosen candidate will fly as a payload specialist on Shenzhou 24 along with two Chinese colleagues, while the other will be on standby as a backup. While the Chinese astronauts will be starting a six-month-long stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will spend roughly a week in orbit aboard Tiangong during a standard crew rotation period. He will then return to Earth aboard the departing Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, along with two Chinese astronauts who will have completed a six-month-long stay in orbit.

It has been revealed that the arrangement means changes to China's usual "three in, three out" Tiangong crew rotations. One of the three Shenzhou 23 astronauts, who arrived at Tiangong on May 24, will stay aboard and complete China's first-ever year-long stay in orbit, while the Pakistani astronaut will take their seat aboard Shenzhou 23 to return home.

During his stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will be responsible for four research payloads selected from more than 300 proposals, according to Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO.

It has been revealed that china has not confirmed a timeline for the launch of the Shenzhou 24 mission, but it is expected to lift off before the end of November. The Shenzhou 23 astronauts currently aboard Tiangong are closing in on 180 days in orbit, nearing an end to their six months in space.

Shenzhou 24 will launch from Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi Desert on a Long March 2F rocket. The identities of the crew for China's human spaceflight missions are typically closely guarded, and will only be revealed in a press conference a day ahead of launch. Shenzhou 24's Long March 2F rocket will be rolled out to the pad around a week ahead of launch.

The partnership between the two countries has already produced Chinese-released Pakistani satellites, including a lunar cubesat, and a Pakistani-built rover due to fly on the Chang'e-8 lunar landing mission.

Sources indicate that andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, New Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.

#297. Industry News: Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1110 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Industry News: Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh national study suggests that the way people consume cannabis may reveal important clues about their likelihood of using it heavily or developing an addiction.
  • In a recent development, cannabis is consumed in several ways, including smoking, vaping, eating edibles, and dabbing, which involves heating concentrated cannabis products and inhaling the resulting vapor.
  • Researchers at NYU Langone Health identified four distinct patterns of cannabis consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh national study suggests that the way people consume cannabis may reveal important clues about their likelihood of using it heavily or developing an addiction. While smoking remains the most popular method among US adults who use cannabis, roughly one in seven consumes it in nearly every available form. Researchers found that this group had particularly high rates of daily use and cannabis use disorder.

In a recent development, cannabis is consumed in several ways, including smoking, vaping, eating edibles, and dabbing, which involves heating concentrated cannabis products and inhaling the resulting vapor. Its use is widespread in the United States. Recent national survey figures indicate that approximately 43.8 million Americans ages 12 and older (more than 15 percent) had consumed cannabis within the previous 30 days.

Researchers at NYU Langone Health identified four distinct patterns of cannabis consumption. Nearly half of owners, 48 percent, primarily smoked cannabis, while 21 percent combined smoking and vaping. Another 17 percent mainly consumed edibles. The remaining 14 percent belonged to what researchers called the "polymodal group," meaning they used cannabis in almost every available form.

Cannabis Addiction Rates Differ Sharply by Consumption Pattern.

Sources indicate that the findings, published online August 8 in the journal Addictive Behaviors, revealed major differences in how frequently these groups consumed cannabis. Approximately half of people in the polymodal group reported using it every day. Daily use was considerably less common among other participants, occurring in 28 percent of those who primarily smoked, 31 percent of those who smoked and vaped, and about 13 percent of those who mainly consumed edibles.

An even more striking difference emerged when researchers examined cannabis use disorder, the medical diagnosis associated with cannabis addiction. About 67 percent of polymodal users met the criteria for the disorder, compared with 47 percent of those who both smoked and vaped, 36 percent of those who mainly smoked, and just 15 percent of participants who primarily used edibles.

In a recent development, "Our findings suggest that using cannabis in multiple forms may be a red flag for heavier use and symptoms of addiction," mentioned study lead author Omar El-Shahawy, MD, PhD, MPH, an assistant professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. "Asking patients not only whether but how they use cannabis could help clinicians identify when a fuller assessment may be warranted.".

Recent findings suggest that to investigate these patterns, the research team examined responses from 17,732 adults who had used cannabis during the preceding month. The information came from the 2022-2023 National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Using statistical methods to identify similarities in participants' consumption habits, the researchers conducted the first national analysis of how different methods of cannabis use naturally group together.

Younger Adults More Likely to Use Multiple Forms of Cannabis.

Sources indicate that the researchers also discovered notable differences in the characteristics of people who preferred particular consumption methods. Young adults ages 18 to 25 accounted for nearly one-third of both the smoking and vaping group and the polymodal group. In contrast, only about one sixth of participants who primarily smoked cannabis belonged to that age range.

Edibles revealed a different demographic pattern. Women made up more than half of those who mainly consumed edible cannabis products, and this method was particularly common among college graduates. However, the study did not investigate what motivated participants to choose specific consumption methods, leaving the reasons for these differences unresolved, according to Dr. El-Shahawy.

Another finding raised concerns about the potential effects of inhaling smoke. People who smoked cannabis were more likely to also smoke cigarettes than those who mainly vaped cannabis or consumed edibles. Because both tobacco and cannabis smoking involve combustion (burning), people who regularly smoke both substances may expose their lungs to additional harmful chemicals.

In a recent development, "The strong tie between smoking cannabis and smoking cigarettes is of concern because this subset of people are breathing in a wider range of chemicals via combustion, and their lungs are at risk," said senior author Joseph J. Palamar, PhD, MPH, a professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

Why Cannabis Prevention Messages May Need to Change.

The findings suggest that health education should account for the different ways people consume cannabis rather than concentrating primarily on smoking. Different consumption patterns may call for different approaches to explaining potential risks, particularly among younger adults and people who regularly combine several methods.

Sources indicate that "Public health messages about cannabis still focus mostly on smoking, but people now use the drug in many different ways," stated Dr. El-Shahawy. "For younger adults, that means talking about the risks of vaping and combining multiple forms, while for people who prefer edibles, the message is to 'start low and go slow' because the effects take time to kick in.".

In a recent development, the researchers hope to investigate the motivations behind these consumption patterns in future work. According to Dr. El-Shahawy, one question is whether people who favor edibles are more likely to use cannabis to manage problems such as pain or difficulty sleeping.

In a recent development, the team also emphasized several limitations. Because participants described their own cannabis habits, some may not have reported their consumption accurately or completely. The observational study also cannot determine whether using multiple forms of cannabis directly increases addiction risk. It establishes an association between consumption patterns and cannabis use disorder, rather than proving that one causes the other.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health through grant R01DA055675.

Additional NYU Langone researchers who contributed to the study included Mohsen Abbasi-Kangevari, MD, MPH; Michelle He; and Xiaoying Zheng, alongside Drs. El-Shahawy and Palamar. Neal Doran, PhD, of the University of California, San Diego, also served as a study co-investigator.

Sources indicate that materials provided by NYU Langone Health / NYU Grossman School of Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#294. The 9 Best TVs for Next-Level Home Entertainment
