The 9 Best TVs for Next-Level Home Entertainment

📅 26 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 16 min read | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We thoroughly scrutinized and reviewed the most impressive TVs available today—and several of our picks are surprisingly affordable.
  • Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In 2026, the best TVs deliver a leap forward in picture quality and come packed with convenient extra features like built-in streaming apps, high refresh rates to improve your gaming experience, and compatibility with your go-to virtual assistant, to name a few.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We thoroughly scrutinized and reviewed the most impressive TVs available today—and several of our picks are surprisingly affordable.

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In 2026, the best TVs deliver a leap forward in picture quality and come packed with convenient extra features like built-in streaming apps, high refresh rates to improve your gaming experience, and compatibility with your go-to virtual assistant, to name a few.

Industry observers note that the TV market is chock-full of great models across the entire price spectrum, so whether you're looking for a budget-friendly upgrade or a home alternative to your local movie theater, there are a lot of great options. I've been testing TVs all year, and with the holiday season closer than it would seem, it's a good time to start shopping for your next big screen.

If you know what kind of TV you're looking for, check out our detailed guides on the Best OLED TVs, 4K TVs, and Outdoor TVs.

My journey testing TVs began almost a decade ago, so I’ve experienced the product category’s evolution practically in real time. For this guide, I handpicked sets from leading brands like Hisense, LG, Samsung, and TCL, among others. I zeroed in on futureproof products at various price points that offer amazing picture quality and handy onboard features to sustain you for years after making the big-ticket purchase.

Recent findings suggest that A follow-up to one of my favorite TVs of 2025, the TCL QM8L builds on the successful design of the QM8K with a fresh, super-bright super quantum-dot (SQD) mini-LED panel. I was hesitant to recommend the 2026 at launch because of its price tag, but with prices now well below $2,000 for both the 65-inch and 75-inch models, it’s a lot easier to say that this set is the best bang for your buck if you’re looking for a mini-LED that’s bright enough to maintain its best image quality in dynamic lighting.

In addition to the newly introduced tech enhancing both brightness and color reproduction, upgraded local dimming leads to better HDR with less haloing, for a sharper picture in high-contrast scenes. You get a beautiful picture with vivid-yet-accurate colors and deep contrast.

It has been revealed that the TCL QM8L also offers excellent viewing angles, so long as direct light reflections literally aren’t in the picture. When the TV is facing a window or a lamp, its picture quality diminishes, especially when displaying dark scenes. This isn’t a dealbreaker, though I’d be super mindful about light sources when placing the set.

Recent findings suggest that on the audio front, the TCL QM8L delivers an impressively powerful experience via a sophisticated speaker setup tuned by the luxury audio experts at Bang & Olufsen. The bespoke B&O audio customization interface is as impressive as its sound output.

In a recent development, LG has long been synonymous with top-tier OLED TVs, and the C6 Series is a great upgrade, especially now that its price has dropped significantly since its debut a few months ago. With millions of individually backlit pixels, its OLED display panel produces vivid colors, infinite contrast, and, thanks to LG’s proprietary evo technology, strong brightness. As a cinema buff, I also appreciated the TV's Filmmaker Mode, which removed picture-quality enhancements to deliver a viewing experience as the movie director intended.

It has been revealed that the brightness-boosting display technology lets the LG C6 deliver an even more immersive HDR viewing experience in any setting, even in rooms with bright ambient light. Curiously, the larger 77-inch and 83-inch versions pack an upgraded Tandem OLED display, which boosts brightness to dramatically improve performance in brightly lit spaces.

Another significant reason to consider the LG C6 Series is that it is a gaming powerhouse, thanks in part to support for both Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium variable refresh rate standards, which will help games run smoothly on both consoles and PC.

What’s more, the TV’s feature-rich webOS platform offers access to Nvidia GeForce NOW and Xbox cloud gaming, so all you need is an external controller to enjoy high-resolution gameplay with smooth refresh rates.

It has been revealed that the LG C6 also has a beautiful design, a capable speaker system for its form factor, and support for all leading smart home connectivity standards. Unlike its competition, this 4K TV comes in multiple screen sizes, from compact 42- and 48-inch models to larger 77- and 83-inch options.

It has been revealed that this more budget-friendly cousin of the QM8L features many of my top mini-LED picks’ best fresh features, including SQD display technology, but costs much less, dropping below $1,000 in many sizes. While it does not have the tools to produce quite as bright or sharp a picture as my top pick, it’s easily the best TV I’ve seen for less than $1,000.

Like many of TCL’s best TVs, the QM7L has an elegant design with ultra-slim screen bezels and a Bang & Olufsen-tuned speaker system. The TV is available with a screen up to 98 inches. The latter currently costs less than $3,000, which is an incredible bargain given its size and picture quality.

According to recent reports, the TCL QM6K 4K TV is the best for upgraders on a tight budget. Priced below $500 for a version with a 55-inch screen, this TV offers a no-nonsense design with a slim display bezel, impressive picture quality for the money, and a feature-packed platform with seamless smart home integration.

Experiencing the TCL QM6K genuinely made me feel like I was viewing a 4K TV from a higher price tier. Its bright QD-Mini LED display easily bests similarly priced big-name competitors by producing stellar peak brightness, rich colors, and deep contrast via hundreds of local dimming zones. The introduction of a mini-LED panel made the newcomer's picture quality a massive leap forward over its predecessor's.

Because its display has a 144-Hz native refresh rate, the TCL QM6K can deliver a high-quality gaming experience with a PS5 or Xbox Series X. Equipped with HDMI 2.1, the TV supports variable refresh rate gameplay at up to a brisk 288 Hz.

It has been revealed that the Hisense UR9 is among the first TVs in a large 2026 wave of RGB mini- and micro-LED TVs, and the best one we’ve tested to date for the average TV watcher. RGB TVs use separate red, green, and blue light diodes rather than a uniform light source, which generates deep contrast and vivid colors that are comparable to an OLED TV, while maintaining a higher peak brightness. Combined with a legion of local dimming zones to maximize high-dynamic range, and the UR9 feels like a do-it-all option, and doesn’t cost quite as much as the alternatives out there from brands like Samsung and Sony.That brightness, combined with Hisense’s “obsidian” anti-glare coating, makes the UR9 vastly better at managing exposure to direct light sources (e.g., windows, lamps) than a standard mini-LED TV. That’s great if you plan to put this TV in a living room with lots of windows, and might have to contend with sunlight washing out the screen from time to time.In a manner befitting its premium price category, the Hisense UR9 also features a rich set of wired and wireless connectivity features, as well as a capable Dolby Atmos speaker system. The latter has been tuned by experts from the luxury French audio brand Devialet. The U9 series took a year off in 2025, but it’s been a favorite of mine in the past. I’m happy to see this colorful glow-up bring it back to top form.

According to recent reports, the TCL X11L is the first major TV launch of 2026 and creates a newly introduced apex for high fidelity among the largest of at-home screens. It boasts a luxurious design, exceptional picture quality, and immersive sound tuned by Bang & Olufsen. It's incredibly expensive, starting at nearly $7,000 for a 75-inch screen, but you're getting a genuinely cutting-edge set that sets a new benchmark for the entire product category.

Recent findings suggest that what's newly introduced and exciting here is the X11L's SQD mini-LED panel, which combines the quantum dot layer found in QLED and QD-OLED TVs with Mini-LED technology to create dynamic lighting across the TV. Combined with incredible brightness—up to 10,000 nits—the so-called "Super Quantum Dot" achieves contrast and color depth that, at least to my eye, looks on par or possibly even better than an OLED screen.

It has small flaws, like a lack of anti-glare coating, but this is a remarkable TV and the model I would recommend if you're looking for a technological centerpiece to put at the center of a large home theater. And I emphasize large, because it only comes in three "XXL" sizes: 75 inches, 85 inches, and 98 inches.

According to recent reports, developed in-house by Roku, the 2025 Pro Series TV is unsurprisingly the best to run the platform and an equally excellent upgrade for first-time users and longtime faithful. It is capable of delivering excellent picture quality and top-notch sound for its form factor. And since it runs a platform that has been a longtime favorite among consumers, it's easy to use, even for first-time smart TV users.

It has been revealed that the mini-LED display panel of the Roku Pro Series TV produces vibrant colors and deep contrast, courtesy of multiple local dimming zones. I like that the product has a setting dubbed Roku Smart Picture Max, which can optimize any content for its screen, saving time digging through settings menus.

Another significant reason to consider this TV is its refined design and clever cable management setup, featuring integrated Velcro straps. The handy bits make it ideal for wall mounting. Another thing that impressed me was the option to adjust the height of its stand without the need to use a screwdriver.

In a recent development, roku’s backlit remote with rechargeable battery is another major product draw, as it’s intuitive and easy to locate if lost. The TV has a button for locating the essential accessory, and I reckon it’ll be a lifesaver for many.

Sources indicate that you can choose from 55-, 65-, and 75-inch versions of the Roku Pro Series. Similarly priced rivals from Hisense and TCL offer higher peak brightness and deeper contrast, but the refined design and intuitive platform make Roku’s product worth considering.

Recent findings suggest that the Samsung S95H OLED TV is the brand’s flagship OLED TV, and the best high-end model I’ve tested this year. It delivers a consistently beautiful viewing experience, with high peak brightness, vibrant colors, and infinite contrast. Its AI-powered upscaling tech even elevates low-resolution content, raising the bar on everything you watch.

The S95H stands out compared to many of the top OLEDs right now because of its high brightness, which makes colors pop and allows it to function well in brightly lit spaces. With Samsung’s anti-reflective coating on the display, it even looks good in direct sunlight. That’s a rare feat for any TV, but especially remarkable for an OLED panel.

And while it’s a secondary concern, I love how the physical TV looks. Its metal frame stands out in a room (in a good way). This set looks like a piece of art and is worth showing off in your living room.

The device's Tizen OS platform, along with a wide selection of apps and cloud-based gaming services, offers seamless integration with Samsung Galaxy phones, tablets, and laptops. If it weren’t for its lack of Dolby Vision support, the S95H would have been my top OLED pick.

Recent findings suggest that samsung offers the S95H in various screen sizes, ranging from 55 to 83 inches. Opt for the Samsung S90H if you are looking for a great Samsung TV on a tighter budget.

The Sony Bravia 7 II is Sony’s very impressive second-from-top-of-the-line flagship RGB TV, which emphasizes precise color reproduction for folks who care deeply about seeing films (or TV demonstrates, or video games) the way their creators intended for them to be seen. It uses the TV’s Studio Calibrated mode, which optimizes color and contrast for accuracy, rather than brightness or contrast. It isn’t about enhancing performance, but optimizing for accuracy. And, given Sony’s position as both a maker of hardware and content, there’s already a rich selection of content that supports it.

Sources indicate that on the gaming front, Sony maintains its tradition of offering a few PlayStation-focused tricks. It seamlessly optimizes HDR settings in some games, ensuring you get the best possible picture. (It’s especially helpful if you have a PlayStation 5 Pro, which unlocks additional graphics options.).

I also like the TV’s design, headlined by a magnetic semi-transparent panel that attaches to its metal stand. It makes the TV look like it’s floating above the surface it’s placed on. Unlike most rivals, the Bravia 7 II is also available in smaller sizes, down to 50 inches. The largest version has a massive 98-inch screen, but at $9,000 before discounts, it’s a tougher sell than the smaller options.

Industry observers note that some mainstream TVs are available in multiple screen sizes, ranging from 43 inches to a head-spinning 98 inches. TVs with 65-inch screens are deservedly popular and the best for most consumers, offering a good balance between immersive viewing, easy home integration (I’ve experienced many in a one-bedroom Upcoming York City apartment), and price. Until not too long ago, TV models with screens of 65 inches or more had high price tags, but that's no longer the case. Top-tier TVs with 65-inch screens now cost below $1,500, and larger 75-inch TVs are available for less than $2,000. Believe it or not, you can even get a 98-inch for around $2,000 instead of a five-digit sum.

A TV with a 4K (UHD) screen is the best upgrade option at the moment. Content in this resolution is widely available across all streaming platforms for reasonable price points, so consider it a must. Switching from an older 4K set to one of the latest models is worth it for the picture quality improvements. The difference is even more evident if you are ditching a Full HD TV because its screen has four times fewer pixels than a 4K unit. A Full HD resolution is acceptable only if you are shopping for a small and (very) cheap set. TVs with stunningly sharp 8K screens, like this pricey Samsung, are also widely available. Still, I wouldn’t consider one because native content in this resolution isn’t widely available. You’d be better off spending on a similarly priced 4K TV.

Sources indicate that when it comes to refresh rate, avid gamers should look for TVs whose screens support more than the industry-standard 60 hertz. A higher refresh rate—120 Hz, specifically—offers fast and smooth on-screen action.

A high refresh rate can also be beneficial for watching live sports, though that’s a matter of personal preference. I don’t recommend this feature to stream movies and series, as this content has been captured at lower refresh rates.

According to recent reports, unless you are shopping on a tight budget, you should have a TV with an OLED or a mini-LED display on your radar. Featuring individually backlit pixels, OLED TVs give you the best picture quality available, so they are worth the price premium over similarly sized non-OLED models. By producing deep contrast (their pixels switch off to display black color) and vibrant colors, these TVs can make even mundane scenes look amazing. However, mini-LED TVs deserve your attention, as they deliver superior brightness to their OLED counterparts at a lower price tier for the same screen size. Thanks to a sophisticated backlighting setup with thousands of local dimming zones, the latest mini-LED offerings are not too far behind OLEDs in contrast, either. Their viewing angles are narrower than those of an OLED, but the higher peak brightness and the cheaper price can’t be ignored. Commonly referred to as QLED, quantum dot is an crucial display feature to keep an eye out for, even if you are shopping for a TV on the cheap. Products whose screens have the tech offer more vibrant color and higher brightness than non-QLED rivals.

It has been revealed that peak brightness is a vital display feature to have on your radar when shopping for a TV. The luminosity is measured in nits, and I suggest you look for TVs with peak brightness that exceeds 1,000 nits, even if you are shopping on a tight budget. A higher peak brightness guarantees a better viewing experience with HDR-enhanced content, as well as superior picture quality in brightly lit spaces.

Sources indicate that regarding connectivity features, HDMI 2.1 and WiFi 6 (or higher) are the two most important ones to look for in a spec sheet. The former ensures that your TV can sync perfectly with a top-tier gaming console like a Sony PlayStation 5 or a Microsoft Xbox Series X and treat you to smooth and hiccup-free gameplay. Futureproof WiFi 6 or newer wireless connectivity ensures your TV can stream high-resolution content and reliably link up with other compatible devices on your home network, though not all of our picks below include this feature. Today’s best TVs pack multiple HDMI ports, so you can easily link a soundbar and additional streaming players if you want. USB ports for additional accessories and a coaxial input for basic TV are also available.

It has been revealed that every latest TV on this list runs a smart platform with access to all massive-name streaming services, so you won’t have to worry about accessing your subscriptions. Support for Apple AirPlay and Google Chromecast for sharing content from a mobile device is also commonly available.

HDR-enhanced content has become common on all streaming services. I suggest you get a TV that supports all leading formats—Dolby Vision, HDR10/10+, and HLG—for movie buffs.

Look for Amazon Alexa, Google Assistant, or Apple HomeKit support if you want to integrate your TV into a smart home setup or control it directly with voice commands. If you don’t own or plan to invest in a soundbar or a surround sound system, be sure to order a TV with a multi-speaker setup and Dolby Atmos support. Thankfully, the functionality is available in many latest sets.

With all the above features in mind, find your upcoming home entertainment centerpiece among these TVs we vouch for.

A DNA analysis has confirmed that a Nazca infant who lived in southern Peru 1,600 years ago had a rare congenital condition called trisomy 13.

Industry observers note that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Recent findings suggest that archaeologists in Peru have discovered the skeleton of an infant with a rare birth defect that left only one central eye socket in the child's skull. DNA analysis of the remains confirmed a chromosomal abnormality caused the deadly condition in the infant over 1,600 years ago, according to a new study.

"We cannot really say how long this individual survived," study co-author Lars Fehren-Schmitz, an anthropologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Live Science in an email. But "the burial of this infant suggests that the Nasca treated this individual in death like most other infants.".

The skeleton of this female infant was discovered alongside a second one inside a ceramic urn at the archaeological site of Jauranga in Peru's Palpa Valley, where numerous geoglyphs known as the Nazca Lines have been found. Archaeologists uncovered several dozen other burials dated to the Middle Nazca (also spelled Nasca) period (A.D. 325 to 440) at the site, but one of the co-buried infants had an extremely rare condition, researchers wrote in a study published Monday (Nov. 9) in the journal PNAS.

The infant had a very small skull and a single eye socket in the middle of her face, along with other developmental issues of the cranial bones. These traits match modern clinical descriptions of cyclopia, a lethal condition that occurs when the front part of a fetus's brain fails to divide into left and right hemispheres.

This condition can also cause alterations in the nasal structures, resulting in a missing nose or a tube-like nose above the single eye.

A medical illustration from 1891 of two infants with cyclopia.

"The cause of the malformation was present at fertilization, but manifestation occurs around the fourth to fifth week in utero [in the womb], when the frontal lobe of the brain has to divide," study first author Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao, an archaeologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told Live Science in an email.

Sources indicate that cyclopia is a rare condition, occurring in about 1 out of every 100,000 births. To learn more about the infant's short life, the researchers sequenced her genome. (DNA suggested the infant carried two X chromosomes, typical of a female.).

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team detected an extra copy of chromosome 13, meaning the infant had a genetic condition called trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome. It's known to be a major chromosomal cause of cyclopia; that said, only a small percentage of trisomy 13 cases involve cyclopia.

While trisomy 13 is associated with advanced maternal age, it is not clear whether that was the case for this infant, Fehren-Schmitz said.

Sources indicate that "This condition has been documented in historic and modern anatomical collections, but to my knowledge this is the first archaeological example of this developmental abnormality," Siân Halcrow, a bioarchaeologist at Durham University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

Industry observers note that the researchers' estimate of the infant's age at death suggests she may have survived for several weeks or months after birth, Halcrow pointed out. "This raises important questions about how infants with profound congenital differences were cared for and treated in past societies," she noted.

It has been revealed that the infant was buried in a ceramic urn, the researchers noted in the study, which was a common burial method in the Nazca period, along with a second female infant who had no skeletal abnormalities. "The baby with cyclopia was at the bottom of the jar, while the other baby was on top. Nevertheless, it appears that they were interred in a single event," Tomasto-Cagigao said. The genetic analysis revealed that the two infants did not have the same mother.

A burial of two infants in one urn is unusual for this culture, the researchers stated, but there is not enough archaeological evidence to conclude that the infant with cyclopia was given a different type of burial.

"The fact that the individual was buried with a 'healthy' individual in a regular cemetery, without any special grave goods, suggests that, to some extent, the individual was not treated differently in death, even though it had such a rare condition," Fehren-Schmitz stated. "It was neither 'excluded' because of it nor treated in a 'special' way.".

According to recent reports, in ancient Andean societies, some people with disabilities took on special societal roles, such as ones associated with religious practices. "If that reflects Nasca society as a whole, we can't say based on one case," Fehren-Schmitz noted, "but it does reflect the community this infant was part of, even if only briefly.".

Tomasto-Cagigao, E., Reindel, M., Isla Cuadrado, J., Lund Valle, M., Kassadjikova, K., Harkins, K., Fehren-Schmitz, L. (2026). A Nasca-period perinatal burial reveals cyclopia associated with trisomy 13 in southern Peru. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2625042123.

Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. #290. Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1266 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that mars may not be as geologically inactive as it appears.
  • According to recent reports, researchers have identified unusual concentrations of hydrogen chloride gas above fractures in the Alba Mons volcanic region.
  • It has been revealed that an international team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy believes the gas could originate from hot magma underground.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that mars may not be as geologically inactive as it appears. New evidence from mysterious gas emissions near an enormous Martian volcano suggests that heat and volcanic processes could still be present deep beneath the planet's surface.

According to recent reports, researchers have identified unusual concentrations of hydrogen chloride gas above fractures in the Alba Mons volcanic region. The findings suggest that gases from the planet's interior may be escaping through cracks in the surface, potentially revealing volcanic activity that has remained hidden until now.

It has been revealed that an international team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy believes the gas could originate from hot magma underground. If confirmed, this would indicate that Mars still has dormant volcanic systems capable of releasing gases to the surface.

Industry observers note that the European Space Agency's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first detected hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere in findings reported in 2021. On Earth, hydrogen chloride is frequently released through openings connected to magma, raising the possibility that similar processes could be occurring on Mars.

"Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," states Daniel Mège, Professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences and co-lead author of the study published in Science Advances.

Mysterious Gas Emissions Defy Mars' Seasonal Pattern.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers noticed something unusual during early summer in the Martian northern hemisphere. Hydrogen chloride concentrations were unexpectedly elevated in a particular region, even though the gas normally becomes scarce at that time of year.

According to recent reports, hydrogen chloride levels on Mars generally follow a seasonal cycle. They typically peak during northern winter before declining to very low levels in summer. Scientists believe much of this behavior is associated with the planet's dust and water cycles.

However, the observations revealed a striking exception. Elevated hydrogen chloride repeatedly appeared in early summer over volcanic fractures on the slopes of Alba Mons. The unusual timing and consistent location suggested that something beyond ordinary atmospheric chemistry might be responsible.

Mars is home to the largest volcanoes in the Solar System, but scientists still do not know whether volcanic processes remain active beneath their surfaces.

Industry observers note that images taken from orbit indicate that some Martian volcanoes experienced eruptions within the past few million years. Instruments on the surface have also recorded marsquakes, demonstrating that the planet continues to experience seismic activity.

Together, these observations suggest that Mars may retain some of its geological energy. However, scientists have never directly observed a new volcanic eruption or fresh lava flow on the planet, leaving the question of present-day volcanism unresolved.

Fresh Cracks Reveal Clues to Hidden Volcanic Heat.

To investigate the unusual gas concentrations, the research team combined atmospheric measurements with detailed observations of the Martian surface.

The Atmospheric Chemistry Suite aboard TGO uses infrared spectrometers to identify gases in the atmosphere. These instruments detected hydrogen chloride concentrated in a relatively small area shortly after the disappearance of winter frost.

Researchers then examined the same region using the orbiter's CaSSIS camera. The images revealed narrow fractures that appeared relatively fresh, with some extending hundreds of meters across the surface. Unusual changes in surface color were also visible around the cracks.

Recent findings suggest that "The Trace Gas Orbiter was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack. It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," explains Daniel.

Recent findings suggest that one possible explanation is that gases originating from magma deep underground travel upward through these fractures. On Earth, comparable volcanic openings are known as fumaroles.

According to recent reports, the researchers propose that extremely cold Martian winters, when temperatures can fall to -120°C, allow ice to seal the fractures and temporarily prevent gases from escaping. As temperatures rise in early summer, the ice sublimates, changing directly into vapor and potentially opening pathways for underground gases to reach the atmosphere.

It has been revealed that the discoloration observed around the fractures could also be significant. It may result from minerals or other substances deposited by escaping gases, similar to the deposits commonly found around fumaroles (volcanic gas vents) on Earth.

Although the connection between the gas emissions and volcanic fractures appeared promising, the researchers needed to rule out other explanations.

"Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," concedes Daniel.

The team carefully evaluated the chemical reactions that could produce hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere, including processes unrelated to volcanism.

Recent findings suggest that "A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food," adds Daniel.

After examining the atmospheric and geological evidence together, the researchers proposed that the gas could be escaping from a dormant magma chamber beneath Alba Mons. Such a chamber would form part of an underground volcanic system that could continue releasing gases even without producing visible eruptions.

Hidden Volcanic Activity Could Help Mars Support Life.

The implications may extend beyond understanding the planet's geological history. Volcanic gases could also provide clues about how Mars evolved and whether it ever supported environments suitable for life.

In a recent development, in the distant past, gases released from magma, including hydrogen chloride, may have helped create a denser atmosphere and warmer conditions. Those conditions could have allowed liquid water to remain across large portions of the Martian surface.

Volcanic activity might also create habitable environments underground. If rising magma or lava comes into contact with groundwater, the interaction can produce warm hydrothermal systems. Such environments could provide both chemical energy and protection from the harsh conditions on the surface.

According to recent reports, "Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," ponders Daniel.

Although the findings do not establish that Mars is currently erupting or that life exists beneath its surface, they offer an intriguing upcoming reason to investigate the volcanic fractures around Alba Mons.

"These findings may prove to be TGO's greatest success yet," highlights Colin Wilson, ESA's project scientist for the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter.

It has been revealed that on Thursday (Nov. 12), the Euclid space telescope released its first major batch of data, capturing the light of more than a billion objects over an area of sky as substantial as 9,500 full moons. The data release lays the foundation for one of the largest-ever 3D maps of the cosmos and many groundbreaking discoveries about the nature of dark energy and dark matter.

Recent findings suggest that the European Space Agency's (ESA) Euclid space telescope has been called the "Dark Universe Detective" because of its capability to investigate the dual mysteries of dark matter, the universe's most mysterious stuff, and dark energy, the force accelerating the expansion of the universe. Collectively, these cosmic elements are sometimes referred to as the dark universe.

In a recent development, the new data release, designated DR1-Foundation, was built from 13 months of observations and is accompanied by a multitude of images, including large sky mosaics. It marks the first major release of mission data since Euclid launched in mid-2023.

Industry observers note that "These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," ESA's Director of Science, Carole Mundell remarked in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery in a latest regime for astronomy and demonstrating the excellence of European technology, science and international collaboration.".

Sources indicate that the ESA put into raw numbers the sheer number of celestial objects viewed by the Dark Universe Detective and contained in DR1-Foundation. That includes light spectra from 160 million sources, over 900 million galaxies, and 60 million candidates for quasars, regions of space dominated by feeding supermassive black holes.

"This is a change in scale from Euclid's previous releases, which included a few days of observations over around 60 degrees squared of sky," ESA's Euclid project scientist Valeria Pettorino noted. "We're now releasing more than a year of data covering a significantly larger area. This unlocks groundbreaking science.".

Euclid can see such a vast number of cosmic objects thanks to the fact that its space-based position helps it avoid interference caused by Earth's atmosphere.

According to recent reports, this includes clusters of galaxies and even larger superclusters. The study of these objects, some of the largest structures in the cosmos, can reveal how matter came together across the larger network of gas, dust and dark matter called the cosmic web.

In a recent development, "Euclid doesn't just look far back in time  — it does so across huge areas of sky," Euclid Consortium member Barbara Sartoris of JL Lagrange Laboratory, Nice, France, explained. "This gives us an unprecedented view of large samples of ancient galaxy clusters that were previously out of reach. "We will explore these in the coming months to learn how these giants grew, and decipher what they reveal about the dark universe.".

It has been revealed that another exciting element of the fresh Euclid data release is the 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates catalogued by the space telescope. Gravitational lensing is an element of the universe first explained in Einstein magnum opus, general relativity, in 1915.

General relativity says that objects with mass cause the very fabric of space to warp, and that gravity arises from this warping. But there is another consequence. When light passes this curvature, its usually straight path is curved. That means when light from a single background source passes an object with great mass, like a galaxy or galaxy cluster, a strong gravitational lens, it can arrive at our telescopes at different times.

As a result of this strong lensing, background sources can be greatly amplified. It is an effect that the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has been using to great effect to study galaxies in the early universe.

Thus, the prospect of mapping 15,000 strong gravitational lenses is monumental, especially in studying the rate at which the universe is expanding and thus the effect of dark energy.

"Strong lensing provides unique insight into the dark universe, allowing us to 'weigh' individual galaxies, including their invisible dark matter, and explore how the universe is expanding," Natalie Lines of the University of Portsmouth, U.K., and member of the Euclid Consortium, stated. "Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionize the field of strong lens discovery. That day is finally here.".

Arguably, the most exciting thing about DR1-Foundation is that Euclid is just getting started. The area of sky covered from spring 2024 to spring 2025 represents just 14% of Euclid's target for its entire six-year survey.

That means whatever scientists discover from this data release could be the tip of the iceberg in terms of how the Dark Universe Detective will change our understanding of the cosmos.

According to recent reports, "DR1-Foundation includes raw data, calibrated images, catalogues, and spectra over a huge sky area, with enough statistics touncover even rare objects," Valeria mentioned. "It will be used to map the large-scale structure of the universe in unprecedented detail.

#287. Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1025 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A remarkable discovery in a nearly 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb has provided the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence that people used cannabis for its intoxicating effects.
  • Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive plants in the modern world, but tracing its use thousands of years into the past presents a major archaeological challenge.
  • Gino Caspari, affiliated with the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, investigated an elaborate tomb in the Republic of Tyva in southern Siberia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A remarkable discovery in a nearly 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb has provided the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence that people used cannabis for its intoxicating effects. By examining ancient cannabis seeds and chemical traces preserved in human hair, researchers have uncovered upcoming clues about the role of the plant in prehistoric burial rituals.

Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive plants in the modern world, but tracing its use thousands of years into the past presents a major archaeological challenge. Flowers, leaves, and resins tend to decompose over time, leaving little physical evidence behind. Ancient communities also relied on cannabis for practical purposes, including producing fiber and oil, making it difficult to distinguish these uses from medicinal or recreational consumption.

An international team led by Dr. Gino Caspari, affiliated with the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, investigated an elaborate tomb in the Republic of Tyva in southern Siberia. The burial site belonged to prominent members of the Scythians, a culture known for its skilled horseback riders who inhabited the vast Eurasian steppe.

Ancient Siberian Tomb Contains 1,000 Cannabis Seeds.

Industry observers note that during the investigation, researchers recovered approximately 1,000 cannabis seeds from the tomb. They used radiocarbon dating to determine the age of six individual seeds. Combined with other dating evidence, the results indicate that the seeds were deposited in the burial site during the early eighth century B.C.

"The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial," claims Caspari, an archaeologist and the study's lead author.

According to recent reports, the researchers also analyzed human hair preserved in the tomb's central burial chamber. Chemical evidence in several samples pointed to cannabis consumption, providing a crucial connection between the plant remains and the people buried at the site.

"This study is particularly insightful because it combines the analysis of plant remains with molecular traces in the human body," says Caspari.

The findings were published in the journal Science.

Chemical Traces in Ancient Hair Reveal Cannabis Use.

Although the cannabis seeds were remarkably well preserved, their presence alone could not establish whether the plant was used for its mind-altering effects. The seeds probably came from wild cannabis plants, and researchers could not determine whether people had deliberately cultivated them for their psychoactive properties.

Recent findings suggest that the strongest evidence came from the preserved human hair. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry and other analytical techniques, the team identified clear chemical signals consistent with cannabinol (CBN) in several samples.

CBN can form when tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary compound responsible for cannabis intoxication, undergoes oxidation. The researchers also detected weaker signals that matched the mass of THC, further supporting the possibility that the individuals had consumed cannabis.

Sources indicate that while these chemical findings indicate cannabis use, they cannot reveal how much was consumed or exactly how the compounds entered the body. The individuals may have inhaled cannabis smoke or consumed the plant in another way, but the available evidence cannot establish a particular method.

In a recent development, other archaeological discoveries from later periods in Central Asia provide clearer evidence of cannabis inhalation. At those sites, researchers have identified cannabinoid residues on heated stones and inside vessels, pointing to the use of heat to release compounds that could be inhaled.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," claims Caspari, who conducts research at the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute for Geoanthropology in Jena (Germany).

Cannabis, Horse Sacrifices, and Ancient Burial Rituals.

The cannabis evidence was discovered within an elaborate ceremonial burial site, suggesting that the plant may have been connected to important Scythian funerary traditions.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," indicates Gino Caspari.

According to recent reports, earlier research at the site identified the remains of 18 horses that had been deliberately positioned on the burial mound. Continued excavations have since uncovered evidence of several dozen more sacrificed horses, along with scattered human bones.

These discoveries reveal the extraordinary scale of the burial ceremonies and provide vital context for understanding why cannabis may have been included among the materials deposited in the tomb.

Oldest Directly Dated Evidence of Cannabis Intoxication.

Taken together, the seeds and chemical traces in human hair represent the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence currently known for cannabis use associated with intoxication.

However, several questions remain unanswered. The researchers cannot determine how much THC the ancient cannabis contained, whether the plants were particularly potent, or whether Scythian communities had begun deliberately selecting or cultivating cannabis varieties with higher concentrations of psychoactive compounds.

To investigate these questions, the team is now studying genetic material recovered from the ancient plant remains. The unusually good preservation of the cannabis DNA could provide valuable insights into how humans domesticated the plant and how it spread across different regions over thousands of years.

According to recent reports, "We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," notes Gino Caspari. "DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon.".

When potential mates are scarce, some types of seaweed can take reproduction into their own hands, so to speak, according to a study published on 12 November in PLoS Biology1.

“Our findings highlight that kelp are even more flexible in their reproduction than previously appreciated,” notes Daniel Liesner, a marine biologist at the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel in Germany.

The brown algae, which provide food and shelter for marine life, “are really weird, they do all kinds of stuff”, indicates Reina Veenhof, an ecologist at the Scottish Association for Marine Science in Oban, UK. What’s interesting about the study is that it helps to explain how changes in gene activity allow kelp to reproduce in different ways, she says.

Recent findings suggest that scientists know that kelp can reproduce asexually, with unfertilized eggs developing into offspring. This process was even documented for one male strain2 — the PLoS Biology study shows that this wasn’t a one-off.

The ability of male reproductive cells to develop without fertilization is striking, claims Olivier De Clerck, a seaweed biologist at Ghent University in Belgium. This is because, unlike eggs, sperm cells are small and have few resources to support development.

According to recent reports, the researchers focused on Laminaria pallida, a species found along the Atlantic coasts of South Africa and Namibia. In the wild, 523 individual kelp showed no clear evidence of asexual reproduction.

In a recent development, by contrast, both microscopic male and female L. pallida grown in separate laboratory dishes could produce offspring without fertilization. During asexual reproduction, the gene expression in males changed, making them more similar to females.

However, when they were lab-grown in the presence of a member of the opposite sex, kelp favoured sexual reproduction, suggesting they can detect nearby partners through chemical signals.

Scientists Just Found a New World of Magnetism We’ve Never Seen Before

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Altermagnets blend traits of two magnetic opposites, and they could power tomorrow’s quantum devices.
  • For the past few decades, the world of magnetism seemed scientifically simple.
  • Now, thanks to scientists at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory at Stanford University, that final piece is finally in place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Altermagnets blend traits of two magnetic opposites, and they could power tomorrow’s quantum devices.

For the past few decades, the world of magnetism seemed scientifically simple. Materials fit into only two groups, ferromagnets and antiferromagnets—end of discussion. Over the past few years, though, that tidy picture has started to crack. Discussion of a third type of magnetism, dubbed “altermagnetism,” has grown from a whisper to a near-consensus. Still, one crucial piece of experimental proof was missing.

Now, thanks to scientists at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory at Stanford University, that final piece is finally in place.

It has been revealed that first, a quick refresher. Ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism, as their names suggest, are two sides of the same coin. In ferromagnets, all electronic spins point the same direction, creating an easily observable net magnetic field. The counterpart is the exact opposite: antiferromagnets containing alternating electronic spins that effectively cancel each other out, producing no net magnetic effect at all. Now, if you had to wager on where altermagnetism fits into this picture, somewhere between these two extremes might be your guess—and you’d be right.

“In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don’t fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy,” Daniel Jost, a SLAC associate scientist and lead author of the latest study published in Science, remarked in a press statement. “Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase—altermagnetism—is real.”.

Industry observers note that for decades, scientists have noticed that some materials don’t fit into the simple dichotomy between ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. That’s because altermagnetic materials, such as manganese telluride (MnTe), exhibit properties of both. Like antiferromagnets, their spins alternate and cancel out, but like ferromagnets, they can still carry spin currents. In 2022, scientists finally put a name to this phenomenon, and two years later, further proof of its existence emerged.

It has been revealed that to experimentally demonstrate the existence of altermagnetism, the authors of the new study brought samples of MnTe (once thought to be antiferromagnetic) to the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) to investigate the material’s chirality, or “handedness.” Understanding chirality is key to delineating between altermagnets and antiferromagnets because both have alternating spins (and thus no net magnetism), but a twist in MnTe’s lattice would provide a distinctive chirality. ESRF then fired polarized x-ray beams at the sample and scientists analyzed the results.

Recent findings suggest that “Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams. Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way,” Jost stated in a press statement. The results revealed a chiral signal that doesn’t exist in antiferromagnets. The team first produced these results in 2024 and confirmed them the following year. “This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own.”.

According to recent reports, that combination could make altermagnets a key ingredient in future quantum tech and memory devices. They’re as stable as antiferromagnets, with no net magnetization to cause trouble, but like ferromagnets, they still let engineers read and write data. As Jost states, “altermagnets combine the best of both worlds.”.

But climate goals are still unlikely to be met.

According to recent reports, when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The world's carbon emissions from oil, gas and coal are projected to decrease by 0.4% this year, driven partly by the expansion of solar and wind power capacity and the price increases caused by the Iran conflict, according to a fresh report.

According to recent reports, the 2026 Global Carbon Budget report was published in the journal Earth System Science Data Nov. 10 and is due to be presented at the U.N. Climate Change Conference's COP31 meeting in Antalya, Turkey, this week.

Recent findings suggest that global carbon emissions have increased steadily since record-keeping began. This year is projected to have a slight decrease in fossil-fuel emissions, but that is partly due to price increases caused by the Iran conflict.

In a recent development, it is the first time annual carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels have fallen since the coronavirus pandemic in 2020. But the overall emissions picture suggests the world is still likely to miss key climate goals.

"It is an encouraging sign that the growth of emissions is slowing and decarbonisation efforts are starting to make a difference," stated Joeri Rogelj, a climate scientist at the Centre for Environmental Policy at Imperial College London who wasn't involved in the research. "However, at 0.4%, the projected decline is very small," Rogelj told Live Science in an email.

The report projects 38.2 billion metric tons (42.1 billion U.S. tons) of emissions of the climate-warming greenhouse gas CO2 from fossil fuel sources this year. Greenhouse gases trap heat by absorbing the sun's radiation, and as their concentrations in the atmosphere increase, so do global average temperatures, leading to altered weather patterns and higher sea levels, as well as other major impacts.

The war with Iran has resulted in restricted fuel availability and high prices, with a corresponding reduction in demand.

Industry observers note that part of the 0.4% reduction in CO2 emissions is attributable to 40 countries that have cut emissions over the past decade while growing their economies. These include the U.S., Australia, Newly introduced Zealand, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Japan and about 30 countries in the European Union, the researchers reported.

When it comes to some of the biggest emitters, annual CO2 emissions are projected to decrease by 0.9% in China, 1.3% in the U.S., 1.5% in the European Union and 1% in Japan, but India's annual CO2 emissions are projected to grow by 4.4%.

In a recent development, carbon emissions are projected to decrease slightly in the U.S., China and the E.U. but to increase in India.

Sources indicate that fossil-fuel-linked CO2 emissions from the rest of the world are projected to decrease by 0.7%, driven mainly by a 1.9% drop in oil emissions. Some of the report authors suggested in an accompanying paper in Nature Climate Change that this is a short-term response to the global supply constraints and increased prices triggered by the Iran conflict.

"The war with Iran has resulted in restricted fuel availability and high prices, with a corresponding reduction in demand," Rogelj remarked.

While fossil fuel emissions and demand for oil are declining globally, overall demand for energy is actually increasing.

"Based only on the demand for energy, which has grown, we would have expected an increase in fossil CO2 emissions by about 0.8 gigatonnes," noted study co-author Judith Hauck, a biogeoscientist at the Alfred Wegener Institute, Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research in Germany.

Industry observers note that about two-thirds of that increase in demand is being met by solar and wind power and electric vehicles, showing that clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions, Hauck remarked. However, the hike in energy prices that resulted from the Iran conflict also decreased demand by 0.4%, she said.

"So only together with the energy crisis did we bring the change in emissions down to negative," Hauck told Live Science, adding that she expects CO2 emissions to rebound if the conflict ends, as they did after the temporary emissions drop caused by the lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The exceptional circumstances that energy markets experienced this year make it clear that the small projected emissions decline is no reason to declare that emissions are now reducing, but there are hopeful signs, Rogelj stated.

Sources indicate that "Despite my muted enthusiasm about whether these lower emissions for 2026 represent the start of a long-term decline, the analysis indicates encouraging signs of deeper long-term structural changes," he said. "But this shift must accelerate to ensure it is not outpaced by energy demand growth.".

The report found that clean energy growth isn't yet fast enough to drive a steady decline in global CO2 emissions attributable to fossil fuels. The study authors expect that to happen in the next few years, Hauck mentioned, as long as there is a continued push to deploy solar and wind power, batteries and electric vehicles.

In a recent development, CO2 emissions from fossil fuels are just part of the picture, though. Because of increases in human-caused peat fires, deforestation and forest fires linked to dry El Niño conditions, total global CO2 emissions from all sources this year are projected to increase slightly from 42.8 billion metric tons (47.2 billion U.S. tons) last year to reach a record 43.3 billion metric tons (47.7 billion U.S. tons) this year, according to the report.

Industry observers note that this means that the total budget of CO2 that can be emitted before global warming reaches 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels is now just 150 billion metric tons (165 billion U.S. tons) ‪—‬ equivalent to less than four years of emissions at the current rate.

Hauck, like many climate scientists, thinks we have already missed our chance to hit the 1.5 C target and could only get back to that level through extensive removal of CO2 from the atmosphere.

In a recent development, "I'm still hopeful for something between 1.5 and 2 C [3.6 F]," Hauck said. "But for 1.5 degrees, we would need to see such a drastic strong drop in emissions. Based on what we've seen in the past years, even with this strong increase in avoided emissions, I don't think we can make that.".

It has been revealed that to halt global warming from increasing ever further, the world needs to be more ambitious in its planned emissions cuts, said Rogeli. We need to bring annual emissions down to zero to protect future generations from a double whammy of “having to try to transform economies so that they produce less climate pollution, while dealing with the impacts and damages of an increasingly adverse climate system," he said.

#282. A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1304 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory.
  • Sources indicate that unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes.
  • According to recent reports, A new study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory. However, new research suggests that the success of such a mission could depend heavily on which side of the asteroid receives the blast.

Sources indicate that unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes. Those differences can dramatically influence how an asteroid moves when exposed to intense radiation.

According to recent reports, A new study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid. In one simulation, the asteroid's speed changed by 3.9 millimeters per second when irradiated from one direction, compared with only 0.8 millimeters per second from another. That represents a nearly fivefold difference in deflection velocity, the change in the asteroid's forward speed caused by the burst.

"We expected aim to matter," said Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories who led the research. "What surprised us was how much.".

Industry observers note that the effects on an asteroid's rotation could be even more dramatic. For another simulated asteroid, the change in how promptly it spun varied by a factor of 17 depending on the direction of the X-rays.

These findings suggest that understanding an asteroid's shape and carefully selecting where to direct a nuclear blast could be essential to protecting Earth from a future impact.

The research received funding through Sandia's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program.

A New Way to Simulate Asteroid Deflection.

To investigate how different asteroid shapes respond to nuclear blasts, Moore and his colleagues developed what they describe as the most accurate asteroid deflection model yet.

Earlier computer models faced a major limitation. Researchers typically had to choose between representing an asteroid's complex shape and performing highly detailed calculations of the physical forces involved. Combining both approaches demanded more computing power than was practical.

The upcoming system overcomes that obstacle, allowing scientists to study realistic asteroid shapes while maintaining the precision needed to calculate their response to an X-ray burst. The result is the most detailed simulation of asteroid deflection produced so far.

"Our newly introduced algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough," Moore remarked. "With the old models, computers just couldn't handle it.".

Moore's interest in improving these calculations grew out of an earlier experiment using Sandia's Z machine. That experiment provided the first demonstration that X-rays could deflect a small piece of asteroid material.

The next challenge was determining how the same physical process might affect an entire asteroid.

"I started wondering how to scale up the calculation to more accurately predict deflection of a full-scale asteroid.".

Recent findings suggest that A major problem was the widespread practice of treating asteroids as spheres. Although this simplifies the mathematics, it overlooks the irregular shapes of real asteroids, which can have ridges, depressions, and uneven surfaces.

It has been revealed that "You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes," he noted. "That's when I latched onto some work one of my colleagues was doing related to outgassing of objects in space. I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this. No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid.".

The solution involved bringing together two sophisticated simulation systems already used at Sandia for very different types of physical problems.

"The ALEGRA code is normally used to model fast, high-energy experiments, like magnetically imploding wires on the Z machine, while SPARTA, a direct simulation Monte Carlo code, is usually used to model comparatively weak, slowly evolving forces, like the drag on a satellite from the solar wind," Moore explained.

"The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches.".

Predicting What Happens After a Nuclear Blast.

The upcoming computer model allows researchers to reconstruct an asteroid using detailed 3D images captured during spacecraft flybys. They can then simulate a nuclear X-ray burst while adjusting the explosion's strength, its distance from the asteroid, and the direction from which the radiation arrives.

The software calculates how much material would vaporize across different parts of the asteroid's surface and displays the results as a heat map. Using that information, it estimates the resulting push, changes in the asteroid's rotation, and the extent of surface damage.

According to recent reports, these calculations are vital because a successful planetary defense mission would ideally change an asteroid's trajectory without breaking it into multiple dangerous fragments. Redirecting one large object could be preferable to creating several pieces that might still threaten Earth.

However, the simulations cannot yet predict every possible consequence of a nuclear blast.

"Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We can't predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore stated.

It has been revealed that developing that capability will require additional research, investment, and more advanced computational tools. An intense X-ray burst can trigger numerous physical effects, some of which influence one another. Accounting for all those interactions makes it exceptionally difficult to predict exactly how an asteroid would behave during a real deflection attempt.

Choosing the Right Blast Could Save Earth.

Recent findings suggest that despite these remaining challenges, the findings offer valuable guidance for future planetary defense efforts. The research demonstrates that the direction of a nuclear blast is not simply a minor detail. It can substantially change how effectively an asteroid is redirected.

"Our study demonstrates how vital it is to aim carefully," Moore stated. "Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day.".

The new simulation tools could eventually help mission planners identify the most effective way to deflect a threatening asteroid. In principle, researchers could enter detailed information about its shape, then calculate the ideal explosive strength, distance, and direction needed to move it away from Earth.

Turning those calculations into a real mission would still be extremely difficult.

For one thing, the software requires reasonably accurate information about the asteroid's shape from every direction. If an asteroid were discovered on a collision course with Earth, there might not be enough time to gather the necessary observations.

Another challenge would be delivering and positioning a nuclear device at precisely the right location relative to an asteroid traveling through space. Even if scientists could identify the ideal blast configuration, executing it would require extraordinary precision.

Nevertheless, the improved simulations could eliminate much of the uncertainty surrounding one possible method of asteroid defense. By better understanding how nuclear X-rays interact with the complex surfaces of real asteroids, scientists are moving closer to predicting which strategies would work best.

For Moore, that progress is an encouraging step toward ensuring humanity has a better chance of preventing a catastrophic asteroid impact.

A 2019 astronaut photo shows the near-perfect cone of a highly active volcano poking its heavily scarred and partially snow-covered head above a thick bank of low-lying clouds over the Kuril Islands.

Sources indicate that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

According to recent reports, where is it? Atlasov Island, off the coast of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula [50.84755357, 155.56126752].

What's in the photo? The summit of Alaid volcano peeking above a thick layer of low-lying clouds.

Who took the photo? An unnamed astronaut on board the International Space Station.

This eye-catching astronaut photo shows a towering, highly active Russian volcano poking its head above a thick bank of swirling clouds over the Kuril Islands.

Recent findings suggest that the lofty peak is located on Atlasov Island, the northernmost of the Kuril Islands — a chain of roughly 50 largely uninhabited volcanic landmasses stretching along a fault line that runs between Russia and Japan in the Sea of Okhotsk. Altasov lies 40 miles (65 kilometers) off Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula, which is also renowned for its volcanic activity.

The island consists mainly of a single, massive volcano, called Alaid, which is known for its near-perfect cone shape. Alaid reaches up to 7,497 feet (2,285 meters) above sea level, making it the tallest peak in the Kuril Islands.

Alaid has erupted at least nine times in the past 50 years, including a major outburst in April 1981 that ejected a 1,250-mile-long (2,000 km) plume of thick smoke and ash into the atmosphere, according to the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program.

Its most recent eruption occurred between September and November 2022, when a river of lava flowed down its flank (see below). During this outburst, the volcano also spit out smoke and ash that was spotted from space alongside another eruption plume coming from the nearby island Paramushir.

Sources indicate that alaid last erupted in November 2022 and unleashed a scorching lava flow down its snow-covered slopes. This photo also indicates what Atlasov Island looks like when it is not obscured by clouds.

In the astronaut's photo, roughly half of Atlasov Island rises above a deep, low-lying bank of swirling clouds. The summit of Alaid, crowned by a roughly mile-wide (1.6 km) caldera, is also obscured by clouds. (The volcano was not erupting when the photo was taken.).

Industry observers note that farther down the volcano's flanks are a series of snow-filled gullies carved out by lava flows from previous eruptions. Eagle-eyed viewers may also be able to spot some parasitic cones — small openings where lava burst through in the past — around the edge of the cloud layer, according to NASA's Earth Observatory.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Industry observers note that the area surrounding a cluster of parasitic cones on the volcano's northwest flank (top right in the photo) is devoid of vegetation ‪—‬ a result of another major eruption in 1972, which scoured the surrounding landscape with hot ash. A 2009 study revealed fresh signs of recovery in the affected area, but noted that it could take hundreds of years for vegetation to return to pre-eruption levels.

Industry observers note that the clouds are not the only thing the island rises above. Alaid is essentially the summit of a much larger underwater volcano that lies beneath the Sea of Okhotsk. The rest of the island has grown around the exposed cone as lava flows have reached sea level and solidified. Millions of years ago, this larger volcano was likely connected to the Kamchatka Peninsula via a land bridge that has since been submerged.

In 1981, a major eruption caused Alaid to unleash a massive plume of smoke and ash that reached up to 1,250 miles long.

Astronauts and satellites have snapped several other stunning shots of intriguing landmasses nearby, including a quartet of end-to-end volcanoes on Simushir Island and a set of volcanic "nesting dolls" on Onekotan Island.

And in 2022, the Landsat 8 satellite also spotted the iconic summit of Mount Vesuvius peeking through a gap in the clouds over Italy, just like Alaid.

It has been revealed that A 2024 astronaut photo shows the icy surface of Pangong Lake breaking apart in the lofty Tibetan Plateau. The point where the ice meets the water almost perfectly matches a disputed border between China and India.

A 2020 astronaut photo shows the unique structure of Ol Doinyo Lengai, an active stratovolcano in Tanzania that was recently adorned with a bright white "ash cone." The explosive peak produces a rare type of lava that is unusually cool but travels remarkably quickly.

Industry observers note that A 2010 satellite photo indicates the point where a small lake bisects the snowy rim of an ancient glacier on Canada's Baffin Island. The rippling, snow-rimmed structure is the last remaining fragment of a colossal ice sheet that once covered large parts of North America.

#279. An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an extraordinary collection of fossils in central Colombia is revealing a surprising chapter in Earth's evolutionary history.
  • In a recent development, scientists from McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) identified this unusual pattern while studying fossils from Colombia's Paja Formation.
  • Drawing on these findings, McGill biology professor Hans Larsson and PhD graduate Dirley Cortés have proposed a fresh concept called a "Biotic Inflection." The term describes an evolutionary turning point when older groups nearing extinction coexist with newer lineages that are beginning to expand and diversify.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an extraordinary collection of fossils in central Colombia is revealing a surprising chapter in Earth's evolutionary history. Researchers have uncovered evidence of a time when ancient animal groups that were approaching extinction lived alongside newer groups that would eventually flourish. The discovery suggests that major evolutionary transitions can occur without the widespread destruction associated with mass extinctions.

In a recent development, scientists from McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) identified this unusual pattern while studying fossils from Colombia's Paja Formation. The ancient marine ecosystem preserves an exceptional mixture of surviving Jurassic lineages and emerging Cretaceous groups, offering a rare glimpse into a period of profound biological change.

Drawing on these findings, McGill biology professor Hans Larsson and PhD graduate Dirley Cortés have proposed a fresh concept called a "Biotic Inflection." The term describes an evolutionary turning point when older groups nearing extinction coexist with newer lineages that are beginning to expand and diversify.

A Perfect Storm for Ancient Ocean Biodiversity.

The researchers believe an unusual combination of environmental conditions helped make this remarkable coexistence possible. Warm greenhouse temperatures, elevated sea levels, and coastal waters rich in nutrients may have supported an unusually diverse range of marine life.

Another vital factor was the emergence of new ocean connections between the eastern Pacific and the early Atlantic through the region that is now Colombia. Together, these conditions likely created opportunities for different groups of animals to thrive within the same ecosystem. Many of these environmental influences continue to shape biodiversity around the world today.

"The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a 'perfect storm' of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, fresh groups were beginning to flourish," Larsson said.

A Lost World of Giant Marine Reptiles and Predators.

In a recent development, the evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia. This fossil-rich region has preserved an astonishing variety of prehistoric marine animals, providing scientists with an unusually detailed picture of an ancient ocean ecosystem. Most of the fossils collected from the formation are housed at the CIP.

"This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others," Cortés explained. "Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date.".

In a previous study, the researchers reconstructed the feeding relationships among animals in the Paja Biota. Their analysis revealed an exceptionally intricate food web, with an unusually large variety of apex predators occupying the highest levels of the ecosystem.

This remarkable complexity makes the Paja Formation especially valuable for investigating how ecosystems change as older evolutionary groups decline and new ones become established.

Could This Discovery Change How Scientists Understand Evolution?

Industry observers note that the proposed Biotic Inflection offers a potentially important fresh way to understand major changes in Earth's biodiversity. Rather than being driven by a mass extinction, some evolutionary transitions may involve periods of extraordinary diversity, when declining lineages and emerging groups coexist.

Recent findings suggest that however, the researchers emphasize that more evidence is needed to establish how common this pattern may have been. Additional fossil discoveries, more accurate estimates of fossil ages, and comparisons with geological formations in other parts of the world will help determine whether similar transitions occurred elsewhere in Earth's history.

"I think we've discovered a new model of global biodiversity change. Now we'll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth's history and how we can quantify its impacts," Larsson remarked.

In a recent development, the research received funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, the Anders Foundation, the 1923 Fund, Gregory D. and Jennifer Walston Johnson, the Fonds de recherche Nature et technologies Québec, and the McGill Biology Department Writing-Year Award 2024-2025.
