Recent findings suggest that A fresh look at Einstein's equations suggests that gravity can sometimes snap and reconnect, similar to magnetic field lines on the sun. The findings hint at a new way that gravity and matter can trade energy.

Sources indicate that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Magnetic reconnection — the process behind the sun's most violent outbursts — may have a counterpart in gravity.

According to a newly introduced theoretical study, sheet-like structures in the gravitational field can break apart and reconnect in new arrangements, much like the magnetic field lines that unleash solar flares.

In a recent development, built entirely on Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, the study spells out when this "gravitational reconnection" can happen. It also offers a way to measure how fast the theoretical reconnection proceeds, and suggests a change to how gravity and matter trade energy. The process could even play a role in black hole collisions, the researchers suggest.

According to recent reports, magnetic field lines are normally "frozen" into plasma — the hot, electrically charged gas that makes up stars — and carried along wherever it flows. The lines can be stretched and twisted, but not cut. Where this rule breaks down, they can snap and rejoin in a process called magnetic reconnection, releasing pent-up energy in explosive bursts such as solar flares.

"In plasma physics, reconnection has become an essential part of our understanding of how magnetic fields reorganize and exchange energy with matter," Luca Comisso, an astrophysicist at Columbia University and first author of the study, told Live Science via email. "Could something similar be true for gravity?".

Industry observers note that "Gravity and magnetism describe very different aspects of nature, so there's no obvious reason to expect them to behave alike," Comisso stated. "But when we express Einstein's equations in a particular mathematical form, some of the same principles that govern magnetic fields also emerge in gravity. We wanted to understand whether those similarities extended to reconnection itself.".

It has been revealed that comisso and study co-author Felipe Asenjo, a physicist at Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile, used a mathematical framework known as the tetrad formulation. "Einstein's theory describes gravity through the geometry of space-time," Comisso explained. But in the tetrad formulation, "certain aspects of gravity can be expressed through quantities resembling electric and magnetic fields.".

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Recent findings suggest that in a prior study published in the journal Physical Review Letters earlier this year, the researchers applied this framework to gravity. That study suggested that gravitational fields can form two-dimensional structures called gravitational field sheets. Of the sheets' two dimensions, one stretches through space and the other through time — so each sheet is the trail a line leaves as time passes. A snapshot at any instant therefore catches each sheet as a line, akin to the field lines drawn around a magnet. And, like magnetic field lines frozen into a plasma, "under certain conditions, these sheets evolve without breaking or changing how they are connected," Comisso said.

An illustration depicting the sun’s magnetic field lines over an image taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. When magnetic loops get stretched to their limit, they snap and reconnect, triggering solar flares.

In the upcoming study, published Oct. 28 in the journal Physical Review D, the researchers found that this is not always the case. "Gravitational field sheets can break and reconnect in a different arrangement, much like magnetic field lines do in plasmas," Comisso said.

The researchers showed that breaking the frozen-in rule doesn't, by itself, guarantee reconnection. Sometimes, the sheets merely slip relative to the flow that carries them, staying intact because they remain frozen into a different flow. Genuine reconnection happens only when no such alternative flow exists.

"We also derived equations describing how quickly this reconnection can occur and how it can affect the transfer of energy and momentum," Comisso noted. In general relativity, gravity and matter can trade energy and momentum, with only their combined total conserved. The study reveals that reconnection changes the local rate of that exchange.

Reconnection also alters gravitational helicity, the gravitational counterpart of a quantity that measures how twisted and interlinked magnetic field lines are. Frozen-in sheets keep their helicity fixed, but reconnection can create or destroy it.

The findings don't require fresh physics. "Everything follows from Einstein's general relativity," Comisso remarked.

It has been revealed that "Einstein developed his theory more than a century ago, and it has passed an extraordinary number of experimental tests," he added. "Yet even after more than a century, there are still newly introduced insights to be gained from those same equations.".

What could trigger gravitational reconnection in nature remains an open question. Among the candidates the researchers suggested are the singularities thought to lurk at the hearts of black holes and the combined effect of gravitational ripples that are too small to track individually. Quantum effects linked to Hawking radiation ‪—‬ the faint glow that black holes are predicted to emit ‪—‬ could also play a part.

"We're still at the beginning, but one of the most interesting possibilities is that gravitational reconnection could play a role in extreme events, such as the merger of two black holes or the collision of neutron stars," Comisso stated. "These are environments where gravity is extremely strong and the geometry of spacetime changes dramatically.".

Such collisions send out ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, which detectors such as LIGO (the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) have been recording since 2015. "We'd like to understand whether gravitational reconnection could contribute to transferring energy, and whether it might leave a recognizable signature in gravitational waves," Comisso added. "We don't know the answers yet, but these are questions that we can now begin to investigate.".

#267. Tech Report: Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Tech Report: Scientists find deadly virus DNA hidden in 1,000-year-old manuscripts

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, some of Europe's most famous medieval manuscripts, including the York Gospels, have revealed an extraordinary secret hidden in their pages.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery was made by an international research team led by University College Dublin (UCD).
  • It has been revealed that sheeppox is highly contagious and can spread through a flock with alarming speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, some of Europe's most famous medieval manuscripts, including the York Gospels, have revealed an extraordinary secret hidden in their pages. Scientists have discovered ancient viral DNA preserved in the animal skins used to make parchment, opening a new window into the 3,500-year history of sheeppox virus (SPPV).

Sources indicate that the discovery was made by an international research team led by University College Dublin (UCD). By analyzing parchment from centuries-old documents, the researchers uncovered the first genetic evidence that this destructive disease was spreading through European sheep flocks long before modern times.

It has been revealed that sheeppox is highly contagious and can spread through a flock with alarming speed. It can kill large numbers of infected animals, particularly young sheep, while also causing major economic losses by reducing wool, meat, and milk production.

Ancient Manuscripts Preserve the DNA of Deadly Viruses.

Sources indicate that published in Science Advances, the newly introduced study reconstructs more than 3,500 years of sheeppox virus evolution. Researchers identified viral DNA in several historically vital medieval manuscripts, revealing that documents preserved for their cultural significance can also contain valuable biological evidence.

Among the manuscripts examined was the 1,000-year-old York Gospels, considered one of the finest surviving illuminated manuscripts from the early Anglo-Saxon period. The researchers also studied older works, including the Corpus Glossary at Corpus Christi College Cambridge, one of the earliest English dictionaries, along with other medieval manuscripts from Britain and continental Europe.

The secret lies in the parchment itself. Before paper became widely available, manuscripts were often produced using carefully prepared animal hides, including skins from sheep, goats, and cattle. These materials can preserve traces of an animal's biological history, including evidence of infections present when it died.

In a recent development, in several manuscripts, the researchers detected sheeppox virus DNA on multiple pages. These findings indicate that infected animals had supplied some of the skins used to produce the documents.

An especially surprising discovery involved viral DNA found on parchment made from calfskin and goatskin. Because sheeppox primarily infects sheep, the results raise two possibilities: the virus may occasionally have infected other livestock species, or viral material may have contaminated the skins during parchment production.

Historic Books Become Unexpected Disease Archives.

It has been revealed that "The recording of ancient DNA of pathogens has completely changed our understanding of infectious disease in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve animal pathogen DNA. It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past," mentioned Louis L'Hôte, PhD candidate at UCD and lead author of the study.

"These genomes help us understand how these pathogens evolved and how they impacted past societies -- such as sheeppox virus, which we show has been affecting Eurasian sheep herds for at least three and a half millennia.".

According to recent reports, the findings suggest that libraries and archives may hold far more information about historical diseases than previously recognized. Manuscripts that have survived for hundreds of years could provide genetic evidence of livestock outbreaks that left few other records.

"Parchment making has been considered a vanishing craft, but we are beginning to understand just how much of the past it has retained. This project reveals that parchments not only preserve our cultural history for hundreds of years, but also the landscape of disease in our livestock in the medieval period," mentioned Dr. Kevin G. Daly, Associate Professor at UCD School of Agriculture and Food Science and the study's supervising author.

"This kind of exciting, surprising discovery is only possible when researchers from a range of disciplines come together to share their expertise and data -- a generosity and trust that collaborative science depends on.".

The project brought together specialists in genetics, history, virology, protein chemistry, and conservation, allowing the team to investigate the manuscripts from both historical and biological perspectives.

Ancient Sheep Teeth Reveal 3,700 Years of Disease.

The medieval manuscripts were only part of the investigation. To trace the disease further into the past, the scientists also examined DNA recovered from sheep teeth dating to the Bronze Age.

Teeth are particularly useful for studying ancient infections because they can protect genetic material for thousands of years, often preserving evidence that has disappeared from other skeletal remains.

The researchers identified the oldest known genetic traces of sheeppox virus in sheep teeth recovered from ancient pastoralist settlements in the Eurasian steppe. When combined with the manuscript findings, this evidence shows that the disease has affected livestock for more than 3,700 years.

To investigate how the virus developed, the team compared ancient viral DNA with genetic sequences from modern viruses. Their analysis suggests that the main branches of the capripoxvirus family (sheeppox virus, goatpox virus, and lumpy skin disease virus) separated from one another sometime between 11,500 and 3,700 years ago.

That estimated timeline coincides with major changes in human history, including the domestication of livestock and the large-scale movement of sheep from the Eurasian steppe into Europe. These movements may have played an important role in the virus's long history of transmission.

A Deadly Virus That Has Barely Changed in Thousands of Years.

One of the study's most striking findings was how little the sheeppox virus has changed genetically over the past several thousand years. Unlike some other viruses, its genome appears to have remained remarkably stable despite its long history of infecting livestock.

Understanding that stability could help scientists identify the genetic changes that originally allowed the virus to become an effective sheep pathogen.

The discovery also has immediate relevance. Sheeppox remains a serious threat to livestock farming, with outbreaks continuing to cause substantial economic damage.

"People around the world are still fighting against this pathogen -- there is at the moment an outbreak of sheeppox in Greece, causing much economic damage," noted Louis L'Hôte.

"Ancient genomes can help us understand how these pathogens affecting us today evolved. We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia.".

L'Hôte added: "This might mean that genetic changes before this point were very vital to how the sheeppox virus evolved to infect its host, which may help us fight the pathogen in the future.".

According to recent reports, by uncovering viral DNA in both medieval manuscripts and prehistoric animal remains, the researchers have demonstrated a powerful new way to investigate the history of infectious diseases. Their work suggests that materials preserved for entirely different purposes may contain valuable clues about the emergence, spread, and evolution of pathogens that continue to affect the world today.

The research was funded by Taighde Éireann-Research Ireland and the European Research Council. Led by UCD, the project involved more than 30 institutions in Ireland and internationally, including Trinity College Dublin, the Helmholtz Institute for One Health, Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, the University of Leicester, Cambridge University, and the University of Copenhagen.

Philae drifted and bounced around the comet for two hours before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P. To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement.

It has been revealed that the European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired.

When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space. The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down.

In a recent development, philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it. Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.

The European Space Agency's Rosetta and Philae expedition was a first-of-its-kind mission, an endeavour to not just rendezvous with a comet and watch it change over time as it approached the sun (that was Rosetta's job), but also to soft-land a probe on its icy and rocky surface to see what a comet is truly made of.

The Rosetta and Philae mission succeeded on both counts, but Philae's historic landing was marred by its turbulent touchdown. Philae actually landed three different times on Comet 67/P, all because the harpoons designed to secure it in place didn't fire as planned.

It has been revealed that after the first landing, Philae bounced up and drifted around the comet for two hours, making another bounce before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it. Scientists figured it was stuck in a shady spot where sunlight couldn't reach its solar panels. Because it was solar-powered, Philae needed to be facing the sun properly to generate enough power for sustained operation on the comet's surface.

Still, Philae did have some power stored in batteries, which lasted for more than two days on the surface. That allowed Philae to perform some science with its 10 instruments in the time it had on Comet 67/P. Most notably, Philae found organic molecules that had never been detected on a comet before.

The Rosetta orbiter continued to orbit Comet 67P until September 2016, and it was in that month -- just weeks before Rosetta itself landed on the comet on Sept. 30, 2016 -- that the spacecraft rediscovered the Philae lander lying on its side in a rocky crevice.

#265. A Lost Landmass Nearly the Size of North America Is Hiding Under the Sea—and It Could Rewrite Human History

A Lost Landmass Nearly the Size of North America Is Hiding Under the Sea—and It Could Rewrite Human History

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Several years ago, I travelled to North Carolina as part of a research trip for a story about the famous Lost Colony of Roanoke.
  • Recent findings suggest that ultimately, trying to wrangle all the many tendrils of that leviathan proved too unwieldy, and many of the ancillary elements have remained confined to my notebooks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A geographer calls it Aquaterra. For 120,000 years, early humans lived there—then the oceans swallowed it.

Several years ago, I travelled to North Carolina as part of a research trip for a story about the famous Lost Colony of Roanoke. Trying to leave no stone unturned, I explored the former colony’s dedicated National Historic Site, poured over archives of antique maps, and even took in a lavish outdoor stage production.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, trying to wrangle all the many tendrils of that leviathan proved too unwieldy, and many of the ancillary elements have remained confined to my notebooks. Yet one moment from that trip has never been far from my mind, and it reshaped how I thought about our quest for answers about early human history.

It came about during a conversation with Dr. Eric Klingelhofer, a respected scholar and Vice President for Research with The First Colony Foundation. Dr. Klingelhofer had overseen several excavations that yielded remnants of Roanoke, but he was worried that many once-buried artifacts had already been claimed by a much more powerful force.

Industry observers note that “Before my retirement,” he told me, “I attended a UNESCO-backed conference on Bonaire in the Dutch West Indies. These causes, rising sea levels and storm surges, plus coastal overdevelopment, endangered every island, as most prehistoric and early colonial sites lie close to the sea.” As we sat there on tranquil, federally protected land, it was hard for me to feel the urgency at the time, but he stressed that we were in a race against time. “At Fort Raleigh,”—the name the National Parks Service gave the National Historic Site—“coastal erosion has already swallowed up excavation units we had dug in 2007. The rate of loss is about twenty feet in twenty years—and it may be increasing.”.

After our conversation, I walked along the island’s shoreline, struck by the thought that although I might be walking the same land as those colonists, the landscape wasn’t really the same. Their shoreline likely sat yards farther out than the one I strolled, and as the water swept that land away, it took with it our chance to learn more about the people who once stood there.

In the study of history, we too often focus on the preservation or replication of what was once on a certain parcel of land, taking it as a given that the land itself stayed constant. We spend all our time debating whether the proverbial Ship of Theseus is still the same after centuries of repairs, never stopping to question if the shoreline of Delos on which he landed still remains.

Yet, recent studies have emerged to remind us that even in the absence of human intervention, the world looked different to the peoples of the past than it does to us today.

The scale of this dilemma, the problem of our submerged history, is far greater than a single island in North Carolina, or a single colony from the 1500s. Our whole understanding of early humankind may be built on faulty ground, due specifically to how much of that ground is now underwater. But don’t let your thoughts drift to that Platonic idea of Atlantis; the proper term, as The Atlantic recently reminded us, is Aquaterra.

Sources indicate that in 2014, the geographer Jerome E. Dobson mounted a case for the recognition of a global landmass he dubbed Aquaterra, a term he first proposed in 1999. In “Aquaterra Incognita,” Dobson argued that “all landmasses are defined by time as well as space,” and therefore, since “so little is known about the seacoast where a significant portion of humankind surely dwelled for the better part of 120,000 years,” we should properly recognize and name the 22.5-million-square-kilometer landmass that once hosted the earliest human civilizations.

When we think about the ice ages that have cycled across Earth’s history, we can easily picture the glaciers and ice sheets that formed, but we rarely consider where all that water came from. During an ice age, sea levels drop, exposing land that’s now underwater. As a result, the shorelines early humans knew looked very different from the ones we see today.

The lowlands these glaciers exposed were not bereft of life, either. The ecosystems they once supported varied, from grasslands to wetlands, forests to estuaries. They attracted wildlife, and later, early human civilizations. “Compare the most recent curve of sea level rise against the timeline of cultural innovations,” Dobson writes, “and you will find that much human progress occurred while seacoasts were still quite low.”.

When the glaciers melted and sea levels rose again, naturally, early humans abandoned their soon-to-be-submerged settlements. But that doesn’t mean we should simply ignore what once stood there. “It would not change the timeline of human progress if, for instance, cities were found as low as -50 meters, since Jericho is known to have existed when sea levels were that low,” Dobson notes. What could revise that timeline, he notes, is “the possibility that precursors of major innovations may exist at even lower depths.”.

“One intriguing possibility is pottery,” he proposes:.

According to recent reports, all this talk about “possibility,” of course, makes the benefits of recognizing Aquaterra seem entirely theoretical. Yet in just the last few years, the archeological world received a stirring reminder that the land we can see is not the only land there ever was, and that whole chapters of our history may have been claimed by the sea.

In a recent development, in 2021, Michael K. Faught and Morgan F. Smith published “The magnificent seven: Marine submerged precontact sites found by systematic geoarchaeology in the Americas.” The study documented not one or two but seven projects, in North America alone, that had found traces of precontact life now drowned beneath the continental shelf. Each of the seven projects worked “from the terrestrially known, to the submerged unknown.” Using methodical but varied mapping and modeling techniques, researchers predicted where people might once have lived, then searched for proof with underwater surveys, sediment cores, and even hands-on excavations.

One of the research efforts happened in the Gulf of Mexico’s paleo-Sabine River. Over the course of a decade, from 1976 to 1986, it turned up “charred wood and vegetation, nut hulls, seeds, fish scales, and bone from fish, reptiles, birds, and small mammals,” some of which dated back 9,000 years. Soon after, researchers in Belize found the drowned outlines of pole-and-thatch buildings, which turned out to be Classic-period Maya salt works now sitting underwater. Other research discussed in the study uncovered stone tools, campsites, and even a stone artifact more than 12,000 years old.

Industry observers note that to truly understand human history, we can’t keep digging only in the land we can see. We also have to search for the land our ancestors knew, much of which now lies beneath the waves. That calls for a change in mindset and a rethinking of how archaeology works. As seas keep rising, how many more once-inhabited places will slip beneath the surface, taking with them secrets as recent as Roanoke’s? If we don’t change course now, the sites we have yet to excavate may be written off by tomorrow’s scholars as mere seafloor.

As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

#264. DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that scientists have uncovered a remarkable collection of DNA hidden within the Shroud of Turin, revealing a surprisingly complex biological history behind one of the world's most mysterious and controversial religious artifacts.
  • Published in Scientific Reports, the study used advanced DNA sequencing technology to examine samples collected from the Shroud in 1978.
  • Unlike traditional DNA testing, which often focuses on genetic material from a single organism, metagenomic sequencing can detect DNA from many different species within the same sample.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that scientists have uncovered a remarkable collection of DNA hidden within the Shroud of Turin, revealing a surprisingly complex biological history behind one of the world's most mysterious and controversial religious artifacts. The genetic evidence includes traces of humans, bacteria, fungi, plants, animals, and even Mediterranean red coral, offering new clues about the environments and people that have come into contact with the famous cloth over the centuries.

Published in Scientific Reports, the study used advanced DNA sequencing technology to examine samples collected from the Shroud in 1978. For the first time, researchers applied a sophisticated technique (rigorous PCR-free next-generation metagenomic sequencing) to these officially collected samples, allowing them to identify genetic material preserved within the linen fibers in unprecedented detail.

Unlike traditional DNA testing, which often focuses on genetic material from a single organism, metagenomic sequencing can detect DNA from many different species within the same sample. This makes it particularly useful for studying historical objects that have been handled, stored, and exposed to changing environments over long periods.

By examining this genetic material, the international research team assembled what they describe as the most comprehensive picture yet of the biological traces accumulated on the Shroud throughout its history.

Human DNA and a Hidden World of Microorganisms.

It has been revealed that among the discoveries were multiple lineages of human mitochondrial DNA, suggesting that genetic material from different human populations has accumulated on the cloth. Mitochondrial DNA is a small portion of our genetic material that is inherited through the maternal line, making it especially useful for studying ancestry and population history.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also identified an unexpectedly diverse microbiome, the collection of microscopic organisms associated with a particular environment or object. These included bacteria commonly found on human skin, various fungi, and microorganisms adapted to living in salty environments.

Some of these organisms belong to a group known as archaea, which are single-celled microorganisms distinct from bacteria. Certain archaea can thrive in extremely salty conditions that would be difficult for many other forms of life to tolerate.

Together, these findings reveal that the Shroud carries a complicated biological record shaped by repeated human contact and exposure to different environmental conditions.

DNA From Plants, Animals, and Mediterranean Coral.

The discoveries extended far beyond human DNA and microorganisms. Scientists also detected genetic traces from numerous plant and animal species, adding another layer to the Shroud's biological history.

Plant DNA included cultivated wheat, carrots, maize, bananas, and peanuts. Genetic material from domesticated animals was also present, including cattle, pigs, chickens, dogs, and cats.

One particularly unusual finding was DNA associated with Mediterranean red coral.

Industry observers note that the wide variety of biological material suggests that the cloth has encountered a diverse range of living organisms and environmental influences. These genetic traces may reflect its long history of handling, storage, and movement through different geographical regions.

In a recent development, importantly, the presence of DNA from a particular species does not establish when that material reached the cloth. Some traces could have accumulated relatively recently, while others may reflect much older interactions. This makes the findings valuable for reconstructing the Shroud's environmental history, but also highlights the difficulty of interpreting DNA recovered from an object that has been exposed to human activity for centuries.

Can DNA Solve the Mystery of the Shroud of Turin?

Despite the remarkable diversity of genetic material, the researchers emphasize that their findings cannot establish the Shroud's age or authenticity.

Industry observers note that the Shroud of Turin is a linen cloth bearing the faint image of a human figure and has long been associated by some believers with the burial of Jesus. Its origins have been debated for generations, making it one of the most extensively investigated historical and religious artifacts in the world.

Because the cloth has been touched and exposed to different environments over many centuries, its DNA represents a mixture of biological material accumulated at different times. This makes it impossible to reliably separate any original DNA that might have been associated with the fabric from the many genetic traces deposited afterward.

Instead, the research demonstrates how modern forensic genomics and proteomics can reveal information that traditional methods might miss. Forensic genomics uses genetic evidence to investigate biological origins and interactions, while proteomics examines proteins, which can also preserve valuable clues about biological materials.

Together, these approaches offer powerful latest ways to investigate how historical objects have been preserved, handled, and exposed to different environments.

Modern DNA Technology Reveals New Historical Clues.

Professor Noemi Procopio, Professor of Forensic Science at the University of Lancashire, contributed to the international research collaboration. She emphasized that advances in forensic technology are making it possible to recover information from historical samples collected decades earlier.

Professor Noemi Procopio, Professor of Forensic Science at the University of Lancashire, stated: "The Shroud of Turin continues to fascinate historians, scientists and the public, and we're thrilled to reveal new information about the biological complexity preserved within samples collected almost 50 years ago by applying new cutting-edge forensic DNA technologies.

"The Shroud represents a rich archive of genetic information that has accumulated over centuries of human interaction and environmental exposure. While the DNA evidence cannot answer all the questions about the age or authenticity of the cloth, it provides novel insights into its biological history and demonstrates how advances in forensic science can unlock new information from historical artifacts.".

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

It has been revealed that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Recent findings suggest that engineers in China have built a newly introduced computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Industry observers note that traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the fresh architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

According to recent reports, huawei unveiled the fresh architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

It has been revealed that representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

Recent findings suggest that "Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models.".

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives mentioned in the statement.

It has been revealed that nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a firm breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to recent reports, according to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the organization claims delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit.".

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also declared the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Industry observers note that huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is presently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

This supernova imposter erupts every 113 days as the compact object gets close to the unstable massive star.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered.

According to recent reports, when a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices.

Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

"For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis," Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville said in a statement.

Sources indicate that several other supernova imposters have been observed over the past decade or two. Until now, no one knew what causes these stars to repeatedly cry wolf. Thanks to Chandra’s X-ray vision, Aghakhanloo has led a team of astronomers who think they have now uncovered an explanation.

The supernova imposter is named AT 2016blu, and is a type of star that we call a 'luminous blue variable,' or LBV. These are the most massive and luminous stars in the universe and their extreme characteristics result in them being highly unstable, undergoing intermittent bouts of mass loss as they eject material from their outer layers into the surrounding space.

However, faking a supernova is not part of their typical behavior, so a new way of looking at AT 2016blu was needed.

"To understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized that we needed X-ray data that was timed so that we’d observe the star when it was in an outburst," team member Núria Torres-Albà, also from the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, remarked.

It has been revealed that aghakhanloo’s team were granted the opportunity to commandeer Chandra to target an outburst of AT 2016blu at the earliest opportunity. That opportunity arose in March 2026.

Industry observers note that chandra had previously and coincidentally looked in the direction of NGC 4559 back in 2001 and 2002 and did not notice anything unusual back then. This time around, however, it captured a powerful blast of X-rays coinciding with yet another false supernova outburst.

Recent findings suggest that the X-ray detection allowed Aghakhanloo’s team to assemble a picture of what is happening. "Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen," he said.

Chandra’s X-ray observations indicate that AT 2016blu has an unseen companion, a compact, high-gravity object that is either a neutron star or a stellar-mass black hole on an elliptical 113-day orbit around the luminous blue variable.

Neutron stars and stellar-mass black holes are the core remnants of massive stars that have gone supernova for real, meaning that at one time AT 2016blu was a binary star system.

According to recent reports, each time the compact object reaches the point in its orbit that is closest to the luminous blue variable, its powerful gravity is able to pull material from the unstable star. This sets in motion a chain of events that results in the brilliant outbursts.

As the stolen starstuff is dragged away from the wounded star and towards the compact object, it forms an accretion disk swirling around the neutron star or black hole so fast and growing so hot that it emits X-rays. These are the X-rays that Chandra saw.

It has been revealed that the X-rays are immense, energizing the surrounding cloud of material that had been ejected by the luminous blue variable years before. The cloud is heated and glows extremely brightly in visible light, creating the impression of a supernova.

"We suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays," mentioned team member Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. "The dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical.".

Calculations suggest that each year a 440 billion trillion pounds of material at minimum is stolen by the compact object, and possibly two orders of magnitude more than that. This is a huge amount, yet it is only 800 millionths of the mass of the sun, and AT 2016blu’s luminous blue variable is at least 33 times the mass of the sun.

Sources indicate that nevertheless, it is far greater than the maximum rate of material that a neutron star can safely accrete, referred to as the Eddington limit. It’s little wonder that the accretion onto the compact object unleashes such extreme energies.

AT 2016blu is also connected with another mysterious and rare astrophysical phenomenon, that of ultra-luminous X-ray (ULX) sources. The identity of whatever it is that is powering ULXs remains unclear, but the involvement of compact objects such as black holes and neutron stars is high on the list.

Industry observers note that AT 2016blu is bright enough to be considered a ULX, so could it act as a Rosetta stone connecting supernova imposters with ULXs? It’s too early to say that; only one other supernova impostor has so far been found to have X-ray emission typical of material being stolen from one star and accreting onto a compact body, and that is SN 2010da, but in that case it is known that the companion is another massive star, a red supergiant, rather than a compact object.

It has been revealed that the X-ray detection of AT 2016blu is described in a paper published on Monday (Nov. 9) in The Astrophysical Journal.

#261. After Testing Bose and Denon, I’m Convinced the Sonos Beam Ultra Is the Best Small Soundbar

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words)
General 🌐 Popularmechanics

After Testing Bose and Denon, I’m Convinced the Sonos Beam Ultra Is the Best Small Soundbar

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between its Beam and Arc Ultra soundbars, Sonos finds a new, more compact sweet spot.
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • The Sonos Beam Ultra soundbar is the whole-home audio brand’s attempt to find a middle ground in the home theater space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between its Beam and Arc Ultra soundbars, Sonos finds a new, more compact sweet spot.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The Sonos Beam Ultra soundbar is the whole-home audio brand’s attempt to find a middle ground in the home theater space. Wedged between its compact Sonos Beam and flagship Arc Ultra soundbar, the Beam Ultra sits in the middle in terms of size, power, and price.

That’s an intriguing proposition: The Beam Ultra has many of the advanced features I loved in the Arc Ultra, including Dolby Atmos with up-firing speakers and A.I.-powered speech enhancement to boost dialogue in the mix. But the Arc Ultra is made for significant TVs and carries a $1,099 price tag: It’s an upgrade for serious home theater fans with a big budget. At $699, the Beam Ultra is still a serious investment, but seems far more attainable than the tubular Arc.

And, after a few weeks of testing, I feel comfortable saying that Beam Ultra sounds more like the Arc Ultra’s little brother than a slightly bigger Beam. Its stellar audio performance, which I’ll break down shortly, deserves the Ultra name. And the Beam Ultra delivers it in a much smaller footprint than the Arc Ultra—at about 30 inches wide, it’s only 4 inches wider than the second-generation Beam, but more than a foot narrower than the Arc Ultra.

If you are a serious cinephile with the budget to upgrade, but don’t have a stand or space to accommodate a full-size soundbar, the Sonos Beam Ultra almost certainly sets a newly introduced gold standard for compact soundbars, delivering top-tier audio with minimal compromises.

In a recent development, compared to other small soundbars, the Sonos Beam Ultra has tremendous firepower behind it, which may explain why it sounds bigger than it is. It’s a 7.1.2 system, which means it has seven forward-facing speakers, a single down-firing unit, and two up-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos virtual surround sound. That’s more than the Bose Smart Soundbar (five audio drivers in a 3.0.2-channel layout) and the Denon Home 550, which I previously would’ve called the top compact options in the space.

Recent findings suggest that more audio drivers don't automatically mean better sound. Still, they do let the Beam Ultra project a wider soundstage and reduce the number of audio channels that need to be combined and condensed. The results are, in a word, powerful. It generates an impressive soundstage, simultaneously expansive and precise. It is certainly more immersive and capable than any soundbar I’ve ever considered describing as “compact.”.

At the same time, it can convey incredible nuance. The eclectic selection of music I played—from bass-heavy downtempo tracks to classical jazz albums—came through with clear separation across bass, treble, and midrange, unlike lesser-equipped alternatives from other makers. For folks who initiative to stream music from their phone, the Beam Ultra supports lossless audio files and can play them over WiFi without compression. (If you connect your soundbar to your phone via Bluetooth, you'll get some audio degradation, whether the soundbar supports lossless or not.).

The more varied your audio diet, the more vital it is to fine-tune the soundbar with EQ settings that match the music, movies, sports, or video games you’re listening to. The Sonos companion app makes it easy to swap modes or tweak settings on-the-fly, including the height of the sound from the up-firing speakers. This trick can further enhance scenes in Dolby Atmos content, especially action sequences (e.g., explosions, flying aircraft, etc.).

You can also adjust advanced features like Sonos’s signature AI-powered voice enhancement. The voice-enhancement feature, which was introduced in the Arc Ultra, works wonders when you’re watching movies or sports, cranking up the volume and clarity of dialogue amid other sounds so you can hear clearly. The feature comes with some drawbacks: Cranking up voice enhancement to “high” takes a toll on overall sound quality. I would avoid going above “medium.” This was not specific to Beam Ultra, though; I experienced similar problems with the Arc Ultra as well.

Beyond audio playback via the Sonos platform, the Beam Ultra soundbar supports Apple AirPlay 2 for streaming audio from an iPhone, a MacBook, or an iPad. Basic Bluetooth is built in, just in case, and, to my surprise, you can also connect a device directly to the soundbar via a USB-C cable.

Like the Arc Ultra soundbar, the Beam Ultra can deliver a truly private Dolby Atmos audio experience by connecting to the excellent Sonos Ace and Ace Ultra wireless headphones. The feature, known as “TV Audio Swap,” is easy to set up and works seamlessly. It allowed me to watch late-night movies and live NBA games without disturbing those around me.

Recent findings suggest that the revamped Sonos app is much better and easier to navigate than the previous edition. Its learning curve is minimal compared to before, and it brings a host of thoughtful extra touches. My favorite is the addition of Live Activities to the iOS app, which lets me access playback and volume controls directly from my iPhone’s lock screen or by long-pressing the Dynamic Island.

Industry observers note that and, as ever, one of the biggest advantages of Sonos is its modular wireless connectivity, which allows you to build out a whole-home audio system over time. A soundbar can turn into a proper surround-sound system by adding a Sonos Sub Mini and a pair of Era 100 rear surround speakers for a full private-theater sound experience. And a home theater system can turn into audio for the whole house if you add more speakers in other rooms.

There is an obvious customer for the Sonos Beam Ultra: a discerning audiophile/home theater devotee with limited space who wants to compromise on quality as little as possible. This is a noticeable upgrade over just about any compact soundbar, and it may sound better than many full-size models, too. It’s very powerful, just as acoustically proficient, and offers processing features that I generally associate with larger bars.

According to recent reports, as impressive as this is, the Arc Ultra remains the best Sonos soundbar, though. With 14 onboard audio drivers, it's simply more capable than the Beam Ultra: You’re getting similar sound, but it’s bigger, punchier, and more expressive. If you have the room, it’s the option to beat. (And Sonos specifically recommends the Beam Ultra for 65-inch TVs and smaller. If you have a 75-inch TV or larger, Beam Ultra may not meet the spec.) Ultimately, the Beam Ultra is incredibly impressive, though, and should open the door for many upgraders who want something that sounds special but can’t or don’t want to break that four-figure price barrier.

#260. Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1495 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that protein is everywhere these days.
  • Recent findings suggest that after examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that protein is everywhere these days. From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products. But while consumers are being encouraged to eat more of it, a major scientific review suggests that cutting back on protein could offer surprising benefits for health and longevity.

Recent findings suggest that after examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan. The potential benefits appear to involve several processes that influence how the body uses energy, responds to nutrients, protects cells from damage, and maintains healthy cellular function.

Recent findings suggest that the findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets. Could many people be consuming far more protein than their bodies actually need?

It has been revealed that "It's absolutely crystal clear that there are benefits of protein to muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," says Dudley Lamming, the paper's corresponding author, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences.".

Why Eating Less Protein Could Promote Longevity.

Scientists have long understood that reducing calorie intake can extend lifespan in numerous organisms. Research has also linked calorie restriction to a lower risk of diseases associated with aging, including cancer. However, consistently eating fewer calories is challenging, making it difficult for many people to maintain such a diet over time.

An alternative approach has attracted increasing scientific interest: reducing protein without necessarily eating less food.

Sources indicate that experiments involving flies and rodents have demonstrated that limiting protein intake can increase lifespan even when total calorie consumption remains unchanged. This suggests that the benefits of dietary restriction may depend not only on how much food is consumed, but also on which nutrients make up that food.

Recent findings suggest that human research has produced encouraging findings as well. Several recent clinical trials have shown that people who reduce their protein intake can lose weight, decrease body fat, and improve fasting blood sugar levels, even when they consume more calories overall. Fasting blood sugar measures glucose in the bloodstream after a period without eating and is an key indicator of metabolic health.

These findings do not establish that protein restriction extends human lifespan, but they suggest that changing protein intake can influence processes associated with aging and disease.

The Debate Over How Much Protein We Really Need.

The picture becomes more complicated when exercise and muscle health enter the equation.

Industry observers note that other studies have demonstrated that higher protein intake can support weight loss and help older adults preserve muscle mass, particularly when combined with physical activity. Maintaining muscle becomes increasingly notable with age because muscle loss can contribute to weakness, reduced mobility, and a greater risk of falls.

In a recent development, research highlighting these benefits helped motivate US authorities to revise dietary recommendations this year, encouraging daily protein consumption of 1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.5-0.7 grams per pound). That represents nearly twice the previous recommended amount.

With protein consumption reaching new highs in the United States and older adults increasingly being advised to eat more, Lamming and a colleague examined decades of research to better understand the relationship between protein intake and aging.

Recent findings suggest that their analysis brought together findings from more than 350 papers, identifying several biological mechanisms that repeatedly appeared across studies. Together, these mechanisms suggest that lowering protein consumption may improve metabolic function, alter the way cells detect nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help preserve the processes that keep cells functioning properly.

A Hormone That May Help Explain Slower Aging.

One particularly intriguing finding involves fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a hormone that becomes more abundant when dietary protein is limited.

FGF21 helps the body adjust to changes in nutrient availability and influences how energy is used. Higher levels of this hormone can increase energy expenditure, support healthier blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.

According to recent reports, these effects are especially interesting because metabolism and chronic inflammation are closely connected to aging. Over time, disruptions in these processes can contribute to conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and other age-related diseases.

It has been revealed that studies in mice have shown that animals with elevated FGF21 levels live longer than mice with normal levels. The lifespan benefit was particularly strong in males, suggesting that biological sex may influence how the body responds to this hormone.

In a recent development, researchers have also established that eating less protein increases FGF21 levels in humans. Whether this hormonal response produces the same longevity benefits seen in mice remains an key unanswered question.

How Certain Amino Acids Could Influence Aging.

Industry observers note that the amount of protein someone eats may not be the only factor that matters. The types of amino acids that make up that protein could also play an important role.

Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to produce proteins, which are essential for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues, and carrying out countless cellular functions. Beyond these basic roles, certain amino acids also act as signals that influence metabolism and cellular growth.

The review identifies three amino acids that appear especially important: methionine, isoleucine, and valine.

Sources indicate that research suggests that excessive intake of these amino acids can stimulate biological pathways that encourage growth. Although growth-related processes are essential for normal development and tissue repair, excessive or prolonged activation of certain pathways may contribute to obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.

Limiting specific amino acids could therefore produce some of the benefits observed in protein-restricted diets. This possibility has attracted attention because it suggests that the relationship between protein and longevity may be more complicated than simply eating more or less of a single nutrient.

"These studies show that the amount of protein sedentary people are eating today may have negative health consequences, at least at the population level," Lamming indicates.

Why Exercise Could Change the Effects of Protein.

The researchers emphasize that protein requirements are not the same for everyone.

According to recent reports, pregnant women, for example, need additional protein to support fetal development, while some older adults require higher amounts to help maintain muscle and physical function. People who exercise regularly may also benefit from greater protein consumption because their muscles use those nutrients to recover, repair tissue, and adapt to training.

For many adults who spend most of their day sitting, however, adding protein to everyday foods may offer little additional benefit.

Lamming points out that athletes frequently consume large amounts of protein without developing the metabolic diseases sometimes associated with protein-rich diets. One possible explanation is that physical activity changes how the body handles those nutrients.

Regular exercise stimulates muscle growth and repair, potentially allowing the body to put additional protein to productive use while reducing some of the harmful metabolic effects associated with high protein intake.

Recent findings suggest that this distinction may help explain why studies sometimes reach seemingly contradictory conclusions about protein. A diet that benefits someone who exercises intensely may not be ideal for someone with a largely sedentary lifestyle.

Rather than recommending the same amount of protein for everyone, the researchers argue that dietary advice should better reflect individual circumstances, especially physical activity levels and age.

"Recent recommendations have encouraged people to eat more protein, but they've also encouraged people to exercise more," Lamming states. "We probably need to personalize protein recommendations based not just on age, but also on how physically active people are.".

Sources indicate that the findings challenge the assumption that adding more protein automatically leads to better health. Although protein remains essential, the growing body of longevity research suggests that for some people, consuming less may offer benefits that have been overlooked in the rush toward protein-rich foods.

The work was supported by the National Institute on Aging, the Wisconsin Partnership Program, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

#259. Tech Report: These 1,500-Year-Old Warriors Were Buried With Riches. Their Wounds Paint a Darker Picture.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words)
General 🌐 Popularmechanics

Tech Report: These 1,500-Year-Old Warriors Were Buried With Riches. Their Wounds Paint a Darker Picture.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The rare cemetery could finally shed light on a shadowy era after Rome’s collapse in what is now France.
  • Recent findings suggest that archaeologists with the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (Inrap) were excavating ahead of a residential construction project near Colmar, on the banks of the Ill River in eastern France.
  • Recent findings suggest that the human burials included 11 adults or older adolescents and three children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The rare cemetery could finally shed light on a shadowy era after Rome’s collapse in what is now France.

Recent findings suggest that archaeologists with the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (Inrap) were excavating ahead of a residential construction project near Colmar, on the banks of the Ill River in eastern France. According to a translated statement, they found both a Gallo-Roman village occupied from the first to the third century C.E., and a fifth-century funerary complex containing 14 human burials and two horse burials.

Recent findings suggest that the human burials included 11 adults or older adolescents and three children. Human bone fragments found west of the necropolis suggest that more burials may lie beyond the site’s boundaries. The burial pits were typically quadrangular or trapezoidal in shape and sized to fit the person buried inside. Some of the pits were also filled with artifacts.

Those artifacts caught the archaeologists’ attention. Two graves contained high-quality goods associated with warriors, including a sword partially preserved in a wooden scabbard, a single-edged knife, a shield, and a barbed javelin. The Inrap experts mentioned the grave goods match those of Germanic chieftains, whose peoples allied with and joined the Roman army in the region near the Empire’s Rhine frontier during the fifth century.

The weapons and the clothing both featured decorative elements made of gold and silver and inlaid with garnets, further evidence of the high status of those buried.

According to recent reports, two graves associated with women also produced impressive finds, including silver-gilt bow brooches, silver bird-shaped brooches, glass-bead necklaces, belt buckles, and a bone comb. Even the horses received grave goods: harness equipment was buried with both animals.

The skeletons, however, told a grimmer story, with signs of injury and poor health found throughout the 14 burials. At least two of the deceased had fractures that were never set, and one of these likely left a man’s lower leg useless. Two other individuals had bone injuries likely caused by edged weapons. “The complete absence of perilesional bone remodeling suggests that death followed these violent acts rapidly,” the experts wrote.

The team was surprised to find so many injuries linked to violence in such a small sample of burials.

It has been revealed that the fifth-century funerary complex was the excavation’s most striking discovery, but it wasn’t the only one. The team also uncovered part of the Gallo-Roman village’s core, including a residential district and a network of streets, showing that people lived there continuously from the first to the third century C.E.

According to recent reports, human activity at the site began in the middle of the first century C.E., and the site was most densely occupied from the second into the third century. Houses built of perishable materials stood on stone footings and were arranged along a street network that changed over time. Archaeologists also found hearths and wells, along with other structures that they said may have been used for industrial work.

After the village declined, a layer of silt covered the area. The silt reveals only occasional use and little human activity through the fourth century, until the burials appeared in the fifth century.

Sources indicate that because evidence from this era is so rare, the funerary complex helps shed light on the poorly understood transition between the end of the Western Roman Empire and the Merovingian era in the Alsace region. “The exceptional nature of this find stems, in particular, from the scarcity of sites that document Germanic settlements during the specific chronological period in the region,” the statement reads. “These new findings will undoubtedly provide a fresh impetus for examining the region’s settlement dynamics, as well as the profound upheavals that shaped this territory during the second half of the fifth century.”.

#258. Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1326 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A specially engineered chewing gum could offer an unexpected newly introduced weapon against viruses and bacteria linked to head and neck cancer.
  • The findings, reported in Scientific Reports, suggest that this experimental approach could eventually help prevent certain infections and support existing cancer treatments.
  • It has been revealed that the research was led by Henry Daniell of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Dental Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A specially engineered chewing gum could offer an unexpected newly introduced weapon against viruses and bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. In laboratory tests using samples from cancer patients, researchers found that extracts from the gum reduced levels of human papillomavirus, or HPV, by as much as 93%. An enhanced version also nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species while leaving beneficial bacteria unharmed.

The findings, reported in Scientific Reports, suggest that this experimental approach could eventually help prevent certain infections and support existing cancer treatments. Researchers believe the plant-based technology could also provide a more affordable option for patients.

It has been revealed that the research was led by Henry Daniell of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Dental Medicine. His team has been exploring ways to use specially engineered plants to produce proteins with potential medical benefits.

Why Scientists Are Targeting Cancer-Linked Microbes.

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that develops in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. It begins in squamous cells, the thin, flat cells that cover many surfaces throughout the body. These cancers can be particularly difficult to treat once they have spread, and patients diagnosed at advanced stages often face poor outcomes.

According to Daniell, recently approved cancer medications have generally failed to produce major improvements in patients' quality of life or their chances of surviving five years after diagnosis. This highlights the continuing need for more effective treatments and new strategies that could help prevent the disease or reduce complications.

One promising area of research involves the microorganisms living in the mouth. Although many oral microbes are harmless or beneficial, certain viruses and bacteria have been associated with the development or progression of head and neck cancers.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers focused on three of these microbes. The first was HPV, a common virus that can cause certain cancers when infections persist. The other two were Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), bacterial species associated with oral disease and poorer outcomes in some cancer patients.

"The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies.".

Oropharyngeal cancer affects the middle portion of the throat, including areas such as the tonsils and base of the tongue. Metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has spread beyond its original location, while adjuvant treatments are additional therapies given to improve the effectiveness of primary treatment.

A Chewing Gum Made From Beans Delivers Surprising Results.

The new study builds on the team's earlier development of a chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). This gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring protein with antiviral properties.

To investigate its potential benefits, the scientists tested extracts from the gum against microbes found in oral samples collected from patients with head and neck cancer.

The results were striking. The bean gum extracts lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples and by 80% in oral rinse samples. These findings suggest that proteins delivered through a chewing gum could potentially help reduce the presence of a virus associated with certain head and neck cancers.

The team then took the technology a step further by engineering the gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Some antimicrobial peptides can attack and destroy harmful microorganisms, making them promising candidates for new infection treatments.

With this additional ingredient, the researchers found that a single dose of the engineered gum extract reduced the two targeted bacterial species, Pg and Fn, to almost undetectable levels.

Harmful Bacteria Nearly Disappear While Good Bacteria Survive.

One of the most encouraging findings was the gum's ability to target harmful bacteria without disrupting the beneficial microorganisms that naturally inhabit the mouth.

According to recent reports, the oral microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microscopic organisms living inside the mouth, plays an important role in maintaining oral health. Many of these microbes coexist harmlessly with the body and help maintain a balanced environment.

In a recent development, some cancer treatments can disturb that balance. Radiation therapy, for example, can reduce populations of beneficial oral bacteria while encouraging the growth of potentially harmful yeast, including Candida albicans.

In contrast, the experimental gum extract sharply reduced the targeted bacteria without affecting the beneficial bacterial populations examined by the researchers. This selectivity could be especially valuable for patients whose oral health has already been affected by cancer or its treatment.

It has been revealed that importantly, the results came from laboratory testing of patient samples rather than clinical trials in which people chewed the gum. Further research will be needed to determine whether the same effects occur in the human mouth and whether reducing these microbes can meaningfully improve cancer outcomes.

Could Chewing Gum Become Part of Cancer Prevention and Treatment?

The researchers believe their findings justify moving the technology toward human clinical trials, particularly because head and neck cancers remain a serious global health challenge.

It has been revealed that "Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," claims Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission.".

According to recent reports, prophylaxis refers to measures taken to prevent disease or infection before it occurs. In this case, the researchers envision a future in which specially designed chewing gum might help limit exposure to harmful microbes or reduce their levels in people already receiving cancer treatment.

Such an approach could offer a relatively simple and potentially inexpensive way to deliver protective proteins directly into the mouth, where the targeted microorganisms are found.

Sources indicate that for now, the technology remains experimental, and there is no evidence yet that chewing the gum prevents or treats cancer in humans. Nevertheless, the ability to substantially reduce HPV and nearly eliminate two cancer-associated bacterial species in laboratory tests offers a promising starting point for further investigation.

If future clinical trials confirm its safety and effectiveness, a familiar everyday product could become an unexpected addition to the medical toolkit against dangerous oral infections and cancers.

Henry Daniell is the W.D. Miller Professor in the Department of Basic & Translational Sciences at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.

Recent findings suggest that other authors are Geetanjali Wakade, Rahul Singh, and Smruti Nair of Penn Dental Medicine; Andrés M. Bur and Sufi M. Thomas of the University of Kansas Medical Center; Eri S. Srivatsan and Marilene B. Wang of the University of California at Los Angeles; and Saroj K. Basak of the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System.
