AI & Tech 🌐 Sciencedaily

Caltech robot makes history by building a structure in space

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first time, a robot has successfully assembled part of a structure in space without astronauts, demonstrating a technology that could dramatically change how large spacecraft and scientific instruments are built.
  • According to recent reports, the robotic system was developed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) with funding from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA).
  • According to recent reports, rather than relying on astronauts to connect individual pieces, the robot uses an automated arm to retrieve structural tubes and connecting joints from nearby storage dispensers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time, a robot has successfully assembled part of a structure in space without astronauts, demonstrating a technology that could dramatically change how large spacecraft and scientific instruments are built.

According to recent reports, the robotic system was developed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) with funding from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). It is part of DARPA's Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program, an initiative exploring ways to manufacture and assemble enormous structures directly in space.

According to recent reports, rather than relying on astronauts to connect individual pieces, the robot uses an automated arm to retrieve structural tubes and connecting joints from nearby storage dispensers. It then joins the components into repeating sections, called bays, that form a larger supporting framework known as a truss.

"This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space," indicates Sergio Pellegrino, the Joyce and Krent Kresa Professor of Aerospace and Civil Engineering, the Lynn Booth and Kent Kresa Department of Aerospace Leadership Chair, the executive officer for aerospace, and a senior research scientist at JPL, which Caltech manages for NASA.

A Historic Step Toward Building Giant Structures in Space.

In a recent development, pellegrino leads Caltech's Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA) demonstration. The robotic system has spent six months in orbit attempting to construct a reflector antenna measuring 1.4 meters across. Its design combines composite fiber tubes, aluminum connectors, and a lightweight reflective surface made from Kapton, a durable polymer film commonly used in spacecraft.

In a recent development, DARPA compares the assembly process to building with sophisticated versions of K'Nex or Tinkertoy construction toys. However, making a robot perform those same tasks reliably in the harsh environment of space presents a far greater engineering challenge.

The team encountered technical difficulties and scheduling constraints that prevented it from finishing the entire antenna. Nevertheless, the robot successfully assembled an initial section, providing evidence that this construction method can work in orbit. Researchers believe the same basic approach could eventually support much larger frameworks carrying enormous reflective surfaces.

The orbital experiment represents the third stage of DARPA's research program. During the first two stages, Caltech researchers developed the construction concept, worked out the engineering design, and verified its operation in laboratory experiments on Earth. The team then had less than 12 months to manufacture, test, and deliver the space hardware to Momentus Inc., the manufacturer hosting the payload.

"Developing a payload of this complexity on such a short timeline was an enormous undertaking for our small team," indicates Pellegrino, who is also co-director of the Space Solar Power Project, which aims to harvest solar power in space and wirelessly transmit it to Earth's surface. "As we wrap up the mission, we are finally able to start thinking about the new avenues of research opened by this demonstration.".

Why Scientists Want to Build Enormous Structures in Orbit.

The ability to assemble large structures directly in space could transform astronomy, communications, and space based energy systems.

For example, future telescopes could use enormous reflective surfaces to collect more light and observe extremely distant objects. Similar structures could also support powerful radio antennas, allowing scientists and engineers to build communications systems much larger than those that can presently be launched.

According to recent reports, one of the greatest obstacles is the limited room available inside a rocket's fairing, the protective enclosure that surrounds its payload during launch. No matter how ambitious a spacecraft design might be, its components must somehow fit inside that confined space.

Industry observers note that traditionally, engineers have addressed this problem in two ways. They either fold large structures into compact packages that can unfold after reaching orbit, or they launch separate components and have astronauts assemble them in space. Both approaches impose practical limits on the size and complexity of the finished structure.

Sources indicate that robotic construction offers a third possibility. Instead of fitting an enormous telescope or antenna inside a rocket, engineers could transport its materials into orbit and assemble the complete system there.

DARPA's Proposal for Kilometer-Scale Space Structures.

DARPA established NOM4D in 2022 to investigate technologies that could eventually "ferry raw materials from Earth for in-orbit manufacturing," according to the program's website.

Caltech's ASTRA experiment is one of only two projects selected to advance to the program's third phase, which involves demonstrating construction technologies in orbit.

Sources indicate that the other project, led by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, will use a module attached to the International Space Station to investigate a technique for hardening carbon tubes in space. This could provide another way to manufacture structural components without having to complete every step on Earth.

"NOM4D's objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space," said Andrew Detor, DARPA program manager for NOM4D, in a written statement. "By 'very large,' I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today.".

Such structures could eventually be several football fields long or even extend for kilometers, far beyond the dimensions of conventional spacecraft.

How Caltech's Construction Robot Reached Space.

ASTRA began its journey on March 30, 2026, when a SpaceX Transporter-16 mission introduced from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California early that morning.

The robot traveled aboard Momentus Inc.'s Vigoride 7 orbital vehicle, which carried 10 separate payloads into low Earth orbit. ASTRA occupied approximately one cubic meter of space, a compact package containing both the assembly machinery and the materials required for construction.

Sources indicate that inside were two previously assembled truss bays, reinforced with diagonal tubes and connecting joints. The payload also included a robotic arm and motorized dispensers loaded with the parts needed to construct the remaining sections.

In a recent development, the successful launch was an emotional moment for the small engineering team watching from Earth. Jaden Suh, a former Caltech postdoctoral scholar who is now an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin, was moved to tears as the spacecraft carrying his team's work headed into orbit.

"As a child, I was super curious about and interested in space structures. Just like many other engineers working in this field, sending your stuff to space is what I've been dreaming of my entire life," Suh notes. "I was extremely lucky to have the opportunity to work on this project, beginning from scratch. A lot of my original ideas are included in this system, and it was just incredible seeing it reach space.".

Building a Structure Hundreds of Miles Above Earth.

After ASTRA reached orbit, researchers began operating the system by transmitting instructions to its onboard computer through the Vigoride spacecraft.

Recent findings suggest that the initial steps involved releasing the mechanisms that had secured the components during launch. The robot then extended the two previously assembled truss bays out of the machine and proceeded to construct a third bay using the onboard assembly system.

Three team members managed the construction commands from Earth: Charles Sommer, a former Caltech systems engineer; Alan Truong, a Caltech research engineer; and graduate student Tara Venkatadri (MS '24).

Although the robot carried out the assembly operations automatically, the researchers monitored its progress using photographs transmitted from orbit. When something went wrong, they examined the images, adjusted their instructions, and attempted the operation again.

These setbacks were an important part of learning whether the technology could function outside a controlled laboratory.

"That's basically the reason you do proof-of-concept testing. There are a lot of differences in the space environment compared to down on Earth," Suh explains. "There are always lots of little surprises.".

Sources indicate that to diagnose problems in orbit, the engineers relied on a second ASTRA system kept at Pellegrino's laboratory at Caltech. This backup unit, known as a flight spare, allowed researchers to recreate difficulties encountered by the spaceborne robot and experiment with possible solutions.

"Every time we confirm there is an matter in space, we come to the laboratory and try to mimic the problem on the ground," Sommer claims.

Communication restrictions made troubleshooting especially challenging. The team could contact ASTRA only during approximately seven or eight brief periods each day, with each opportunity lasting about 15 minutes.

That meant engineers had to make the most of their limited communication windows. They used the laboratory twin to investigate problems, evaluate different solutions, and determine which adjustments were most likely to work. Once a solution was ready, they sent the revised instructions to the robot in orbit.

This process helped the team work through numerous unexpected difficulties while gathering valuable information about what future autonomous construction systems will need to operate more reliably.

ASTRA's intended construction process involves repeating a carefully coordinated series of movements.

Sources indicate that first, the robotic arm retrieves structural components from their storage dispensers. It positions the tubes and joints on an assembly plate and connects them to create a new truss bay.

According to recent reports, once the framework is assembled, the robot is designed to attach a thin reflective film containing many tiny openings. This material forms two reflective cable nets that are held under tension against one another by springs, helping the resulting surface maintain its intended shape.

The special film was jointly invented by researchers at Caltech and the University of Pennsylvania, where the collaborating team was led by Professor Igor Bargatin.

Unlike the knitted metallic mesh typically used in reflectors designed to fold and unfold, the perforated film requires less tension to maintain its shape. That allows engineers to reduce the amount of supporting structure needed, potentially making the entire assembly substantially lighter.

Lower weight is especially valuable in space engineering because every additional kilogram increases the demands placed on a launch vehicle.

When a bay is finished and its reflective components have been prepared, the robotic system pushes the completed section outward into space. It then begins assembling the next bay.

The full ASTRA antenna design calls for 11 connected bays, each attached to the reflective nets and extended outward from the assembly system.

A Small Demonstration With Enormous Implications.

Despite successfully demonstrating the construction technique, the researchers do not expect ASTRA to finish assembling all 11 bays before the mission concludes in December.

The experiment has revealed several ways the robotic hardware and assembly procedure could be simplified and improved. Even without a completed antenna, the team believes it has collected enough evidence to establish that the approach is technically feasible.

The implications extend well beyond the relatively small antenna used in this demonstration.

Future robotic construction systems could help scientists build gigantic space telescopes that collect more light, radio antennas capable of supporting advanced communications, and enormous solar arrays designed to capture sunlight in orbit.

Such solar power systems could potentially transmit collected energy wirelessly to receivers on Earth, an idea being explored through Caltech's Space Solar Power Project.

More broadly, the successful test suggests that the size of future space infrastructure may not always have to be dictated by the dimensions of the rockets used to launch its components.

"Once you get to the size limit where structures cannot be prebuilt on the ground and unfolded, you have to think about how to build them in space," Pellegrino states. "So, this work could be useful not only for astronomy and astrophysics but also for communications and other areas, such as building very large solar arrays for space solar power.".

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

According to recent reports, when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 latest alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other notable spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is at the moment around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Industry observers note that researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

According to recent reports, first, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, debuted and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

It has been revealed that thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, mentioned in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, noted in the statement.

In a recent development, in total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

In a recent development, given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the newly introduced space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins remarked. "That's a lot of science!".

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking.".

Recent findings suggest that there is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

According to recent reports, roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

According to recent reports, we have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

In a recent development, after Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome.".

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, remarked in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it.".

Recent findings suggest that NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.).

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he mentioned it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Recent findings suggest that roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.).

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us.".

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#243. The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

📅 12 Jun 2020 | ⏱️ 22 min read | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Be prepared for unexpected power failures and off-the-grid camping trips.
  • Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In a recent development, portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Be prepared for unexpected power failures and off-the-grid camping trips.

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators.

According to recent reports, portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout. Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels.

We evaluated eight power stations of varying sizes, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed their listed max output to see how well they could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.

Sources indicate that once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using its AC adapter, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

Our test team for this article includes David Dritsas, an editor who covers generators, lawn and garden, and more; Bradley Ford, an editor with more than five years of experience testing and writing about generators, generator maintenance, power tools, and lawn and garden equipment; and Tony Carrick, a frequent Popular Mechanics contributor who covers landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security.

Bluetti manages to pack a lot of power into the Elite 200 V2. It has a max output of 2,600 watts with 3,900-watt startup power and a 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, all while being relatively compact.

We hooked up a miter saw, blender, and space heater, all three of which it powered simultaneously. It easily handled the spike to 4,000 watts to start up the saw, above its listed 3,900-watt starting power, before maintaining an even flow of around 2,500 watts.

Industry observers note that the Elite 200 V2 also impressed with the quality of its battery. We recorded 92 percent of its listed 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, well over the 85 percent average for most portable power stations. It has a quick recharge time for its capacity, going from 0 to 80 percent in 81 minutes and to full in just 107 minutes. And because it uses a LiFePO4 battery, it discharges and recharges for 6,000 cycles before it drops below 80 percent capacity.

The Elite 200 V2 gives you plenty of output and input options for its size, too. Four AC outlets allow you to load up multiple appliances. There are four USB ports for charging smaller devices, a car accessory outlet, and a DC output. Along with its power cord, there’s a port for charging from a car accessory port or with up to 1,000 watts of solar panels.

With a great power-to-weight ratio, the latest version of the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is a great portable power station for powering a camper or providing backup power for the essentials.

Industry observers note that A latest and improved version of Jackery’s extremely popular Explorer 1000, the Explorer 1000 V2 features a slightly larger storage capacity, up 70 watt-hours, and a much higher 1,500-watt output—a 50 percent jump from 1,000 watts of the original. This allows you to power devices with higher loads, like an electric grill or a large microwave. Jackery managed this while maintaining the Explorer 1000’s compact size and weight, so it’s still easy to carry with you on a camping trip.

Sources indicate that the Explorer 1000 V2 features three standard 120-volt AC outlets, two USB-C ports (30- and 100-watt), one USB-A port (18-watt), and one 12-volt DC outlet. Paired with Jackery’s app, you can monitor the power station locally via Bluetooth or from anywhere when it’s connected via WiFi. The app allows for checking charge levels and estimated run time, as well as toggling any of the outputs on or off. Plugged into the wall, the power station charges in under two hours. It’s also possible to charge it from your vehicle in up to 12 hours.

Performance-wise, the 1000 V2 did well powering a 25-cubic-foot refrigerator for 18 hours and 22 minutes, which is better performance than we’ve gotten from other tested 1000-watt models. Under a constant load of 475 watts (that’s a little less than a small coffee maker), it ran for 1 hour and 57 minutes.

In a recent development, this power station offers a lot of bang for the buck. Sure, it isn’t going to power your house through a days-long outage, but it offers a lot of nice features for the price, making it one of the better values out there, especially if you pick it up on sale.

According to recent reports, what is most impressive about the Anker S2000 power station is its ability to maximize its runtime. During our testing, we were able to run a full-sized refrigerator for just over 24 hours, which is nearly six hours longer than other power stations we’ve tested with comparable capacity.

It does this using a technology that recognizes the type of device plugged in and adjusts the inverter's frequency to match the type of demand. This, in theory, helps reduce the amount of wasted power. From what we can tell, it works very well.

It has been revealed that the S2000 is fairly well equipped, too, with five outlets for AC power (two are in the back) and a bank of USB ports for home use, and can operate as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for 10-millisecond automated backup. With only 1,500 watts of output, it may struggle with some high-power appliances like a large microwave, but for many people, this station can deliver power during a blackout and keep you up and running for a long time.

In a recent development, with the Bluetti Apex 300, the name of the game is flexibility. Alone, it delivers up to 3,840 watts of continuous power and handles up to an impressive 7,680 watts of surge power. Capacity is a solid 2,764.8 watt-hours for decent runtime, though it depends on the amount of power you intend to draw from it. If you happen to have 240-volt appliances or circuits, this model has you covered, too.

It has been revealed that but everything on this power station is scalable. It’s possible to add up to six additional batteries for a very high capacity of 19,353.6 watt-hours, and connect up to two other Apex 300 units and run them in parallel. This expandability makes it a great entry-level home power station that expands into a larger backup system that delivers whole-home power.

The Apex 300 features four 120-volt outlets across the front, plus a 120-volt 30-amp outlet and a 120/240-volt 50-amp outlet on the side for powering devices individually, plugging into an RV, or delivering home power through a transfer switch.

It has been revealed that one downside for me was the lack of direct DC outputs, e.g., USB-C ports. For that, you have to purchase an optional hub. There are also power inputs for a standard AC plug, a 30-amp connection, and two solar connections. The Apex 300 uses two inverters as opposed to one, giving you two banks of 120-volt, 1,920-watt output (two outlets in each bank). We easily ran two high-powered appliances at the same time, including a space heater and a toaster, with no concerns at all.

This station is serious about solar recharging, too. There are two ports for connecting solar panels up to 1,200 watts each. Having the option of 2,400 watts of solar input is uncommon in a station of this size and price point. Plus, you can reach even higher input by pairing with a Bluetti SolarX 4K voltage regulator, which is designed for connection to larger solar arrays.

Industry observers note that most of the control options are accessed with the Bluetti Mobile app, and it’s one of the best we’ve seen. It’s easy to finely tune settings in ways that other companies don’t offer, such as adjusting the recharging level from as little as one amp to 50 amps.

If you’ve been eyeing power stations but aren’t sure if you want one more for portable power or more for home backup power, this is the model for you. It delivers a great amount of power for portable use, but lays the groundwork for building a more dedicated system in the future.

This is one of the most rugged power stations we’ve seen yet. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra features an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system and cooling structure that help keep water out of the enclosure. All work together to resist the elements better than most power stations can.

The unique cooling system was particularly interesting. A titanium alloy plate within the structure helps dissipate heat without the need for multiple fans, and eliminates the need for any side vents (typical in most power stations) that could allow droplets of water in. Meanwhile, you can remove an external plate on the bottom and dry it if water does make its way in.

The 1,800 watts of output power and 1,536 watt-hours of battery capacity are decent if you’re taking this camping for the weekend and need to recharge devices, run a low-powered small appliance or two, and plug in some lighting. But don’t expect to run something like a space heater for very long, though.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review.

The S5000 is the second power station in Anker's S-series, which features inverter efficiency technology that helps to reduce wasted energy when the inverter is idling or running lower-powered devices. We were impressed with how this technology performed in the S2000, and this model matched that performance.

According to recent reports, we ran this through several tests, and the battery efficiency proved to be around 97 percent (the industry average is around 89 percent). For example, we left the AC inverter idling for 18 hours, and the battery remained at 100 percent capacity. Meanwhile, another station we idled at the same time lost 19 percent of its available power. That was impressive.

The next most impressive attribute about the S5000 is its size. It’s at least half the size of other power stations that feature 5,000 watt-hours of capacity and includes just as many outputs, including a 240-volt, 30-amp outlet. It also has both high- and low-powered DC inputs that enable up to 3,000 watts of solar power input if you have the panels to generate that. You can also recharge at up to 4,500 watts using a direct DC connection to Anker's 5500 Smart Tri-Fuel generator.

With only 4,500 watts of total output, we wouldn’t call this a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that), but the S5000 can deliver a decent amount to power an RV, run lights and appliances during an emergency, or even a couple of critical circuits.

During our hands-on test, Goal Zero’s newest Yeti 1500 impressed us with its capable performance and sturdy construction. It’s the replacement for an older model and improves on its predecessor with improved weatherproofing, more outputs, and a better battery.

This 2,000-watt power station is clearly designed for outdoor use with an IPX4 water-resistance rating and new outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs when you’re not using them. That’s great for dusty conditions. Each section is nicely illuminated by an LED light and can be individually turned on/off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a duration of time). These additions make it perfect for camping or other outdoor uses. You can’t leave it out in the rain, but getting a bit of water on it won’t be a concern.

We loved the increased number of outputs on the Yeti 1500. There are now four 120-volt AC outlets and six USB ports: four USB-C (two are high-powered) and two USB-A ports, plus four 12-volt connections (though two of those are proprietary for Goal Zero accessories and not all that useful in our estimation). There are also inputs for AC power, 12-volt DC, and inputs for both low- and high-voltage solar power that can be used simultaneously. Theoretically, you could recharge this station with up to 900 watts of eco-friendly electrical current.

Recent findings suggest that as part of our test, we simulated a blackout at home and managed to run a cable modem/Wi-Fi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while simultaneously charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

According to recent reports, the mobile app was easy to use and chock-full of great information on energy consumption. The only problem we had was maintaining a stable Bluetooth connection. It needed to be manually paired every time we went to use it, which was annoying. Wi-Fi is available, but that’s not so useful when you are off-grid.

Recent findings suggest that we should warn you that the Yeti 1500 is heavy at 53 pounds. If you’re taking it on a trip, you’ll need a bit of strength to lug it around. That aside, the 2026 Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping, especially when there are dusty or wet conditions. We’d happily take it on our next camping trip.

Though it’s no longer EcoFlow’s flagship backup power solution, the original Delta Pro is still a massive power station with a good amount of electrical output. The brand claims it powers nearly any appliance, and after testing, we’re inclined to agree. With an output of 3,600 watts, it can handle multiple appliances, and it’s possible to bump the output to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if you need more power.

It has been revealed that in testing, we ran it with a continuous 470-watt load for 6 hours and 57 minutes, as indicated on the Delta Pro’s display. Of course, in a home backup during a power outage situation, we would run only the bare essentials to conserve power. To that end, we used it to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator, which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes.

Recharging the power station from empty using a standard 120-volt home outlet, it recharged to full capacity in 2 hours and 36 minutes. There’s also an included adapter for charging the system at EV charging stations, with solar panels (sold separately), with a car charger, or combinations of these to speed things up.

The Delta Pro’s display screen provides all the crucial information you need to manage your power consumption. We frequently checked the screen during testing to see the unit’s charge level, current load, and estimated run time at the current discharge rate.

All of this information is accessible through EcoFlow’s app, which was the most intuitive and easiest to use of those tested. We connected the app both locally using Bluetooth and remotely via Wi-Fi to monitor the power station from anywhere. We could also toggle outlets on and off remotely, which is helpful if you’re trying to manage power station output to extend the battery life.

We’ve tested the brand’s Whole-Home Backup Kit, which includes two of the power stations and a dual-voltage hub used to connect to your home service panel, via a transfer switch. We used this setup to power critical circuits in a Northeast Pennsylvania home in late winter.

The Delta Pro Whole Home Kit ran just over 24 hours, powering kitchen outlets, a full-size refrigerator, a chest freezer, a cable modem and wireless network, and a hot water boiler. Plus, having charged these two Delta Pro power stations previously, we found that they were able to hold a full charge over a full 8 months.

Testing was performed under normal usage conditions—run time could easily be extended by employing standard power-conservation strategies like lowering the thermostat, powering the fridge and freezer for four hours on and four hours off, and only opening them when absolutely necessary.

EcoFlow’s Delta Pro Whole Home Kit is a legitimate home backup system that can operate inside your home, with none of the risks or potential hassles of running a generator, such as dangerous carbon monoxide gas from exhaust fumes and dealing with fuel and oil.

A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you proposal to plug into it.

Some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds that you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.

Sources indicate that A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, if you have a power station with 2,048 watt-hour capacity, and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.

In a recent development, keep in mind that the usable watt hours are not the same as the watt hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.

These days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.

In a recent development, while all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.

Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.

Mid-size models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station, which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.

Recent findings suggest that large portable models can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.

Portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.

Industry observers note that since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.

If you’re looking for a large capacity power station that will back up critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.

Sources indicate that portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn inputs off and on and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.

According to recent reports, often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that they stay charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.

Most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, this can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or run the pump and filter on a fish tank.

Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most latest portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.

How much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.

Industry observers note that that depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

Recent findings suggest that for example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.

Some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s important to check if you blueprint on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

SpaceX has a message for itself, and for the spacecraft set to make history today (Nov. 13): Don't panic.

The manufacturer's Starship megarocket will conduct its 15th test flight this afternoon, a landmark liftoff that will feature the first-ever attempt to catch both of its stages with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), SpaceX rolled the Flight 15 upper stage, a vehicle known as Ship 42, out to the launch pad at its Starbase site in South Texas to prep. The company shared photos of the move on X, and in two of those shots we can see some intriguing words inked on the spacecraft: "Don't panic.".

The phrase is familiar to fans of Douglas Adams' sci-fi classic "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy": In the novel, the electronic guidebook that helps travelers find their way across the cosmos has "Don't panic!" on its cover.

And Ship 42 itself is connected to the beloved book, by virtue of its serial number. In "The Hitchhiker's Guide," a supercomputer named Deep Mind is asked to come up with "the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything." It thinks for 7.5 million years and comes up with "42.".

SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has voiced his affection for "The Hitchhiker's Guide" in the past — and he has already paid tribute to it with a well-placed "Don't panic.".

The debut launch of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket back in February 2018 sent Musk's red Tesla Roadster into orbit around the sun, with a spacesuit-clad mannequin named Starman at the wheel and its entertainment display programmed to read "Don't panic!".

Recent findings suggest that starship Flight 15 is scheduled to launch today during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). You can watch it here at Space.com.

If all goes according to proposal, Starship's Super Heavy first stage will come back to Starbase for a chopsticks catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

Ship 42, meanwhile, will head to orbit, a destination that Starship reached for the first time on Flight 14, which took place on Sept. 28. Ship 42 will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites today — the second batch of the spacecraft to reach orbit. (The first set of 26 were delivered on Flight 14).

Industry observers note that ship 42 will stay up for a while after that, circling Earth 14 times before coming back for its own chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after launch.

That's the proposal, anyway; SpaceX will only go through with a Ship catch attempt if all systems on the vehicle look good. If there are any problems, the company will divert to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, near either Hawaii or Chile.

Industry observers note that both of Starship's stages — Super Heavy and the Ship — are designed to be rapidly reusable. And "rapidly" is a bit of understatement: SpaceX wants to launch 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030, Musk has mentioned.

Industry observers note that the chopsticks-catch strategy is a big part of that vision. Bringing both Starship stages directly back to the launch mount will greatly reduce the time needed for inspection, refurbishment and reflight, according to SpaceX.

The firm has already caught Super Heavy on three previous Starship test flights. It has never tried to do so with Ship, instead targeting ocean splashdowns with the upper stage.

The double catch attempt may be unprecedented, but SpaceX seems to be taking its own advice: There's no panic around Flight 15 or its bold goals.

"I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," Musk mentioned last month, during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call.

#241. Breaking: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words)
Business & Policy 🌐 Sciencedaily

Breaking: After 40 years, CERN finds evidence of a one-in-10-billion particle decay

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after more than 40 years of searching, physicists at CERN have reached a major milestone in their hunt for one of the rarest known particle decays.
  • According to recent reports, the finding, announced during a seminar at CERN, marks the first time a single experiment has produced sufficient evidence for this extraordinarily rare event.
  • In a recent development, at the center of the discovery is a particle called Bd, which contains a beauty quark and a down antiquark.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after more than 40 years of searching, physicists at CERN have reached a major milestone in their hunt for one of the rarest known particle decays. Researchers working with the LHCb experiment have detected evidence of a process expected to occur only once in approximately 10 billion beauty particle decays.

According to recent reports, the finding, announced during a seminar at CERN, marks the first time a single experiment has produced sufficient evidence for this extraordinarily rare event. Beyond its rarity, the decay is particularly valuable because it could help scientists investigate particles that are too massive to be created directly in the Large Hadron Collider.

In a recent development, at the center of the discovery is a particle called Bd, which contains a beauty quark and a down antiquark. Scientists found evidence that this particle can decay into a pair of muons (μ+μ-). Muons are similar to electrons but have greater mass. The results agree with predictions from the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions, and help narrow the possibilities for new particles beyond it.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics.

One reason physicists are so interested in these unusual decays is that quantum effects allow other particles to influence how they occur. Even particles too heavy to be produced in the Large Hadron Collider can potentially leave subtle traces in the rates of these processes.

Sources indicate that by measuring extremely rare decays with high precision, researchers can look for differences between experimental results and theoretical predictions. Such discrepancies could provide indirect evidence of previously unknown particles. Generally, the rarer a decay is, the more sensitive it can be to these hidden influences.

In a recent development, the decay known as Bd → μ+μ-belongs to a special category that physicists have long considered 'golden channels' for investigating physics beyond the Standard Model. During this process, a beauty quark and an antiquark with the opposite electric charge annihilate each other. Their energy is transformed into a muon and its antiparticle.

Scientists have previously observed a related process involving a different beauty particle, called Bs. In 2015, a joint analysis by the LHCb and CMS collaborations reported the first confirmed observation of Bs → μ+μ-, along with initial evidence for the much rarer Bd decay.

However, subsequent analyses incorporating data collected through 2018 could not confirm the earlier evidence for Bd → μ+μ-. The difference in rarity is substantial. The Bs decay occurs approximately three times per billion beauty particle decays, while the Bd process is predicted to happen about 30 times less frequently.

Upgraded CERN Detector Makes the Breakthrough Possible.

A significant improvement to the LHCb experiment helped researchers overcome the enormous difficulty of detecting such a rare event.

In a recent development, following a major upgrade, the experiment began collecting data in 2024 at five times the rate achieved between 2010 and 2018. The upgraded detector also became better at identifying different kinds of particles, giving researchers a clearer picture of the activity produced during collisions.

The team combined these improvements with machine learning techniques to distinguish the exceptionally rare signals from the vast number of other particle processes. Without these advances, the events scientists wanted to study would have been overwhelmed by the background.

"Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than forty years," mentioned Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team of 19 scientists. "Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background.".

Four Decades of Searching Finally Produce Strong Evidence.

In particle physics, scientists use a statistical measure called standard deviations to evaluate how likely an apparent signal is to result from random fluctuations rather than a genuine physical process.

Industry observers note that A result must reach three standard deviations to qualify as evidence of a new phenomenon. At that level, the probability of random fluctuations producing a signal at least as statistically extreme is approximately 0.3%.

According to recent reports, using data collected during 2024 and 2025, the LHCb researchers identified evidence of Bd → μ+μ- at a significance of 3.0 standard deviations. When they combined those measurements with earlier data gathered between 2011 and 2018, the statistical significance increased to 3.2 standard deviations, exceeding the widely accepted threshold for evidence.

The same investigation also produced the most precise measurements ever obtained for the related Bs → μ+μ-decay, providing additional information about these exceptionally uncommon processes.

Recent findings suggest that although the newly introduced findings represent a major achievement, physicists have not yet reached the threshold required to declare a confirmed observation. That milestone requires a significance of five standard deviations.

If future measurements achieve that level of certainty, Bd → μ+μ-would become the rarest beauty particle decay ever observed.

Future Large Hadron Collider Upgrades Could Uncover Hidden Particles.

Researchers expect upcoming improvements to the Large Hadron Collider to make these measurements even more powerful.

The High Luminosity LHC, also known as the HiLumi LHC, is scheduled to begin operating in 2030. Another major upgrade to the LHCb experiment is planned for the middle of the following decade. Together, these developments could eventually increase the experiment's data collection rate by another factor of ten.

Collecting much larger datasets would allow physicists to detect more of these extremely rare decays and measure their properties with greater precision. That increased sensitivity could make it possible to identify subtle effects associated with particles that remain beyond the direct reach of existing accelerators.

"Seeing evidence of this rare decay is incredibly exciting, opening up newly introduced possibilities to probe beyond the direct reach of the LHC," explained Harry Cliff, LHCb's Rare Decays Convener and Analysis Co-lead.

"The future LHCb upgrade will allow us to observe many more of these decays, providing even greater sensitivity to undiscovered particles.".

Sources indicate that for physicists who have pursued this elusive signal for more than four decades, the fresh evidence represents a long-awaited advance. It also offers a promising way to investigate whether the known laws of particle physics are part of a much larger picture.

#240. Why Aging Stars Suffer A Sudden Luminosity Dip

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words)
General 🌐 Universetoday

Why Aging Stars Suffer A Sudden Luminosity Dip

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Universetoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • From a naked eye perspective, stars are stable and predictable.
  • Powerful telescopes bring millions of stars of different types and ages into view.
  • As low-mass stars like the Sun exhaust their hydrogen supplies and evolve, they become Red Giant Branch (RGB) stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From a naked eye perspective, stars are stable and predictable. Not much goes on but shining. The Sun itself is fairly plane and nondescript and will shine relatively steadily for billions of years. It's considered a low-mass star compared to the most massive stars, which are rarer and contain many times its mass.

Powerful telescopes bring millions of stars of different types and ages into view. Astrophysicists and astronomers watch the Sun and its low-mass brethren, and note changes in their shining, just as they do all types of stars. Their observations reveal the changes stars experience during their long lifetimes.

As low-mass stars like the Sun exhaust their hydrogen supplies and evolve, they become Red Giant Branch (RGB) stars. This is not only theoretical, it's an observational conclusion. RGB stars are easy to observe and study for two reasons: they're bright, and they're numerous. Arcturus, Aldebaran, and Pollus are all bright, naked-eye stars and are all RGB stars. (Well-known Betelgeuse is a Red Supergiant, not quite the same.).

Industry observers note that as RGB stars age and cool, they swell in size and become more luminous. It's a pretty steady change. But for some reason, there's a brief and abrupt dip in their brightness known as the RGB luminosity bump. The bump is called that because of how it appears in the colourâmagnitude diagrams of stellar clusters.

Astrophysicists know why the bump ends. But what initiates the bump is still unexplained. Astrophysicists don't like this gap in their knowledge and they've been trying to fill it in.

Industry observers note that newly introduced research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters has an explanation for the bump. It's titled "The Role of Specific Entropy in the Onset of the Luminosity Bump," and the sole author is Saskia Hekker. Hekker is a Professor of Theoretical Astrophysics and the Group Leader of the Theory and Observations of Stars Group at the Heidelberg Institute for Theoretical Studies.

"During their evolution, stars follow a distinct path in luminosityâtemperature space. Low-mass stars that have exhausted hydrogen in their core follow the so-called red-giant branch (RGB), which is predominantly in the direction of increasing luminosity and decreasing surface temperature," Hekker explains. "The luminosity bump is a temporary decrease in luminosity against this otherwise increasing trend.".

The inset grey box is the Hertzsprung-Russel diagram for a 1 solar mass star progressing from the subgiant branch to the tip of the Red Giant Branch. The tiny grey box inside it is magnified in the larger part of the image, highlighting the RGB luminosity bump. Image Credit: S. Hekker 2026 ApJL 1008 L61.

The bump is understood theoretically and also confirmed with observations. But there's one discrepancy between theory and observation. In models, the bump appears at higher luminosities than the observed bump, meaning it appears later. "To understand why the bump appears later in the models than in observations, the physics of the bump needs to be unravelled," Hekker writes.

Industry observers note that stars, including our Sun, are layered, and RGB stars are no exception. But unlike the Sun, RGB stars have exhausted the hydrogen in their cores, and most of what's left is in their envelopes. Since the core has exhausted its hydrogen by fusing it into helium, the core is inert helium. An RGB's fusion occurs in a thin shell. In both these regions, energy is transported via radiation.

Above this radiative region is a convective outer envelope.

In a recent development, as an RGB star ascends the branch, the core contracts and the surface expands. Since the core is inert helium, it exerts no outward pressure and is forced inward. "This causes the deepest layer of the convective envelope to move inwards, reaching layers that have changed their chemical composition due to (burning) processes earlier in the evolution of the star," Hekker explains.

This is when dredge-up occurs, as deeper layers are forced into the convective zone. Since the convective zone is convective, the material from the radiative zone mixes into the convective zone, changing its composition.

Now there's a situation where there's a shifting boundary deep inside the star called the Base of the Convective Zone (BCZ). It's organized around a thermodynamic property called specific entropy. It basically measures how disordered the gas is at the BCZ. As the BCZ moves deeper inside the star, the entropy difference across the boundary shrinks. Past a certain point, entropy across the boundary layer drops past a critical value, and that triggers the luminosity bump.

This diagram demonstrates the interior of an RGB star (not to scale). An inert helium core is in the center, and it's contained in a thin hydrogen-burning shell. Above that is a radiative zone separated from the star's convective envelope by the base of the convective zone (BCZ). Earlier dredge-up and mixing created this boundary between helium-enriched and hydrogen-rich gas. This work ties the RGB luminosity bump to this boundary. The author argues that the onset of the bump occurs when the entropy across this boundary crosses a critical value. (Image Generated with AI).

Industry observers note that previous explanations for the bump rested on mechanics. In those explanations, the thin hydrogen-burning shell reaches the boundary and something inside the star changes, triggering the bump. In this explanation, the bump happens when an entropy threshold is crossed inside the star's thermodynamics. It's not simply that layers meet.

In a recent development, we can't see inside stars. Astrophysicists use physics to try to understand what's going on there, and they test those physics against the only part of the star they can really see, the outside. It's a constant back and forth to refine theories until they match observations.

âThis succinct explanation of the onset of the bump, is the first quantitative description proposed so far,â remarked Hekker.

This new work will make its way into the larger body of astrophysical theory.

Sources indicate that "This viable description of the mechanism behind the onset of the bump provides crucial and fresh insights for the exploitation of the bump as an anchor point in stellar evolution theory," Hekker writes. "Such added knowledge of the onset of the bump could potentially be used to make more informed choices for changes to the physics in stellar models that go beyond calibration of the overshoot, to place the bump in stellar evolution models at the correct luminosity while at the same time aligning them with measured surface abundances.".

If you’re looking for an efficient way to heat your home during the cold winter months, pellet stoves offer several advantages over wood stoves or fireplaces.

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The novelty of a wood burning fireplace wears off when you have to trudge outside to grab a bundle of logs. Installing a wood burning stove can be expensive, and once it’s running, it produces ash that needs to be cleaned out. Pellet stoves, however, are an efficient, convenient option for heating a room while appreciating the glow of a live fire.

Powered by compressed hardwood pellets stored in a hopper that can hold over 100 pounds, pellet stoves can provide a fire that burns for dozens of hours without needing to be tended. Those pellets drop into a combustion chamber where they are burned to produce heat. Exhaust is then vented through a flue pipe out a sidewall or your roof.

Sources indicate that A pellet stove offers consistent, reliable heat without a lot of fuss. More expensive models will cost several thousand dollars, but often come with programmable digital thermostats and larger hoppers that allow a fire to burn longer without the need for additional pellets being added.

In a recent development, wood stoves require a bit more effort and knowledge—you’ll have to learn about the different burn rates of wood and clean out ash more regularly. Still, wood burning stoves are typically quieter and may last longer than pellet stoves because they don’t have electronic components.

As for installation, freestanding pellet stoves need an available outlet with an open plug and a vent to the outside, which may require the installer to cut a hole in the wall. If your power goes out often during storms, that means your pellet stove won’t work without a generator or separate power source. Pellet stoves that insert into your fireplace require a chimney liner, a pipe that vents gas outside.

It has been revealed that pellet stoves are designed to warm up everything from your patio to your rec room. Different models can stand on their own, be mounted to the wall, or inserted into a fireplace. Here are the 10 best pellet stoves to buy now that bring the heat.

It offers a large window where you can watch the fire burning inside. With a 55-pound hopper, the ash from the fire falls down into a removable pan that only needs to be emptied every 2 weeks. The stove offers five power settings, and on the lowest setting, you can get up to 20 hours of continuous heat.

The PelPro Pellet Stove is an efficient option that gives you plenty of heat for your buck. The EPA-certified stove has a large hopper (the manufacturer says the stove can run for 40 hours before needing to be reloaded) and convenient features like an automatic ignition at a lower price point.

The main compromises are a manually controlled dial thermostat and only a 1-year warranty on parts.

The stove has a three-sided bay window that makes it a great focal point for your living space, and it can heat up to 2,500 square feet. It has a large hopper that can hold up to 66 pounds of pellets, providing a long run time between refills, and the unit’s quiet blower won’t disturb your family while it’s running.

In a recent development, one of the downsides of pellet stoves is they require electricity to operate their augers and inner fans, and this means you’re left without heat when the power goes out. However, this pellet stove from US Stove Company is one of the few designed to work without electricity. Instead, it uses a gravity-fed hopper and manual start.

If you’re hoping to heat a large area or even your whole house, this pellet stove can warm up to 3,000 square feet when temperatures are mild.

The EPA-certified stove has a unique heat exchanger design and powerful blower that help to produce maximum heat from pellets, and there are five power settings and a programmable thermostat that let you adjust the warmth to your liking.

On the lowest setting, the 51-pound hopper has enough fuel to run for up to 19 hours, and the stove is reasonably priced considering its high heat output.

The Ashley Pellet Space Saver Stove is like a genie in a bottle—lots of power in an itty bitty living space. With a small profile thanks to thoughtful curves and an efficient design, this steel stove can heat up to 2,200 square feet for 32 hours.

Adjust the temperature and heat output via remote control and the side panels pop off for maintenance. A large glass window lets you enjoy a lovely view of the fire.

Industry observers note that if you don’t have space for a freestanding pellet stove, this unique model can be mounted to your wall instead. It’s ideal for spaces up to 1,000 square feet and has a direct vent design that doesn’t require the traditional chimney installation.

Industry observers note that I’ve worked with pellet grills and wood stoves to get through Midwest winters, so I know the differences and potential benefits of different stoves. Also, I delved into message boards and talked with pellet stove owners to understand what was frustrating and what was delightful about owning one.

Recent findings suggest that I also weighed the cost and size of each model, as well as the warranty. Finally, I relied on some of the previous research done for this article by writer Camryn Rabideau. Here are the 10 pellet stoves that will warm your heart and your living room.

A pellet stove can be a significant investment—multiple thousands of dollars to cover the stove and installation—so it’s key that you find one that fits your room and heats it efficiently.

Pellet stoves come in three main styles: freestanding, wall mounted, and insert. A freestanding stove—which can be larger or more powerful than the other options—evokes a classic cabin feel and sits on the ground or on feet. A wall-mounted stove hangs free of the floor and kicks out heat like the heads of a mini split. Inserts are meant to slot inside your fireplace and could take a non-functioning fireplace and make it a focal point of your room once again.

More Cozy Options to Consider: Best Electric Fireplaces • Best Space Heaters • Best Heated Blankets.

It has been revealed that pellet stoves are efficient, producing less creosote (the tarry byproduct of burning wood) and ash than wood stoves. The compact pellets—thanks to their small size and low moisture content—burn hot and rapidly. Pellet stoves that receive certification from the United States Environmental Protection Agency typically offer between 70 and 83 percent fuel efficiency. In some cases, certification comes with a tax credit so check before you purchase a given model.

Pellet stoves often have multiple settings. Higher settings release more pellets so the stove can burn hotter, whereas the lowest setting will enable you pellets to last longer, but you might not get as much heat. A stove with a smaller hopper running outdoors may only last 6 hours per full hopper, like the Even Embers Pellet Stove, which is fine if you’re looking to gather in the backyard at night. Larger pellet stoves can burn unattended for more than a day, like the PelPro Pellet Stove which can run for 40 hours.

Industry observers note that the larger the hopper, the longer the burn time, and the longer you can go between pellet refills. Most hoppers will need to be refilled once a day. But larger hoppers (60 pounds and up) typically mean bigger stoves, so you’ll have to consider whether or not it will fit your space. Likewise, it can be cumbersome to pour heavier bags—50 pounds at a time—into the hopper.

In a recent development, the heating ability of pellet stoves is measured in British Thermal Units (BTUs) per hour. The higher the BTUs, the easier it will be for a stove to heat a room or multiple rooms. If you’re considering heating multiple rooms or a whole home, a pellet stove rated at 60,000 BTUs can heat approximately 2,000 square feet.

Warranties typically cover parts and repairs for several years. A well-maintained pellet stove should last longer than the warranty—a decade or more if properly maintained; but it’s a comfort to have some financial coverage in the first few years after investing a decent amount of money in a pellet stove.

Empty your ash pan and clean the firebox once or twice a week. If your pellet stove has baffles, clean them every few months. And you’ll need to do a deep clean of the venting probably once a year.

Check your manual for the specific instructions, but cleaning can follow a simple rule—if you see ash build up, clean it out once your stove has cooled.

Recent findings suggest that pellet stoves heat up swiftly—it’s one of their best features. They’ll be raising the temperature of your room often inside of 30 minutes.

Pellets may be more expensive; but they’re convenient. Pellets take up less space and produce less ash than firewood. Wood stoves can be used for cooking (even if it’s just s’mores) and require tending that you’ll either see as a nice part of the ritual or a chore that you’d rather not do.
