#238. Tech Report: NASA reveals bold new proposal to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1446 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Tech Report: NASA reveals bold new proposal to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA has revealed new details about its accelerated effort to return American astronauts to the Moon in 2028.
  • During an October 23 briefing, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders outlined the next steps for the Artemis program.
  • The announcement builds on priorities introduced earlier this year through NASA's Ignition initiative.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA has revealed new details about its accelerated effort to return American astronauts to the Moon in 2028. The updated strategy includes testing two competing lunar landers, streamlining rocket preparations, and introducing a lighter spacesuit to help make the first moonwalks possible sooner.

During an October 23 briefing, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders outlined the next steps for the Artemis program. The revised approach centers on two major missions: Artemis III, a test flight scheduled for 2027, and Artemis IV, which is intended to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

The announcement builds on priorities introduced earlier this year through NASA's Ignition initiative. Agency officials also highlighted recent progress in spacecraft development, mission preparations, and partnerships with private aerospace companies. These efforts are intended to reduce technical risks, accelerate the schedule, and establish the foundation for a lasting American presence on the Moon.

"This is a very energized NASA, and these updates are only a small part of that story. We are bringing extreme focus to the mission to ensure delivery of world-changing outcomes as quickly, safely, affordably, and successfully as possible," mentioned Isaacman. "NASA is driving outcomes to make Moon missions a reality, and we're not waiting for others to bring their looks to us -- the campaign must move with urgency as strategic competitors pursue a permanent presence beyond Earth.".

Artemis III Will Test Two Lunar Landers in Earth Orbit.

It has been revealed that before attempting another crewed Moon landing, NASA prepares to conduct a major rehearsal in Earth orbit. The Artemis III mission will bring together NASA's Orion spacecraft and experimental lunar landers developed by SpaceX and Blue Origin.

Four astronauts will travel aboard Orion, launching on NASA's powerful SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. During the planned 14-day mission, the crew will practice rendezvous and docking procedures with both companies' lander test vehicles. Rendezvous involves guiding two spacecraft to meet in orbit, while docking allows them to connect so astronauts can move between vehicles.

These demonstrations are designed to verify important spacecraft capabilities before Artemis IV attempts to carry astronauts to the Moon's surface.

The tests will take place in a carefully planned sequence. Blue Origin will first launch a test version of its Blue Moon lander into Earth orbit. NASA will then send Orion and its four astronauts into space aboard the SLS rocket, where Orion will rendezvous and dock with the Blue Moon vehicle.

According to recent reports, next, SpaceX will launch a test version of its Version 3 Starship lunar lander. Orion will separate from Blue Moon and perform another docking maneuver, this time with Starship. By testing both systems during a single crewed mission, NASA aims to gather essential operational experience while reducing uncertainties before the 2028 landing attempt.

NASA Cuts Rocket Preparation Times and Costs.

Recent findings suggest that the latest mission details follow other recent Artemis progress reports. According to NASA, the hardware needed for Artemis III remains on schedule, and improvements in processing have reduced preparation timelines by approximately 50%.

In a recent development, the agency also reported a significant engineering achievement involving a critical rocket fuel-line component. Rather than relying on an outside supplier, NASA engineers redesigned, manufactured, and tested the component themselves in just five months. The work cost roughly one-tenth of an earlier estimate from an external vendor.

"NASA should be expected to do this kind of work, and we have some of the best technical knowledge in the world on rocket hardware and operations to do it," stated Jeremy Parsons, the agency's Artemis program manager. "It's an example of how we are rebuilding our core competencies and developing centers of excellence in technical functions instead of continuing to outsource expertise.".

The improvements reflect NASA's broader effort to strengthen its internal engineering capabilities, shorten development schedules, and reduce the cost of preparing missions for launch.

SpaceX and Blue Origin Offer Different Paths to the Moon.

Industry observers note that for Artemis IV in 2028, NASA intends to launch astronauts aboard Orion using the SLS rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Once in space, the crew will rely on a lunar landing system developed by either SpaceX or Blue Origin to reach the Moon's surface.

It has been revealed that both companies have revised their original mission designs to make operations simpler, more efficient, and more adaptable. Although they share the same objective, their approaches to transporting astronauts to the lunar surface differ considerably.

SpaceX intends to use its Starship spacecraft, which will take on additional propellant while orbiting Earth. After refueling, Starship will meet Orion and carry the spacecraft toward the Moon. Refueling in orbit is an crucial part of SpaceX's strategy because it allows the vehicle to receive the propellant needed for its journey after leaving the launchpad.

It has been revealed that blue Origin is developing a different approach using its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander. Its initiative calls for additional propulsion stages in Earth orbit to send the lander toward the Moon. The lander will then meet Orion in a relatively low lunar orbit before carrying astronauts down to the surface.

Both companies are working toward having their systems ready to support a crewed Moon landing in 2028. Maintaining two potential landing systems gives NASA greater flexibility as development and testing continue.

NASA Explores New Rocket Options for Artemis IV.

NASA is also considering two possible upper stages for the SLS rocket used on Artemis IV. An upper stage is the portion of a rocket that provides additional propulsion after the earlier stages have completed their work, helping send a spacecraft toward its destination.

According to recent reports, one option is the interim cryogenic propulsion stage already used by SLS. The other is an extended version of United Launch Alliance's Centaur V upper stage, which would hold additional propellant.

Recent findings suggest that by developing both possibilities, NASA hopes to preserve flexibility in its launch aims and avoid becoming dependent on a single technical solution. Having alternatives could help the agency respond to engineering challenges without jeopardizing the broader Moon landing schedule.

A New Lightweight Spacesuit Could Speed Up Moonwalks.

Another important change involves the spacesuits astronauts will wear while exploring the lunar surface.

NASA is working with Axiom Space on a second, lighter design known as the "Sortie suit." The new suit is intended specifically for the first Moon surface excursions and weighs approximately half as much as Axiom's larger primary spacesuit.

The lighter design could simplify preparations for the earliest landing missions and help astronauts begin exploring the lunar surface sooner.

In a recent development, however, the Sortie suit is not intended to replace the primary design. Axiom's more capable suit will remain part of NASA's aims for future missions that require longer periods outside the spacecraft and more demanding surface activities.

Building a Permanent Human Presence on the Moon.

NASA's ambitions extend well beyond returning astronauts to the lunar surface for a single mission.

Industry observers note that as the Artemis program advances, the agency intends to send crews on increasingly challenging expeditions near the Moon's South Pole. This region is an important focus of future lunar exploration, and the missions are designed to expand how much of the Moon humans can investigate directly.

NASA describes the effort as part of a new Golden Age of innovation and exploration. The agency expects its lunar missions to support scientific discoveries, generate economic benefits, and encourage the development of technologies needed for more ambitious space exploration.

Ultimately, the goal is to establish an enduring human presence on the Moon rather than repeat the brief visits of earlier lunar expeditions. The experience gained from operating spacecraft, supporting astronauts, and carrying out increasingly complex missions on the lunar surface will also help NASA prepare for another historic objective: sending the first astronauts to Mars.

A upcoming study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

Recent findings suggest that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Recent findings suggest that obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

In a recent development, "BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a newly introduced study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the latest findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

According to recent reports, additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

Sources indicate that the proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.).

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," remarked Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in Newly introduced Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the fresh study.

In a recent development, under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," stated Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the upcoming criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the latest criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang noted. She noted potential challenges in implementing both upcoming aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

In a recent development, providers also may struggle with the fresh distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

It has been revealed that rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

Industry News: First Direct Measurement of Cosmic Hydrogen Could Change How We Map the Universe

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Advances in computing and astronomy have led to increasingly complex attempts to chart the large-scale structure of the Universe.
  • According to recent reports, today, it remains the most abundant element in the Universe and can be found everywhere - the interstellar medium (ISM) and the intergalactic medium (IGM) - in abundance.
  • The MeerKLASS (MeerKAT Large Area Synoptic Survey) Collaboration is an international group of astronomers conducting cosmological surveys using the MeerKAT radio telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Advances in computing and astronomy have led to increasingly complex attempts to chart the large-scale structure of the Universe. For the past decade, scientists have been working to map one aspect in particular to see whether it matches observations of the cosmic web: cosmic hydrogen. Between 380,000 and 1 billion years after the Substantial Bang, neutral hydrogen was the most common element in the Universe, a period (known as the "Cosmic Dark Ages"), and provided the feedstock for stars, galaxies, and the cosmic web.

According to recent reports, today, it remains the most abundant element in the Universe and can be found everywhere - the interstellar medium (ISM) and the intergalactic medium (IGM) - in abundance. For the past decade, scientists with the MeerKLASS Collaboration have been trying to measure how neutral hydrogen "clumps" in the distant Universe. In a study published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), the team declared the first direct measurement of the large-scale structure of cosmic hydrogen.

The MeerKLASS (MeerKAT Large Area Synoptic Survey) Collaboration is an international group of astronomers conducting cosmological surveys using the MeerKAT radio telescope. Their survey relies on a technique known as HI intensity (or 21-cm intensity) mapping to detect the combined emissions of galaxies within large segments of the sky. This enables the creation of 3D maps of the cosmos that show the distribution of matter (gas, dust, stars, galaxies, clusters, etc.) in the cosmic web.

Recent findings suggest that members of the MeerKLASS collaboration at their biannual 'Busy Week' meeting, hosted at the University of Torino in September 2025. Credit: SARAO.

Recent findings suggest that this is no easy task, since the 21-cm signal must be extracted from all the other emissions of the Universe (the "foreground noise"), which are about 10,000 times stronger than the hydrogen signal itself. To accomplish this, the team chose to operate each dish in the array as an independent telescope, rather than combining all 64 dishes into a single interferometer. This was an entirely new observation mode for MeerKAT that traded sharp angular resolution for very high survey speed.

In a recent development, for their survey, the team analyzed data collected by the MeerKAT array across ~250 square degrees of sky. This enabled the detection of a neutral hydrogen signal that originated 4.5 billion years ago (or 9 billion years after the Substantial Bang). The team's measurements produced many independent maps from different dishes and observing times. These were then cross-compared to suppress individual instrument effects and reinforce the structure of cosmic hydrogen.

Their results showed that cosmic hydrogen mirrors the large-scale structure of the cosmic web, advancing a technique that could transform how cosmologists map the Universe. Dr Steven Cunnington, a Senior Research Fellow at Purdue University's Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation, led the development of the analysis pipeline that enabled the mapping of cosmic hydrogen. Since 2015, he has also co-led one of the working groups within the MeerKLASS Collaboration.

As he expressed in a University of Portsmouth release:.

Sources indicate that this result feels particularly special because it's the culmination of a journey that began when I started my PhD at Portsmouth over a decade ago. I am now fortunate to be part of a much wider international collaboration sharing this common goal. Many of the challenges addressed in this work have shaped my own research career, so seeing our team deliver this measurement is a remarkable milestone to witness.

This slice of the DESI data maps celestial objects from Earth (center) to billions of light-years away, showing nearby bright galaxies (yellow), luminous red galaxies (orange), emission-line galaxies (blue), and quasars (green). Credit: DESI Collaboration/DOE/KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/C. Lamman.

It has been revealed that this information can be used to constrain the most pressing cosmological measurements facing scientists today. This includes the expansion rate of the cosmos (the Hubble-LemaÃ®tre Constant), the influence of Dark Energy, and the distribution of Dark Matter. Stated Professor MÃ¡rio Santos, Principal Investigator of the MeerKLASS survey at the University of the Western Cape:.

This is a milestone in establishing 21-cm intensity mapping as a novel tool for cosmology. This measurement took a decade of patient work by researchers spread across seven countries and three continents - and many of them are early-career scientists who have spent their whole career on this project. Such an ambitious result requires sustained and genuine teamwork from many people. And none of it would exist without the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory, which built and operates MeerKAT and helped sort out the many challenges with this survey along the way. It is a reminder that science at this level is a large collaborative effort.

Here are the most vital things to keep in mind while shopping:.

There is all manner of exotic formulae for determining the exact distance you should sit from a large screen TV—X-times the screen height, X-times the screen’s diagonal size—but there isn’t a right or wrong answer. The best rule of thumb is if the screen fills your frame of vision from where you’re sitting, and you don’t have to turn your head to see one side of the screen or the other, you’re fine. (Note: Sitting too close to a 4K TV won’t ruin your eyes despite what your mother may have told you.).

Sources indicate that what size TV you choose, however, may be predetermined by your room geography and/or furnishings, such as the interior of an existing TV cabinet, or dictated by a spouse’s objections to a larger-size set. If you plan to buy a new TV larger than your current set, measure the width, height, and depth of your home’s TV space, and then check the actual width and height of the TV with stand, not the diagonal screen size. A flat panel 65-inch screen 4K TV usually measures less than 60 inches wide, less than 36 inches tall, and about 15 inches deep with the stand.

In a recent development, planning to hang your TV on a wall? All TVs follow a version of the VESA (Video Electronics Standards Association) wall-mounting standard, including variations such as VESA MIS-D, MIS-E, and MIS-F, which mainly address a TV’s rear mounting-hole spacing, supportable weight, and size.

A VESA wall mounting kit can work with virtually any wall-mountable TV, but double-check your TV’s specifications to confirm any VESA variation.

Industry observers note that A 4K TV’s display is composed of 3840 x 2160 pixels, but that’s only the screen resolution. A dizzying array of screen technologies creates different levels of stunning 4K images. These technologies include:.

Recent findings suggest that A TV screen's image speed is measured by its refresh rate, expressed in hertz (Hz). This equals frames flashed per second; for comparison, movie film is projected at 24 frames per second, while Normal TV broadcasts refresh at 60 Hz, or 60 frames per second.

If you’re a heavy gamer, you want a display that more accurately reflects the eye-blinking speed of the animated action, which means you’ll want a TV with a refresh rate of at least 120 Hz or higher, and a set equipped with VRR (variable refresh rate), which automatically adjusts the refresh rate depending on the content being displayed.

Industry observers note that another screen technology gamers want is low latency, or input lag, which is how swiftly the display responds when you push a button on your controller or joystick. Many higher-end TVs include Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), which automatically switches your TV to a faster, more responsive mode measured in milliseconds (ms).

It has been revealed that yes, but you only need to concern yourself with the types your 4K TV includes. Nearly all bigger-screen 4K TVs are equipped with a type of HDR (high-dynamic range) that creates visibly punchier, higher-contrast images when viewing 4K content from Blu-ray or streaming channels.

Different HDR versions include the standard and most common HDR, as well as the more specialized HDR-10, HDR-10+, Dolby Vision, and HLG (Hybrid Log Gamma), designed to deliver HDR benefits to lower non-4K broadcast, cable, and satellite TV fare.

While there are subtle visual benefits associated with each type of HDR, and while some TV makers, 4K Blu-ray producers, and streaming channels opt to deploy some HDR versions but not others, compatibility really isn’t an issue since all include a plain and widely compatible HDR version.

Bottom line: Any set featuring any type of HDR will produce a visibly better 4K picture than a set without HDR.

In a recent development, 8K TV makers may not want to hear this, but probably never. 8K TVs offer a display with a resolution of 7,680 x 4,320 pixels, or 33 million pixels, more than four times the 8 million pixels that comprise a 4K TV display.

Prices are coming down to near 4K TV price levels for 8K models. But, for a variety of reasons, there is no existing 8K content—no 8K broadcast or cable, no 8K streaming, no 8K Blu-ray—and there isn’t likely to be for the foreseeable future.

Industry observers note that the only benefits of an 8K TV are via upscaling or up-conversion of lower-resolution programming to 8K. But realistically you’ll need at least a 75-inch TV to appreciate the difference between 4K and 8K.

Imagine watching the movie "Jaws" without feeling that "bum-bum, bum-bum" bass in your gut, or not being able to understand character dialogue over a swelling orchestral passage, or subtle sounds that lend a dramatic scene its key ambience.

A 4K TV may produce excellent picture quality, but most do not produce equally excellent sound, which can dull or ruin your viewing experience. There is a fix for this. Instead of relying on a TV’s poor audio, you may want to pair your 4K TV with a soundbar via an ARC (Audio Return Channel) or eARC (enhanced Audio Return Channel) HDMI connection.

An ARC-compatible soundbar connected to a TV via an ARC HDMI jack lets you control your TV’s picture and sound with a single remote, as if the soundbar were your TV’s speaker.

Just make sure to measure the space between your TV tabletop and the bottom of the TV display area so your prospective soundbar won’t block either the screen or the TV’s IR remote control sensor.

#234. Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising latest approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China.
  • In a recent development, the findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system.
  • How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising latest approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

In a recent development, the findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis.

Industry observers note that at the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Industry observers note that dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

It has been revealed that "Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," notes Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored.".

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis.

In a recent development, the researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

Industry observers note that when the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

According to recent reports, vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

Recent findings suggest that this connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

The team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang indicates.

Common Supplement Indicates Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial.

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

Sources indicate that however, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

It has been revealed that "Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang claims. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases.".

#233. Industry News: ALMA Reveals a Jet of Cool Gas from a Microquasar

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1191 words)
General 🌐 Universetoday

Industry News: ALMA Reveals a Jet of Cool Gas from a Microquasar

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Universetoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there's a strange gamma-ray emitter in the Large Magellanic Cloud that has astronomers stumped about its source.
  • So, a research team from two Japanese universities decided to give the object, called LMC P3, a closer look.
  • In a recent development, according to astronomer Yasuo Fukui of Nagoya University, who worked with team leader Bhuvana Gadikere Rajendra of Gifu University, what they detected at LMC P3 is unusual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there's a strange gamma-ray emitter in the Large Magellanic Cloud that has astronomers stumped about its source. It lies within the ashes left behind by a supernova that created a compact object that's part of the system. The supernova remnant provides a piece of evidence to explain the emissions, but not the whole story.

So, a research team from two Japanese universities decided to give the object, called LMC P3, a closer look. Instead of tracking the gamma rays, they looked at the object with the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile. This is a series of radio telescopes that provide highly detailed radio views of objects in the sky. ALMA focused on radio emissions from carbon monoxide (CO) molecules in proximity to the cold cloud in the area around LMC P3. It's one of the few such objects found outside the Milky Way, and astronomers have dubbed it a microquasar. It consists of a giant O-type star and a compact object that could be explained by the existence of a black hole or a neutron star.

In a recent development, according to astronomer Yasuo Fukui of Nagoya University, who worked with team leader Bhuvana Gadikere Rajendra of Gifu University, what they detected at LMC P3 is unusual. âWe discovered a gigantic molecular jet,â stated Fukui. The jet consists of molecular gas that stretches out across 26 light-years of space. For reference, the bright star Vega lies 25 light-years away from us, so the jet would connect us and that star quite easily.

According to recent reports, the strange thing is, the molecular jet itself is cold (by our standards), but astrophysically "heated" to a temperature of about 35 to 60 Kelvin. By comparison, that's warmer than the 15 Kelvin surrounding gas but still very cold. That temperature difference means that the gas is interacting with another jet— this one a high-energy stream of particles coming from the nearby compact object with enough energy to power gamma-ray emissions. The object turns out to be a micro-quasar, which would have the energy to do the job.

Micro-quasars are interesting objects. They actually consist of two objects: a stellar-mass black hole or neutron star coupled with a companion star. The black hole constantly sucks material from the star, and that creates a swirling accretion disk around the black hole. It's a fairly energetic interaction that leads to X-ray and gamma-ray emissions. It also creates high-speed jets that travel out at nearly light-speed velocities. They're called micro-quasars because they're a smaller type of quasar, which is a highly active region around a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy.

Industry observers note that fukui noted the relatively high temperature observed over a large fraction of the molecular cloud makes it a very strong case that the gas is interacting with a high-energy jet coming from the compact object â precisely the kind of jet that can also power LMC P3âs gamma rays. This also provides a boost to the idea that the object is a black hole, leftover from the collapse of a supermassive star in a supernova explosion.

Industry observers note that prior to this discovery, scientists had two competing theories about what could be powering the emissions. One is that pulsar winds could have been causing the emissions. That means the object has to be a pulsar, which would send out streams of energetic particles in pulsations as the object spins. Neutron stars are created when a supermassive star collapses, but a stellar remnant remains behind consisting solely of neutrons packed tightly together in a space about the size of a city.

Recent findings suggest that the other theory is that the object is indeed a microquasar. The discovery of the newly found "cold" jet strongly suggests that the compact object could be a stellar-mass black hole or neutron star that draws in material from its companion to form an accretion disk. Since black holes drive more powerful jets than neutron stars, the fact that LMC P3âs gamma-ray emission is particularly high is a smoking gun pointing toward the micro-quasar origin of the signals found by ALMA. âIt provides very strong support for the possibility that its central object is a black hole," mentioned Fukui.

In a recent development, object LMC P3 was first discovered in 2016 thanks to its very strong gamma-ray emissions. It was also the first one found outside the Milky Way. From the beginning, astronomers suspected it was an X-ray binary, and Chandra X-ray Observatory studies seemed to confirm that. Then, the FERMI telescope observed it and found a 10.3-day period in gamma-ray emissions from the object. That suggested a number of ideas, including jets.

Recent findings suggest that detailed observations with ALMA focused on the surrounding gas clouds and found the "cold" jet streaming away. That raised questions about the "launch mechanism" for such a jet. In the paper the team published about their observations, they wrote: "We interpret that the high temperatures are due to shock heating of a microquasar jet driven by the gamma-ray binary, where the compact object has an accretion disk fed by the O-star winds. The CO jet matches existing predictions from magnetohydrodynamical simulations, which show that a CO jet can form from the interaction of the microquasar jet and an ambient interstellar medium (ISM) cloud. These results provide strong evidence that CO jets are a signature sculpted by microquasar jets, lending support for mass accretion in LMC P3 as the gamma-ray origin.

According to recent reports, this discovery has notable astrophysical implications for the study of high-energy emissions and the objects that provide them. Coupled with ongoing studies of such objects as SS 433, which is the first microquasar ever found, discoveries such as LMC P3 give upcoming insight into the actions of compact objects and their interactions with surrounding objects.

According to recent reports, update: United Launch Alliance has delayed the launch of its Vulcan Centaur rocket to Saturday (Nov. 14) at 12:32 p.m. ET (1732 GMT) due to a power problem in a liquid gaseous nitrogen factory that pumps propellant into the rocket. Industry observers note that united Launch Alliance's (ULA) Vulcan Centaur rocket will fly on Saturday (Nov. 14) for the first time in nine months, and you can watch the action live.

According to recent reports, A Vulcan Centaur topped with 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites is scheduled to lift off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Nov. 14 at 12:32 p.m. ET (1732 GMT).

You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of ULA, or directly via the firm. Coverage will start 20 minutes before liftoff.

Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which has just a half-dozen launches left on its manifest.

Sources indicate that vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has flown three more times since. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024, and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).

In a recent development, in both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both releases, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addresses the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.).

ULA has been working hard on that front, and the company is confident that Vulcan is ready to return to flight.

"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update.

According to recent reports, "To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission," ULA added. "By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers.".

Amazon Leo will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Today's launch will be the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.

Recent findings suggest that if all goes according to plan Saturday, Vulcan Centaur will deploy the 40 Amazon Leo satellites over a 25-minute span beginning about 70 minutes after launch. They'll be released roughly 270 miles (435 kilometers) above our planet.

#231. Automated Assembly in Space is the Future and NOM4D is Showing the Way

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1497 words)
General 🌐 Universetoday

Automated Assembly in Space is the Future and NOM4D is Showing the Way

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Universetoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if we want massive things in space, we'll have to build and assemble them there.
  • Telescopes like the JWST feature ingenious folding designs that unfold in space like insects metamorphosizing.
  • Sources indicate that what's far more feasible is sending smaller components into space inside fairings and then assembling them into a larger structure once there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if we want massive things in space, we'll have to build and assemble them there. Rocket fairings are not large enough to accommodate the large things we want to have in space. Not only that, but the stubborn rocket equation refuses to bend itself to our desires.

Telescopes like the JWST feature ingenious folding designs that unfold in space like insects metamorphosizing. That was a very impressive way to bypass the restrictions imposed by rocket fairings. But that's not practical in every case.

Sources indicate that what's far more feasible is sending smaller components into space inside fairings and then assembling them into a larger structure once there. That's what NOM4D, the Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials and Mass-efficient Design program is demonstrating. NOM4D reached an important milestone recently when it successfully demonstrated automated in-space assembly for the first time.

Industry observers note that the demonstration involved a gantry robot, also known as a linear robot, building a typical truss structure. Gantry robots move in straight lines along x, y, and z axes. The payload came from Caltech and consisted of individual components with custom joints put together to form the structure. The individual components were not only assembled, but a thin reflective mesh that mimics what a space-based antenna might have was also simultaneously applied.

âNOM4Dâs objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space,â mentioned Andrew Detor, NOM4D program manager. âBy âvery large,â I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today.â.

This concept image demonstrates a space-based antenna autonomously assembled by a NOM4D-type device. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz.

There is no shortage of ideas of how space-based manufacturing and construction could be used, but it all starts with programs like NOM4D. NOM4D is fairly simple at this point, like a child's construction toy, but that's its strength.

According to recent reports, âYou can think of the Caltech approach as similar to Tinkertoys or Kânex construction toys: individual truss members are joined at nodes, one section at a time, to create a larger structure,â Detor mentioned. âWithin the automated assembly box, each section is built piece by piece, a reflective mesh is attached, and the assembled sections are deployed as they are complete. There are no complicated robotics or advanced algorithms; itâs just solid engineering from the Caltech team to combine operations in a way that scales.â.

Decades ago, thinkers proposed different types of rotating space stations that could be homes for thousands of people. The O'Neill Cylinder is probably the most well-known one of these, and space-heads and sci-fi dreamers of a certain age may have carried around a dog-eared copy of Gerard K. O'Neill's "The High Frontier: Human Colonies in Space.".

"More notable than material complications, I think there is reason to hope that the opening of a new, high frontier will challenge the best that is in us, that the new lands waiting to be built in space will give us new freedom to search for better governments, social systems, and ways of life, and that our children may thereby find a world richer in opportunity by our efforts during the decades ahead," O'Neill wrote.

The O'Neill Cylinder lies in the realm of science fiction or the distant future for now, as do O'Neill's hopes for humanity. But that was 50 years ago, and technology has advanced considerably, even if how humans conduct themselves hasn't advanced at the same pace.

But there are other proposed space structures that are closer to reality, and they may be stages towards O'Neill's hopeful vision that can be built by NOM4D or its successor.

It has been revealed that it may begin with Low-Earth Orbit transfer stations and lunar orbit stations that would expand our presence in space. The proposed Lunar Gateway was one of these, and was envisioned as a modular design built in space from pre-made components. It would be a docking station and communications relay facility for trips to the lunar surface and operations there. These types of orbital facilities could be hybrids of pre-made components and structural frameworks made by NOM4D or something like it.

According to recent reports, this concept image shows how a NOM4D-inspired device might autonomously construct a circular truss structure in space. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz.

According to recent reports, another future use for scalable construction concerns lunar lava tubes. The Moon has what appear to be networks of subsurface lava tubes that provide natural protection from hazards. Robotic assembly could feasibly be used to reinforce these natural tubes and turn them into habitats.

According to recent reports, another idea is liquid mirror telescopes. Building a huge telescope mirror and sending it into space would be near impossible, but a liquid mirror telescope could be built in a lunar crater out of components shipped individually into space. And NASA's Lunar Crater Radio Telescope (LCRT) is a concept for a crater-based telescope on the lunar far side, isolated from Earth's radio pollution. These ideas are waiting for the engineering to catch up.

Recent findings suggest that âIn a future space economy, weâre going to need large things,â Detor mentioned. âThink large space depots or habitats, large solar arrays to collect power, or large radio antennas to explore the edges of the universe. Those things require size, and NOM4D gives us a path to accelerate creation of upcoming capabilities.â.

Recent findings suggest that the rapid advancement of the NOM4D program surprised even NOM4D personnel themselves. This successful on-orbit demonstration wasn't expected to happen so soon.

Back in February 2025, NOM4D changed its timeline. What was expected to be a third phase of more laboratory tests was instead changed to on-orbit tests, and SpaceX debuted Caltech's NOM4D payload into space in March 2026.

âCaltech [California Institute of Technology] and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have demonstrated tremendous advances in the first two phases and have now partnered in Phase 3 with space-launch companies to conduct in-space testing of their novel assembly processes and materials,â Detor mentioned at the time. âOriginally, Phase 3 was going to be about making things more precisely in the lab than we did in Phase 2. But we said, âYou know, the maturity is there, and there would be more impact if we took the capabilities we have now and actually go demonstrate them in space to show that it can be done,â"Detor said.

Sources indicate that now, way ahead of its original schedule, NOM4D has demonstrated its capabilities and is maturing rapidly. As Detor makes clear, leaping from the laboratory to space is a huge jump.

Industry observers note that âItâs the speed and the scale that made this a DARPA project. We went from the idea of an on-orbit demo to launching a working prototype into space in 15 months,â Detor remarked. âOperating in space is much harder than operating on the ground â thereâs virtually no margin to address issues that may arise. Testing in the operational environment is instrumental to rapidly maturing the technology.â.

There's still another test upcoming for NOM4D now that it's demonstrated successful on-orbit assembly. Next, the NOM4D team from University of Illinois Urbana-Champagne will launch a test project to the ISS. This will be more than just assembly; it will demonstrate composite material processing. A monomer resin will be used to build a high-strength structure in space. It will use an energy-efficient method to heat the resin and create a strong polymer. This is similar to how resins are used in Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) manufacturing to build things like aerospace components, where strength and light weight are critical.

If that test is successful, then it really will be time to start thinking big, according to Detor.

This concept image shows what the future of NOM4D-like construction might look like. Large space structures like these could be built entirely in space. Image Credit: DARPA | Colie Wertz.

Industry observers note that âThe NOM4D Caltech demonstration is not an endpoint; itâs a beginning,â Detor mentioned. âNow that weâve demonstrated a process that can scale to large structures, what do we go make? What wild ideas get assembled thousands of miles above us and what latest capabilities do those structures enable?â.

Is it time to open Gerard K. O'Neill's seminal book again?

#230. Tech Report: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Tech Report: Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant.
  • Sources indicate that scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an key part of the answer.
  • In a recent development, dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are naturally inclined to avoid. Yet millions of people eventually come to enjoy that same taste, often looking forward to their morning cup. What changes?

Sources indicate that scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an key part of the answer. Their research reveals a little-understood dopamine pathway linking the digestive system and the brain, helping explain how we develop a liking for certain flavors through repeated experience.

In a recent development, dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning. Researchers have long known that it helps the brain recognize experiences worth repeating. However, most studies have examined rapid dopamine signals that appear within seconds of encountering something rewarding, such as the sight of a favorite meal.

Sources indicate that the latest research, published November 4 in Nature, examines a different system. This slower pathway responds to information coming from inside the body, allowing the brain to learn about the benefits of food after it has been consumed.

"We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," stated Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

In a recent development, the findings offer a possible explanation for why an initially unpleasant flavor can gradually become enjoyable. Once the brain connects the taste of coffee with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better.".

How the Gut Sends Reward Signals to the Brain.

According to recent reports, scientists have spent decades investigating dopamine and its influence on behavior. Its familiar, rapidly acting signals help us respond to opportunities for reward. But dopamine also operates on a slower timescale, through a system that has received far less attention.

According to Knight, this slower process largely unfolds outside our conscious awareness.

Industry observers note that when food enters the digestive tract, specialized sensors detect nutrients, including sugar and fat. Information about those nutrients travels toward the brain, where it can produce a dopamine response that develops gradually and continues for several minutes.

To investigate this process, Knight worked with James Grove, PhD, who was a graduate student at the time. They introduced nutrients directly into the stomachs of mice while monitoring dopamine activity throughout their brains.

The researchers used either sugar water or a liquid resembling a milkshake. Delivering these substances directly into the stomach allowed them to separate the effects of nutrients from the experience of tasting food.

The results revealed a powerful, prolonged dopamine response in a specific brain region called the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA.

Industry observers note that the amygdala is involved in emotional processing and learning, including forming associations between experiences and their consequences. Scientists already knew that dopamine was released in this particular region, but its purpose had remained unclear.

"We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role," he stated.

Scientists Find a Brain Circuit That Changes Food Preferences.

It has been revealed that finding the dopamine signal was only the beginning. The researchers next wanted to determine whether it actually influenced how animals learned to prefer different flavors.

They first interrupted the newly identified pathway in mice. The animals continued eating normally, indicating that the disruption did not prevent them from consuming food. However, they lost the ability to learn that an unfamiliar flavor was associated with receiving calories.

The team then conducted the opposite experiment.

Industry observers note that after mice tasted a flavor containing no calories, the researchers artificially activated dopamine fibers in the BLA. Remarkably, the animals developed a preference for that flavor even though it provided no nutritional reward.

In effect, stimulating the pathway reproduced the learning signal that nutrients would ordinarily generate.

Together, the experiments indicated that this dopamine system plays a critical role in teaching the brain which flavors predict rewarding nutritional effects.

A Surprising Discovery in the Left Side of the Brain.

The researchers also looked for evidence that a comparable process occurs in humans. Brain imaging studies conducted by Knight's collaborators revealed a strikingly similar pattern.

Dana Small, PhD, a psychologist at Yale University, revisited data from an earlier positron emission tomography (PET) study involving 13 men. Participants had consumed either a milkshake or a drink without calories.

Her analysis found that dopamine release following nutrient delivery was especially concentrated in the left side of the BLA.

A separate study led by Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and his colleagues provided additional evidence. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in brain activity associated with blood flow, the researchers examined 38 adults after they consumed glucose, a simple sugar.

They observed increased activity in the same brain region.

One of the most unexpected findings was that the response was not evenly distributed between the brain's two hemispheres.

In both mice and humans, nutrients produced a considerably stronger dopamine response in the left BLA than in the corresponding region on the right.

That imbalance surprised Knight because brain networks responsible for essential functions, such as feeding, are generally expected to work in a relatively symmetrical fashion.

Recent findings suggest that why the left side plays such a prominent role remains unanswered. Knight's laboratory is now investigating what causes this unusual difference.

Could This Discovery Help Scientists Change Food Cravings?

Identifying the pathway provides researchers with a clearer picture of how the digestive system influences the brain's learned responses to food. It also raises an intriguing possibility: Could scientists eventually use this knowledge to change which foods people find appealing?

In a recent development, one area of interest involves GLP-1 medications, a class of drugs that mimic a hormone naturally released by the gut. These medications can substantially alter appetite and eating behavior.

Knight's team did not investigate GLP-1 drugs in the newly introduced study, so it remains unknown whether they influence the dopamine pathway the researchers identified.

In a recent development, still, Knight suggests that one possible explanation for some of their effects could involve reducing the dopamine signals generated when nutrients reach the digestive system. If that happens, foods might gradually become less rewarding because the brain would receive weaker signals reinforcing their flavors.

For now, this remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect of the medications.

Industry observers note that the broader implications extend beyond hunger and fullness. Many approaches to changing eating behavior focus on reducing appetite or increasing feelings of satisfaction after a meal. The newly mapped pathway suggests that the brain's process of learning food preferences could eventually become another target.

By influencing how the brain connects flavors with their consequences, future treatments might someday help people develop different preferences rather than simply making them feel less hungry.

"By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods," Knight mentioned.

Industry observers note that the discovery offers a fresh perspective on why our tastes can change over time. From learning to enjoy bitter coffee to developing a preference for calorie-rich foods, what we love to eat may depend partly on a quiet conversation between the gut and brain that continues long after the first bite.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-DK106399, R01-DK138127, R01-NS116626, and R01-DK145100 and F31-NS120468).

#229. The Universe May Be Twice as Old as We Think. A Rebellious Theory Claims We Can Prove It.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words)
General 🌐 Popularmechanics

The Universe May Be Twice as Old as We Think. A Rebellious Theory Claims We Can Prove It.

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A model built only on matter we can see still nails the Major Bang’s first elements—and doubles the universe’s estimated age.
  • According to recent reports, we can all agree that the universe is more or less 13.8 billion years old, right?
  • What would happen if we tried to figure out the age of the universe with only tangible matter and energy?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A model built only on matter we can see still nails the Major Bang’s first elements—and doubles the universe’s estimated age.

According to recent reports, we can all agree that the universe is more or less 13.8 billion years old, right? That figure comes largely from the European Space Agency’s Planck satellite, which mapped the cosmic microwave background (the leftover glow of the Major Bang), with results released in 2013 and finalized in 2018. Ground-based observations from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) in Chile later arrived at nearly the same number. Both fit the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). There’s just one problem: That age depends on the existence of dark matter and dark energy, neither of which has ever been directly detected.

What would happen if we tried to figure out the age of the universe with only tangible matter and energy? Physicists Rajendra Gupta and Nikolaos Samaras of the University of Ottawa are asking this exact question. Frustrated by theories built on invisible matter and on an expansion driven by energy no one has detected, Gupta and Samaras developed their own cosmological framework, called covarying coupling constants plus tired light (CCC+TL). In this model, only quantities measured in units of length change together over cosmic time, while dimensionless constants stay fixed. The researchers tested whether CCC+TL could reproduce Big Bang nucleosynthesis, the process that forged the universe’s first light elements in its earliest minutes. It could. The same model puts the age of the universe at 26.7 billion years, nearly twice the standard estimate.

“In this framework, only quantities with explicit length dimensionality covary through a universal scaling function, while dimensionless constants and dimensionless ratios remain invariant,” the researchers wrote in a study recently published in Universe, also adding that their model ensures “[Big Bang nucleosynthesis] predictions are preserved.”.

In 1929, astronomer Edwin Hubble (namesake of the Hubble Space Telescope) found that the farther away a galaxy is, the more its light is shifted toward the red end of the spectrum. Most astronomers came to read this redshift as evidence that the universe is expanding. That same year, astronomer Fritz Zwicky proposed a different explanation, known as “tired light”: Light gradually loses energy as it crosses vast distances, so light from more distant galaxies arrives redder simply because it has traveled farther. Most cosmologists set tired light aside decades ago, but Gupta has revived a version of it as part of CCC+TL.

It has been revealed that gupta and Samaras are challenging the prevailing view. In ΛCDM, the hot plasma of the newborn universe expanded and cooled, and ordinary (baryonic) matter then gathered inside vast haloes of dark matter to form galaxies. Dark energy, meanwhile, is thought to be driving the universe’s accelerating expansion. CCC+TL abandons both of those hypotheses. Instead, the fresh theory modifies the standard equations for gravity and expansion, yet still reproduces the observed expansion of the universe and the amounts of hydrogen, helium, and other light elements formed in its first minutes. It can also reproduce galactic rotation curves, which measure how fast stars and gas orbit at different distances from a galaxy’s center.

It has been revealed that gupta has also argued, in earlier papers, that CCC+TL gets around the objections that sank tired light the first time, including time dilation. In an expanding universe, light from distant supernovae is stretched out in time, so the supernovae seem to brighten and fade more slowly than nearby ones. Simple tired-light models don’t provide an explanation for that phenomenon. Time dilation itself comes from Einstein: Because light always travels at the same speed, observers moving at different speeds experience time differently, and time passes more slowly for someone moving very fast. That’s why astronauts aboard the International Space Station, which circles Earth at about 17,500 mph (28,000 kph), age very slightly more slowly than people on the ground. Gupta notes his new theory works better because the tired-light effect runs alongside cosmic expansion, instead of replacing it.

Dark matter and dark energy have been used to explain phenomena that would otherwise make no sense. CCC+TL tries to explain the same phenomena with modified gravitational effects instead. It also changes the cosmic timeline. In a 2023 paper, Gupta used CCC+TL to put the age of the universe at 26.7 billion years. That would give the first galaxies billions of years longer to form, which could explain surprisingly mature galaxies in the early universe and the Methuselah star, which some age estimates make older than the universe itself.

Recent findings suggest that “A central requirement for any alternative cosmology is that it preserves the key empirical successes of standard Massive Bang nucleosynthesis,” Samaras and Gupta wrote. They concluded that “the CCC+TL model is consistent with the [Big Bang]-predicted primordial helium and other light-element observations.”.

In a recent development, the idea remains well outside the mainstream. Most cosmologists still see ΛCDM, for all its unknowns, as the best fit to a wide range of observations, from the cosmic microwave background to how galaxies are spread across the sky. CCC+TL will have to pass many more tests to win them over.

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

Sources indicate that "There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable.".

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes newly introduced genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

It has been revealed that some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

In a recent development, they collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik remarked.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked.".

Sources indicate that to understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith mentioned. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

According to recent reports, the findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

According to recent reports, but the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith stated.
