#178. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words)
General 🌐 Sciencenews

Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every print subscription comes with full digital access.
  • Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions.
  • This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access.

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions.

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that there are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the fresh analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” claims Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sources indicate that researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a massive mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu indicates. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

Industry observers note that the chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu claims. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”.

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, claims Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#177. Tech Report: When Einstein's Gravitational Waves Meet Newton's Tides

Tech Report: When Einstein's Gravitational Waves Meet Newton's Tides

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Universetoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1687, Sir Isaac Newton released his magnum opus, PhilosophiÃ¦ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), in which he described his theories of motion and gravity.
  • According to a recent study from the Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories.
  • In a recent development, the study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1687, Sir Isaac Newton released his magnum opus, PhilosophiÃ¦ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), in which he described his theories of motion and gravity. His theory of the latter accurately described the motion of the Earth's tides, something that scientists had been wrestling with for centuries. For over three hundred years, Newton's work remained scientific canon and the last word on gravity, until Albert Einstein introduced his Theory of General Relativity.

According to a recent study from the Freie UniversitÃ¤t Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories. While the pull of the Sun and Moon and their influence on the tides can be predicted very accurately using Newtonian gravity, GR offers a fuller description that includes gravitational waves (GWs). The new study merges these two theories into a single model that could offer a new way to test our understanding of gravity.

In a recent development, the study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB. His work extends the classical model of lunar tides to include the cross polarization of gravitational waves, one of the key ways GWs can deform spacetime as they pass through. As he explained in a FUB press release:.

It has been revealed that isaac Newton explains the tides extremely well. Albert Einstein shows us that gravity is also dynamic and that changes in spacetime can propagate as waves. Our work brings both perspectives together and asks what traces of this might be found in high-precision measurements.

Sources indicate that GWs were originally predicted by Einstein's Theory of General Relativity and refer to ripples in spacetime caused by the merger of massive objects. To date, thousands of GW events have been detected, the majority of which were caused by the merger of black holes or neutron stars. However, GWs can also result from smaller gravitational interactions, such as those produced by the interactions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.

Recent findings suggest that one issue addressed by Eser's study is the difficulty of distinguishing possible additional signals from measurement errors, the choice of reference frame, and uncertainties in calculating the positions of the Sun and Moon. By identifying which influences must be accounted for, Eser indicates how a signal could be isolated and the possible physical effects identified. The study therefore presents a quantitative basis for future studies of tidal patterns that deviate from what Newtonian Gravity predicts. Mentioned Eser:.

Recent findings suggest that we are not claiming to have discovered a new gravitational effect. What we show is how one could look for it in a targeted way. The EarthâMoon system is particularly interesting for this because we can already describe and measure its tidal effects very precisely.

#176. Scientists Discover a Hidden Immune System Difference That Could Explain Why Obesity Affects Men and Women Differently

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (684 words)
General 🌐 Scitechdaily

Scientists Discover a Hidden Immune System Difference That Could Explain Why Obesity Affects Men and Women Differently

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered that immune cells in fat tissue behave differently in males and females, potentially helping explain sex-specific responses to obesity.
  • A type of immune cell best known for its role in allergies and asthma may help explain why obesity affects males and females differently.
  • The findings, published in PNAS Nexus, challenge the long-held assumption that these cells, called eosinophils, perform a relatively narrow range of functions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered that immune cells in fat tissue behave differently in males and females, potentially helping explain sex-specific responses to obesity.

A type of immune cell best known for its role in allergies and asthma may help explain why obesity affects males and females differently. Researchers at the University of California, Riverside found that certain immune cells in fat tissue appear to protect female mice from obesity-related inflammation, while others become more inflammatory in males fed a high-fat diet.

The findings, published in PNAS Nexus, challenge the long-held assumption that these cells, called eosinophils, perform a relatively narrow range of functions. Instead, their effects may depend on their molecular characteristics, biological sex, and interactions with neighboring immune cells.

Using high-resolution single-cell sequencing, scientists identified six distinct eosinophil populations in adipose (fat) tissue. Each population displayed different patterns of gene activity, suggesting that eosinophils perform specialized functions rather than acting as a single, uniform group.

Sources indicate that “Eosinophils are more complex than we once thought,” said Meera Nair, a professor of biomedical sciences at the UCR School of Medicine who co-led the research with biomedical scientist Adam Godzik. “Some populations can protect against obesity, and if we can identify and activate the pathways that produce these protective cells, we may find new ways to improve metabolic health.”.

It has been revealed that in female mice, researchers identified a protective eosinophil population that communicated more effectively with macrophages, another class of immune cells found in fat tissue. This relationship appeared to be supported by RELM alpha, a protein produced by macrophages that may help maintain protective immune activity. Earlier experiments showed that supplying RELM alpha to mice had protective effects, providing additional evidence for its role in regulating the immune environment.

Male mice demonstrated a different response to a high-fat diet. Their fat tissue tended to contain more eosinophil populations associated with inflammation, and these cells displayed gene-expression patterns that suggested weaker protective functions.

In a recent development, “This means the relationship between eosinophils and obesity is not simply a matter of how many eosinophils are present,” said Rebecca E. Ruggiero-Ruff, a postdoctoral researcher in Nair’s laboratory and co-first author of the study. “Their functional characteristics and how they communicate with other immune cells are also critical.”.

Although eosinophils have been detected in the fat tissue of people with obesity, scientists have not yet established whether they perform the same protective or inflammatory functions observed in mice. Determining whether similar cell populations exist in humans could help researchers investigate treatments that influence specific immune pathways rather than broadly altering immune activity.

“A drug may not activate the same pathways or produce the same effects in males and females, particularly when it targets the immune system,” noted co-first author Xinru Qiu, a postdoctoral researcher in Godzik’s laboratory. “We need to investigate sex-specific biology more thoroughly so that treatments can be optimized for different patients.”.

The researchers are now developing three-dimensional adipose organoids, laboratory-grown structures that reproduce certain features of human fat tissue. These models could allow scientists to examine how eosinophils interact with fat cells and macrophages, and whether modifying those interactions can encourage healthier tissue responses.

“We ultimately hope to develop human adipose organoids that will allow us to investigate whether manipulating immune-cell communication can promote healthier tissue responses,” stated Godzik, a professor of biomedical sciences and the Bruce D. and Nancy B. Varner Presidential Endowed Chair in Cancer Research.

It has been revealed that reference: “Single-cell heterogeneity of adipose eosinophils is shaped by sex and RELMα and linked to macrophage communication networks in obesity” by Rebecca E Ruggiero-Ruff, Xinru Qiu, Lauren Vance, Yuxin He, Djurdjica Coss, Adam Godzik and Meera G Nair, 24 October 2026, PNAS Nexus. DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag365.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, UCR School of Medicine, and California Institute for Regenerative Medicine.

The powerful Euclid space telescope is making the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, and ESA has just shared the first enormous piece of it.

Sources indicate that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

It has been revealed that on Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, stated in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery.".

According to recent reports, captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Sources indicate that scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In a recent development, in its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, "Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here.".

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

It has been revealed that the Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Sources indicate that among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid demonstrates a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image demonstrates the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

#174. Breaking: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (884 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Breaking: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow.
  • Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow. These developing hair follicles form intricate geometric arrangements that differ from species to species. But what determines where each follicle appears, and how does the body create such orderly patterns?

Researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery. By studying how cells move in response to chemical signals, the team developed a model that successfully recreates the formation of hair follicle patterns in two mammalian species. Their findings, published in PNAS, suggest that elaborate biological structures can emerge naturally from basic interactions between neighboring cells.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature. Hair, feathers, and most types of scales begin as small structures called placodes that appear during embryonic development. Scientists have spent decades investigating how these early structures establish the distinctive arrangements seen across different animal species.

Challenging a Long-Standing Theory of Hair Growth.

According to recent reports, for laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the leading explanation has traditionally been the expansion-induction model. This theory proposes that when a fresh placode appears, it releases a chemical that prevents additional placodes from developing too close to it.

As the embryo's skin grows and stretches, some areas move far enough away from existing placodes to escape the chemical's influence. Newly introduced placodes can then develop in those spaces, gradually creating a more complete pattern across the skin.

Although this explanation has gained widespread acceptance, scientists have not experimentally established that it can account for the diversity of follicle patterns found across species.

A Simpler Mechanism for Hair Follicle Formation.

To investigate another possibility, researchers led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor, both in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE's Faculty of Science, focused on a process called chemotaxis.

Industry observers note that chemotaxis occurs when cells move in response to differences in chemical concentrations. The same basic process helps guide white blood cells toward areas of inflammation, allowing the immune system to respond where it is needed.

The researchers created a mathematical model that tracks how mobile cells in the dermis interact with an attracting chemical signal released by the epidermis, the skin's outer layer. They then simulated the growth of embryonic skin to see whether these interactions could produce the gradual appearance of placodes.

Remarkably, the model recreated the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, including the same sequence of follicle formation that scientists had previously explained using the expansion-induction theory. This suggests that a complex system of instructions may not be necessary to determine where follicles develop.

Industry observers note that "Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form," explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. "Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals.".

One Simple Process Creates Different Hair Patterns.

The team next investigated whether the same mechanism could explain follicle arrangements in another mammal with a very different coat structure.

Recent findings suggest that they selected the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles develop in an unusually regular pattern with a strong directional alignment. This distinctive organization cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental information gathered from three-dimensional images of developing embryonic skin, the researchers adapted their simulations to reflect the spiny mouse's particular biochemical characteristics and the way its skin grows.

The results showed that the same underlying process of cells responding to chemical signals could also reproduce the spiny mouse's highly organized follicle pattern. The differences between the two species could be explained by variations in their cellular interactions, chemical properties, and skin growth rather than entirely different mechanisms.

These findings suggest that the remarkable variety of structures found throughout the animal kingdom may arise from a shared set of relatively simple biological rules. By adjusting how cells interact and respond to their surroundings, nature can generate dramatically different patterns without requiring a separate developmental blueprint for every species.

"Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution," concludes Athanasia Tzika. "The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals.".

#173. Your Brain Chemistry Could Change How You Understand Language

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (593 words)
General 🌐 Scitechdaily

Your Brain Chemistry Could Change How You Understand Language

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A single word can overturn your understanding of a sentence, and your brain chemistry may shape how hard you work to make sense of it again.
  • Industry observers note that even a single word can change the meaning of an entire sentence, forcing the brain to rethink what it just read.
  • A study published in PNAS found that increasing dopamine and noradrenaline (catecholamines) strengthened a brain response associated with untangling ambiguous grammar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A single word can overturn your understanding of a sentence, and your brain chemistry may shape how hard you work to make sense of it again.

Industry observers note that even a single word can change the meaning of an entire sentence, forcing the brain to rethink what it just read. But how efficiently the brain handles these grammatical surprises may depend partly on its chemistry.

A study published in PNAS found that increasing dopamine and noradrenaline (catecholamines) strengthened a brain response associated with untangling ambiguous grammar. Researchers led by the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics (MPI-PL) in Nijmegen observed the largest effects in healthy adults with lower baseline working memory capacity.

“Catecholamines are known to regulate attention, working memory, and cognitive control, but their role in language remains poorly understood,” says Peter Hagoort, senior investigator and director emeritus of MPI-PL’s Neurobiology of Language Department and the Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behavior.

According to recent reports, “Our earlier work suggested that catecholamines can affect semantic aspects of sentence comprehension. Whether these neuromodulatory systems also influence syntactic processing—how the brain combines words into grammatical structures—was largely unknown.”.

Sources indicate that understanding a sentence involves more than knowing what its words mean. Readers also have to work out how those words fit together, sometimes revising an interpretation as fresh information arrives. The researchers used temporarily ambiguous “garden-path” sentences to examine that process.

Consider “The fan attacked the drummer, and the guitarist packed the instruments up.” When the words appear one at a time, readers may initially group “the drummer and the guitarist” together as the people being attacked. The word “packed” reveals that the guitarist is instead performing a separate action, requiring readers to rebuild their interpretation.

It has been revealed that to test whether brain chemistry influences this revision, the team recruited 30 healthy adults. Each completed two sessions, once after taking methylphenidate, a stimulant commonly prescribed for ADHD that increases catecholamine levels, and once after taking a placebo.

Participants read ambiguous and unambiguous sentences and answered comprehension questions after each one. Meanwhile, researchers recorded their brain activity using EEG (electroencephalography), allowing them to examine the response at the precise word that exposed the grammatical ambiguity.

Sources indicate that after methylphenidate, participants highlighted a stronger P600 response at the critical word, such as “packed.” This well-known EEG signal is associated with demanding grammatical processing and reflects increased cognitive effort. Its enhancement suggests that higher catecholamine levels changed how the brain recruited resources to resolve the sentence.

The increase was greatest among participants whose working memory capacity was lower before treatment.

It has been revealed that “The findings suggest that catecholaminergic systems contribute to the dynamic allocation of cognitive resources during syntactic processing,” notes Hagoort. “Their influence on language therefore appears to extend beyond semantic processing to syntactic unification, and the magnitude of this effect may depend on individual baseline working memory performance.”.

“The results support the development of neuropharmacolinguistics as a field linking neuromodulatory systems to language processing.”.

It has been revealed that reference: “Neuropharmacology of language: ERP evidence for catecholaminergic modulation of syntactic processing” by Yingying Tan, Ashley G. Lewis, Iris C. Schmits, Robert-Jan Verkes, Roshan Cools and Peter Hagoort, 22 October 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2606806123.

Oscar-winning director Brad Bird ("The Incredibles," "Ratatouille") returns to our screens with his fresh substantial-budget animated sci-fi project, "Ray Gunn," and this latest trailer has us primed.

"In Metropia, a gigantic city in an alternate future as seen from 1939, private eye Raymond Gunn (Sam Rockwell) is drawn into a case involving aliens, murder, and a multimedia starlet named Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson)," states the official synopsis.

Netflix Films and Skydance Animation's "Ray Gunn" is a stylistic pastiche of classic film noir tropes populated by down-and-out detectives and femme fatales living in the inspiring air of technological optimism viewed through a pre-war America lens.

#171. Pink noise played during sleep shows promise for Alzheimer’s memory loss

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (521 words)
General 🌐 Newscientist

Pink noise played during sleep shows promise for Alzheimer’s memory loss

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Newscientist

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Check your subscription status, update your details and more.
  • Brief bursts of ‘pink noise’ played while people with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease sleep might give them a slight memory boost, a small study suggests.
  • Pink noise is best described as a low-pitched hiss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check your subscription status, update your details and more.

Brief bursts of ‘pink noise’ played while people with early-stage Alzheimer’s disease sleep might give them a slight memory boost, a small study suggests.

Pink noise is best described as a low-pitched hiss. There is some evidence that exposure to pink noise during sleep may help clear waste products from the brain. As such, researchers are beginning to assess whether pink-noise therapy has benefits for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease.

Can we harness the brain’s deep-cleaning system to prevent Alzheimer’s?

Industry observers note that an international team of researchers has explored this possibility. They worked with 37 people, each with diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and experiencing mild cognitive impairment affecting memory. On two occasions, 14 days apart, the 37 participants were invited into the lab in the evening and asked to memorise 30 word pairs. They then slept in the lab while the researchers monitored their brain activity.

It has been revealed that javier Mínguez at Elevvo Therapeutics in Spain, and a member of the research team, says slow brainwaves and brief bursts of neural activity known as sleep spindles help the brain consolidate memories, a process Alzheimer’s can disrupt. The researchers used a system developed by Spanish neurotechnology tech giant Bitbrain that can identify when slow brainwaves are approaching their peak. Throughout the first night in the lab, the researchers played a 50-millisecond-long pulse of pink noise to the sleeping participants each time these peaks occurred.

“Timing is critical, because the useful window is only about 200 milliseconds wide,” states Mínguez.

On the second night in the lab, the study participants were not exposed to pink noise as they slept.

According to recent reports, after both nights, the participants were asked to recall the word pairs they had learned the evening before. They remembered slightly more word pairs after exposure to pink noise than after the night without pink noise: 0.88 word pairs more, on average, after the pink-noise exposure. This is equivalent to about a 19 per cent improvement in memory, the researchers say. The clinical significance of this result remains uncertain.

“These results are meaningful theoretically and fit with an increasingly strong set of findings linking memory storage with overnight brain activity,” claims Ken Paller at Northwestern University in Illinois, who wasn’t involved in the study.

Industry observers note that the study hasn’t yet been peer-reviewed. Several authors have commercial connections to Bitbrain or its spin-off Elevvo Therapeutics, and three are inventors on a pending patent covering the method, states Mínguez.

Recent findings suggest that mínguez sees the study as a proof of concept. To find out whether the benefits can last, the researchers are now expanding their experiments. They have given study participants equipment to use at home that offers pink noise stimulation during sleep, and they will assess the effects of continued exposure over a 6-month period.

medRxiv DOI: 10.64898/2026.09.14.26360893.

#170. Scientists Discover California Has Way More Bugs Than Anyone Imagined

Scientists Discover California Has Way More Bugs Than Anyone Imagined

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • California is teeming with thousands of insect species science has yet to name, and its wild places hold more distinct worlds of tiny creatures than researchers realized.
  • It has been revealed that california is home to an astonishing variety of insects, from the deserts of the Mojave to the forests of the Sierra Nevada.
  • Industry observers note that A newly introduced study in Ecography estimates that California supports more than 60,000 insect species, far exceeding earlier estimates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

California is teeming with thousands of insect species science has yet to name, and its wild places hold more distinct worlds of tiny creatures than researchers realized.

It has been revealed that california is home to an astonishing variety of insects, from the deserts of the Mojave to the forests of the Sierra Nevada. But scientists are discovering that the state’s insect diversity is far greater than previously believed.

Industry observers note that A newly introduced study in Ecography estimates that California supports more than 60,000 insect species, far exceeding earlier estimates. Scientists have formally described only about two-thirds of them. Led by researchers at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, the study also found that nearly every location sampled had its own distinct insect community.

The findings suggest that conserving California’s insect life will require protecting a wide range of habitats. Even places with similar climates and landscapes can harbor different species, making it difficult for any single protected area to represent the state’s extraordinary diversity.

It has been revealed that the research is the first publication from the California Insect Barcode Initiative (CIBI), a $6 million project with an ambitious goal: collect and identify every insect species in California. Although insects are the most diverse group of animals on land, they remain underrepresented in large-scale conservation assessments.

Sources indicate that researchers used DNA barcoding on more than one million insect specimens. The technique compares short sections of DNA to help distinguish species, giving scientists a way to investigate diversity that can be difficult to recognize from appearance alone.

It has been revealed that the effort brought together the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, California Department of Food and Agriculture, UC Berkeley, UC Riverside, San Diego Natural History Museum, and California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco. Researchers gathered tissue samples from museum collections, deployed Malaise traps across 72 ecoregions, and made collecting expeditions to 454 additional locations statewide.

It has been revealed that museum specimens extended the project’s reach beyond what researchers could collect in the field. Fresh sampling added another essential piece, with volunteers helping keep traps operating week after week. Although Malaise traps capture insects passively, collecting their contents and maintaining them takes sustained effort.

“This is an example of community science. Volunteers stepped forward to help with sampling by managing traps, which we would not have been able to do for continuous weekly sampling,” notes study co-author Giar-Ann Kung, the museum’s entomology collections manager.

Recent findings suggest that kung joined researchers and volunteers across California in setting traps and collecting insects. Some participants maintained sampling sites for years, providing a continuity that the research team could not have achieved alone.

In a recent development, “There are people like Sara Fairchild and Michael Nance who managed a Malaise trap for over three years at a site in the high desert, which is the longest continuous site for the project. That could not have been accomplished without them.”.

It has been revealed that to explore how insect diversity varies across California, the researchers compared ecoregions, areas grouped by the Environmental Protection Agency according to shared ecosystem characteristics. They used Level 3 classifications, including the Mojave Basin and Range, Southern California Mountains, and Sierra Nevada. Of these regions, the Mojave Basin and Range had the greatest number of insect species.

Recent findings suggest that although similar environments shared some patterns, each region had its own mix of insects. “The deserts are kind of more similar to each other, and the mountains in northern California are a little bit more similar to each other, but every part of the state hosts a really different insect fauna,” states Dr. Barkdull.

Those differences also appeared at a smaller scale, with individual collecting sites within the same ecoregion harboring distinct insect communities. Together, the findings highlight the need to protect a wide range of California’s wild places.

#169. Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1674 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered upcoming clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels.
  • Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death.
  • Industry observers note that reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered upcoming clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels. Their findings point to biological processes involving other fat-carrying particles in the blood that may contribute to cardiovascular damage in ways that go beyond cholesterol buildup. By identifying these previously poorly understood mechanisms, the research could help pave the way for more targeted strategies to prevent heart disease and potentially save lives.

Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes responsible for more than 80% of those deaths. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits containing cholesterol (cholesterol) build up inside the arteries that supply blood to the heart. If left untreated, the condition can eventually cause a heart attack.

Industry observers note that reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack. However, bringing LDL cholesterol into the recommended range does not eliminate the danger. Some patients continue to develop coronary heart disease despite successful treatment, suggesting that other particles transporting fats through the bloodstream play an notable role. Until recently, the biological reasons behind this remaining risk were not well understood.

"For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs," states Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology, in Sweden.

Industry observers note that cholesterol is a substance similar to fat that circulates in the bloodstream. The body needs it to build cells and manufacture certain vitamins and hormones. Problems can arise when too much cholesterol accumulates in blood vessel walls, creating deposits called plaques.

In a recent development, these plaques can narrow arteries and interfere with blood flow. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot may form rapidly and completely obstruct the affected vessel, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Industry observers note that because cholesterol and other fats cannot travel through the blood on their own, they are transported by specialized particles known as lipoproteins. Three major classes of these particles contain a surface protein called apolipoprotein B (apoB). When too many of these particles circulate in the blood, they can deliver excess cholesterol into artery walls. The cholesterol they carry is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol.".

Recent findings suggest that to investigate these unanswered questions, the scientists used proteomics analysis to examine how three types of fat-carrying particles (LDL, TRL and Lp(a)) affect the body and may contribute to heart disease. This approach allowed the team to investigate biological changes associated with the particles rather than focusing exclusively on the cholesterol they carry.

All three types can contribute to cholesterol deposits inside artery walls, although LDL, which stands for low-density lipoprotein, is the most common. In a previous study, the same research group found that counting harmful lipoprotein particles was the most effective way to predict future heart disease risk.

According to recent reports, the researchers also identified two particularly important contributors beyond LDL: triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, or TRL, and lipoprotein(a), known as Lp(a). Their earlier findings suggested that each of these particles poses a greater risk individually than an LDL particle. As a result, TRL and Lp(a) are considered major contributors to the cardiovascular danger that can persist even after LDL cholesterol has been successfully reduced.

Proteomics is the systematic, large-scale examination and measurement of proteins within cells, tissues, or body fluids at a particular point in time.

According to recent reports, while genomics investigates a person's relatively stable DNA, proteomics focuses on proteins, which are constantly responding to changes inside the body. These molecules help construct tissues, process food, transmit hormonal messages, and defend against infections.

Because protein patterns shift in response to factors such as diet, stress, aging, and disease, analyzing them can provide a snapshot of current biological activity. Proteomics can help researchers identify biomarkers, diagnose medical conditions, and track how patients respond to treatment.

Blood Proteins Reveal Hidden Heart Disease Risks.

The new investigation focused on proteins, which perform countless essential functions throughout the body. Unlike genetic information, which remains largely unchanged, protein levels and activity can respond to diet, stress, aging, and illness. Studying these changes can therefore provide valuable insights into the body's current biological condition.

Recent findings suggest that researchers analyzed measurements of nearly 3,000 proteins found in blood samples and compared the results with genetic information and long-term health records. This combination helped them identify protein patterns associated with different lipoprotein particles and provided clues about how those particles might contribute to damage inside the arteries.

It has been revealed that one of the most striking discoveries involved TRL and Lp(a). Although these are distinct types of particles, their associated blood protein patterns showed substantial similarities. Those overlapping patterns also appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that these particles carried proteins capable of attracting immune cells, potentially encouraging inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. This suggests that TRL and Lp(a) may contribute to cardiovascular disease through some of the same biological processes, rather than simply depositing cholesterol in the arteries.

LDL demonstrated a different pattern. Its associated proteins were primarily connected to cholesterol accumulation in artery walls, highlighting an important distinction between the ways these three types of particles may contribute to heart disease.

Sources indicate that "The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings," indicates Morze. "It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future.".

How LDL, TRL, and Lp(a) Affect Heart Health.

The three types of lipoproteins examined in the study, LDL, TRL, and Lp(a), transport different amounts of cholesterol and other fats through the bloodstream. Each contains the structural protein apolipoprotein B, or apoB.

All three can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty material accumulates inside blood vessel walls. As these deposits develop, they increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

LDL: Low-density lipoprotein transports most of the cholesterol circulating in the blood. An LDL cholesterol measurement indicates how much cholesterol is contained within these particles.

TRL: Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins transport cholesterol along with triglycerides, which the body uses as an important energy source. As triglycerides are removed from these particles, the remaining fragments can deposit cholesterol inside artery walls. In this study, the TRL measurements primarily reflected liver-produced particles called VLDL and the remnants they leave behind.

Lp(a): Lipoprotein(a) resembles an LDL particle but contains an additional protein known as apolipoprotein(a). Higher levels of Lp(a) are already recognized as an established risk factor for coronary heart disease.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Disease Prevention?

By identifying biological pathways associated with cardiovascular risk beyond LDL cholesterol, the findings offer researchers newly introduced possibilities for developing more personalized prevention strategies. In particular, the shared inflammatory and blood vessel effects linked to TRL and Lp(a) could become promising areas for further investigation.

It has been revealed that however, the research did not evaluate a new treatment or establish a blood protein test ready for routine clinical use. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether measuring these biological processes, or developing treatments that target them, can improve protection against heart disease.

Industry observers note that "Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention," says Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. "Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments.".

Industry observers note that the results reinforce the importance of controlling LDL cholesterol while revealing why cholesterol reduction alone may not address every source of cardiovascular risk. Understanding the additional ways blood particles affect arteries could ultimately help scientists develop more precise approaches to protecting heart health.

The study, "Apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins: distinct roles in atherosclerosis revealed by plasma proteomic profiling," was published in the European Heart Journal.

The research authors are Jakub Morze, Elias Björnson, Michael Y Mi, Martin Adiels, Giorgio E Melloni, Gonçalo Rosas da Silva, Andrzej Rynkiewicz, Nicholas A Marston, Marta Guasch-Ferré, Michael Y Tsai, Jerome I Rotter, Robert E Gerszten, Qi Sun, Frank B Hu, Rikard Landberg, Göran Bergström, Chris J Packard, Jan Borén and Clemens Wittenbecher.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Cleaning is soothing for some, but for others, it’s simply another task to add to an overwhelming to-do list. Hauling your clunky upright vacuum out of the closet every time you need to tidy up a minor spill or dust bunny makes the task of cleaning even more inconvenient. That’s why handheld vacuums are such a practical companion to your regular vacuum. They help you reach narrow spaces such as stairs, corners, under car seats, and around furniture and cut down on how much large, clunky equipment you need to carry around.

Recent findings suggest that but don't retire your go-to vacuum just yet. Handheld vacs are better suited for tackling small messes in between your deeper cleans. Since they have lower dustbin capacities and less suction power, they aren’t equipped to handle whole rooms or entire floors and can’t penetrate deep enough into your carpet fibers. However, if you’re looking for a machine that can supplement your usual cleaning tools, then a handheld vacuum might be right for you.

We evaluated a host of handheld vacuums from top brands like Black+Decker, Dyson, and Shark. We looked at their capability, features, and capacities to find the best devices to help you maintain cleanliness. These are the eight models we recommend, along with expert insight and valuable tips before you shop.

We also considered some of the more practical details like emptying the dustbin, maintaining the filter, and overall ease of use.

For models we haven’t tested firsthand, we drew on our extensive vacuum-testing knowledge, researching leading contenders and focusing on key features like battery life, filtration, suction performance, and attachments.

We prioritized cordless, rechargeable handheld vacuums that work well for a range of messes, such as pet hair and crumbs. This list reflects our top selections for handling everyday messes and more demanding cleanup jobs.

Lightweight, user-friendly, and full of power, the Dustbuster HHVK515J is an excellent vacuum to take on an array of tasks across the home, the shop, and even inside your car.

According to recent reports, the nozzle at the end of the vacuum stretches an additional 7.5 inches—all you have to do is pull it forward to get into all the hidden nooks and crannies. It has two cleaning speeds, one of which is a power boost in case you need to maximize suction for a bigger mess.

The Dustbuster uses a foam filter and a pre-filter to trap debris and other common allergens, both of which you can wash from time to time. This vacuum doesn't come with any additional attachments besides the adjustable nozzle, so it might be best used for immediate messes that you need to clean up right away.

It has been revealed that the Black+Decker Dustbuster AdvancedClean is reasonably priced, lightweight, compact, and has a good amount of suction power. The battery only lasts for about 15 minutes off of a single charge, but that's more than enough time to clean up a workspace, countertop messes, and other light debris.

Industry observers note that even with its smaller build, the Dustbuster comes with a built-in flip-up dusting brush and crevice tool, so you don’t have to deal with storing any attachments. It uses a washable pleated filter, but it’s not HEPA, so some dust and allergen particles may not be trapped completely.

The dustbin holds about half a liter of debris at a time, and it empties with a quick press of a button. The Dustbuster comes with a wall mount for quick and convenient storage.

What we appreciate about this handheld vacuum is that Shark has packed in similar features to some of the pet hair vacuums we love, like a paddled roller brush for scooping up deeply embedded hair and making continuous contact with surfaces. Industry observers note that this handheld vacuum uses two cyclonic air streams, one for powerful suction and one to separate debris away from the motor to protect its lifespan. We also like how the design uses a two-stage filter, and you can wash and use it again. The vacuum runs for up to 10 minutes off of its rechargeable lithium-ion battery.

According to recent reports, the Dyson Car+Boat is a handheld vacuum that can easily alternate between detailing the interior of your car and cleaning small messes from bare floors, carpet, and furniture. Similar to Dyson cordless stick models, the Car+Boat uses a fully sealed filtration system to pick up and trap almost 100 percent of airborne particles as small as 0.3 microns.

Sources indicate that it also comes with a mini motorized brush, a crevice tool, and a combination tool for messes both big and small. The main caveat is that you have to keep a trigger button depressed for the duration of your cleaning session in order for the vacuum to stay powered on.

The DeWalt DCV517B stands up to tough chores, tackling anything like a bowl of breakfast cereal dumped on the floor (milk and all), or a handful of metal shavings on top of your garage workbench.

The HEPA filter traps debris of varying sizes effectively, and the vacuum has two cleaning modes so you can alternate between the nozzle head and extendable hose. This model also has a half-gallon tank that easily detaches for emptying.

According to recent reports, the DCV517B uses DeWalt-brand batteries, which may add some considerable heft to the body itself (it weighs 4.5 pounds to start). But a high-capacity battery gives superior vacuuming strength and provides the suction needed to clean both wet and dry messes.

According to recent reports, the Shark Wandvac is the sleek, modern hand vacuum that could just as easily serve as an accent piece in your living room as it does for cleaning up spills. While the exterior might be flashy, the bones of the machine are solid as well.

Sources indicate that during our testing, the Duster Crevice Tool was quite effective for hard-to-reach corners, ceilings and otherwise ignored spaces like under the fridge, but we were most impressed by the Surface Pet Tool. In combination with a bit of elbow grease, it lifted tons of hair and dander out of carpets, furniture, and other upholstery. Recent findings suggest that the Pet Hair Eraser has a pleated post-motor filter, a washable inner foam filter, and a mesh pre-filter for trapping dust and allergens. The dustbin is easy to empty once you remove the filter, and you can give it a quick rinse if you want to remove any lingering debris. The vacuum lasts for up to 17 minutes, but it takes a long time to fully recharge.

Don’t want to deal with rechargeable batteries? A corded handheld vacuum is a great option if you prefer to have continuous power for your cleaning tools. The Dirt Devil Scorpion has a 15-foot power cable so you don’t have to always be within range of an outlet, along with a 2.5-foot detachable hose and built-in crevice tool for picking up dirt and debris in hard-to-reach areas.

Sources indicate that the dustbin holds a little less than half a liter, which is right around the capacity we recommend to cut down on trips to the trash can. This model also uses a washable filter to reduce the amount of maintenance and replacements needed.

Sources indicate that use this alongside your corded upright, and you’ll have the suction power you need to tackle tough household messes. We just wish it came with some more attachments to really take it to the next level.

A quality handheld vac should be ready to use whenever you need it, which means having a dependable battery with a run time that lasts long enough so you don’t lose power mid-clean. Many of our selections use a lithium-ion battery that can last anywhere from around 10 to 50 minutes between charges. Just be prepared that some models take several hours to go from fully dead to fully charged, so keeping the vacuum docked and hooked up to power consistently is key.

Handheld vacuums have a smaller dustbin capacity and fill up faster than full-size, upright versions, but that’s because they handle light spills, not whole-home cleaning. If you regularly reach for your handheld vacuum, look for models that hold up to half a liter or more of debris, so you don’t have to make as many trips to the garbage can.

A handheld vacuum with multiple attachments may be a worthwhile investment if you have kids that are prone to dropping crumbs or furry friends that shed profusely. Crevice tools get into the nooks and crannies of the couch, whereas bristled or motorized brushes pick up stubborn pet hair.

Recent findings suggest that additional hose pieces can also be beneficial if you need extended reach. These types of attachments focus airflow and suction to a designated area, and may be used on different surfaces like upholstery, carpet, and hardwood floors.

Handheld vacuums often come with cloth, foam, or pleated filters that trap dust, hair, grime, and allergen particles—and most of these versions are washable to avoid buying replacements all the time.

Recent findings suggest that some handheld vacuums include an additional filter, called the pre-filter, which traps larger particles before they reach the main filter. Others might have a HEPA filter that removes up to 99.7 percent of airborne particles and is useful for allergy sufferers.

Recent findings suggest that we recommend shopping for a handheld vacuum with at least a two-step filtration system or a HEPA filter if you’re trying to keep your home or car clear of common allergens like pollen and pet dander. Otherwise, a washable filter will do just fine for general cleaning tasks.

What is a good suction power rating for a handheld vacuum?

First, it’s important to note that brands don’t all advertise suction power the same way. Some list air watts (AW), some use pascals (Pa), and some don’t provide a suction rating at all and focus more on the motor.

These measurements aren’t directly interchangeable, but for everyday messes and light debris I would look for a handheld vacuum rated around 20 to 40AW or between 5,000 to 10,000Pa.

How often should I clean or replace the filter?

In a recent development, A light cleaning should be done every few weeks or whenever you notice reduced suction power. Foam and felt filters can be washed every 1 to 3 months, and should be replaced every 3 to 6 months.

Sources indicate that HEPA filters are not washable unless specified by the vacuum manufacturer and should be replaced between 6 to 12 months. You can adjust the frequency of maintenance based on your cleaning needs and how much debris you typically pick up.

There’s no one-size-fits all for how long a handheld vacuum lasts because it largely depends on build quality, frequency of use, battery health, and maintenance. Cleaning the filter and dustbin regularly helps preserve the battery and motor, too, but if the vacuum is losing suction or the battery can’t hold a charge, it might be time for a replacement.

Recent findings suggest that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England.

According to recent reports, the Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also demonstrated signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

In a recent development, the unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall claims. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”.

Scientists Develop a Groundbreaking Rechargeable Battery That Runs on Vitamin B12

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The same vitamin found in everyday foods could eventually help store surplus renewable electricity, after an experimental zinc-air battery using B12 completed up to 250 recharge cycles.
  • It has been revealed that the search for safer, more sustainable batteries is leading scientists to some unexpected places, including the chemistry of vitamins.
  • Recent findings suggest that the researchers developed a zinc-air battery, which generates electricity through chemical reactions involving zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The same vitamin found in everyday foods could eventually help store surplus renewable electricity, after an experimental zinc-air battery using B12 completed up to 250 recharge cycles.

It has been revealed that the search for safer, more sustainable batteries is leading scientists to some unexpected places, including the chemistry of vitamins. Researchers at the University of Córdoba in Spain have found that vitamin B12, a nutrient essential to human health, can also help power a rechargeable battery. Their experimental design completed up to 250 charge and discharge cycles, opening another possibility for future energy storage technology.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers developed a zinc-air battery, which generates electricity through chemical reactions involving zinc and oxygen from the surrounding air. Unlike conventional batteries that store all their reactive materials internally, zinc-air batteries draw oxygen from the environment. This makes them lighter and gives them high energy density, meaning they can store substantial energy relative to their weight. They are already used in small devices such as hearing aids.

In a recent development, zinc also offers advantages because it is abundant and recyclable. These batteries use nonflammable, water-based electrolytes, making them potentially safer than conventional lithium-ion batteries, whose raw material extraction raises economic, social, and environmental concerns.

According to recent reports, making zinc-air batteries rechargeable, however, presents a challenge. They need a catalyst, a substance that helps chemical reactions proceed, that can support both the production of electricity and the reverse process needed to recharge the battery.

Vitamin B12, also known as cobalamin, offered a possible solution because its molecular structure contains cobalt (III), a form of the metal cobalt that helps drive these reactions. Although better known for its role in nutrition, B12 is produced naturally by certain bacteria and manufactured commercially for food and pharmaceutical applications. Found in foods of animal origin, it is used to address nutritional deficiencies and has also become popular alongside other B vitamins as a hangover remedy because it can help reduce fatigue.

Researcher Antonio Jesús Fernández Romero explained that vitamin B12 “has proven to meet the necessary conditions to act as a good catalyst because, during discharge, it catalyzes the reduction of oxygen to water and, during recharging, it promotes the production of oxygen”.

Recent findings suggest that the difficulty was keeping the vitamin inside the battery. Because B12 dissolves readily in water, it could not simply be added to a battery that uses a water-based electrolyte. The researchers solved this problem by attaching the vitamin to single-walled carbon nanotubes, extremely thin carbon structures that hold it in place while allowing it to support the chemical reactions. Their approach mimicked “the process by which amino acids bind together in proteins.”.

The prototype was developed by the Physical Chemistry research group (FQM-204) at the University of Córdoba’s Chemical Institute for Energy and the Environment (IQUEMA). As study author Manuel Cano Luna explained, “we looked at the properties we can find in naturally occurring materials to use them in latest batteries.”.

This is the group’s third battery prototype using a biological molecule as a catalyst. Earlier experiments involved hemoglobin, which contains iron (II), and catalase, which contains iron (III). The key advance with vitamin B12 is that the resulting battery can be recharged, completing up to 250 cycles in the researchers’ tests.

Although the prototype remains experimental, the findings suggest that naturally occurring molecules could contribute to cheaper, more sustainable energy storage systems. With further development, rechargeable zinc-air batteries could eventually help store surplus electricity from renewable energy sources, addressing one of the challenges of transitioning toward cleaner energy.

Reference: “A vitamin B12-based air electrode for high-performance rechargeable zinc–air batteries” by García-Caballero, Valentín, López-León, Miguel, G. Argudo, Pablo, Camacho, Luis, Rodríguez Mellado, José M., Martín-Romero, Maria T., Abad, José, Fernández Romero, Antonio J. and Cano, Manuel, , Journal of Materials Chemistry A. DOI: 10.1039/d6ta02773c.

The authors would like to acknowledge the financial support from MICIU/AEI/10.13039/501100011033 and FEDER/UE (PID2022-139191OB-C32 project). M. L.-L. Acknowledges the Ministry of Science, Innovation, and Universities for an FPU predoctoral contract (FPU24/03131).

#164. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1199 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • Industry observers note that unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • According to recent reports, by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Industry observers note that unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

According to recent reports, by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," states Yiwen Chu.

According to recent reports, the breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an key role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

In a recent development, chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Sources indicate that quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are at the moment beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

In a recent development, one of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

It has been revealed that in the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

In a recent development, many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

It has been revealed that however, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Sources indicate that another vital benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments highlighted that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

Sources indicate that one of the most significant findings is that the newly introduced system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

Industry observers note that however, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising upcoming route toward making those machines a reality.
