#108. Tech Report: Why we buy: 5 thinking errors companies exploit to make you shop

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words)
General 🌐 Newscientist

Tech Report: Why we buy: 5 thinking errors companies exploit to make you shop

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Newscientist

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Check your subscription status, update your details and more.
  • The Queen of Christmas, Mariah Carey, has declared “It’s time!!!!”, which can only mean one thing: the holiday season is officially upon us, with all the extra spending that entails.
  • If past years are anything to go by, I suspect that many of my impulse purchases will spark more guilt than joy, as they gather dust in the corners of my home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check your subscription status, update your details and more.

The Queen of Christmas, Mariah Carey, has declared “It’s time!!!!”, which can only mean one thing: the holiday season is officially upon us, with all the extra spending that entails.

If past years are anything to go by, I suspect that many of my impulse purchases will spark more guilt than joy, as they gather dust in the corners of my home. So, I was extremely interested to read a copy of Influenced: The science of why we buy by Aarron Atkinson-Toal, published last week.

Industry observers note that an assistant professor in marketing at Durham University in the UK, Atkinson-Toal has spent much of his career studying the forces that influence consumer decision-making. Like many before him, he argues that our judgements are often driven by cognitive shortcuts called heuristics that help the brain to appraise a situation without consciously deliberating over every piece of data it receives.

Sources indicate that the late Nobel prizewinning psychologist Daniel Kahneman described this intuitive thinking as System 1, as opposed to the conscious, careful calculations of System 2. Leaning on System 1 can save us a lot of time and effort in the information overload of daily life. Unfortunately, this efficiency comes at the cost of accuracy and logic, since it can be easily swayed by our emotions and tends to bypass our self-control.

“It is believed that up to 95 per cent of daily decisions are made in this subconscious and reactive way,” writes Atkinson-Toal. “That is a lot of decisions being made without full awareness of actions and consequences.”.

In Influenced, he sets out the many ways that marketing schemes have been designed to exploit this – and highlights some of the most important errors that may influence our shopping – and describes our feelings after we have made our purchases.

How rethinking your relationship with time could give you more of it.

In the run-up to Black Friday, we’ll see many time-limited deals that promise huge savings. When we are rushed, we are especially likely to fall into System 1 thinking, as we prioritise speed over accuracy.

Imagine you see a new phone, discounted from £1000 to £800. Under time pressure, you will be more easily swayed by your fear of regret for missing out on the bargain, since you know that you can save £200 if you buy it now. If you had more time to decide, however, you might conclude that £800 is still too much to spend for a relatively minor upgrade.

Devices like countdown timers on online retailers’ websites when you put something in your virtual cart “are attempts to make the fast decision-making process of shoppers even faster,” writes Atkinson-Toal.

To make matters worse, these limited-time offers promote the idea of scarcity, which we tend to associate with a higher value, leading us to believe that we’re getting a better deal, argues Atkinson-Toal.

When you see a “low stock alert” on a website, or an emptying shelf in a physical shop, you are primed to make a similar judgement – compelling you to buy the product.

The anchoring effect was one of the first cognitive biases that Kahneman and his colleague the late Amos Tversky documented. In one study, they asked participants to spin a “wheel of fortune” containing the numbers 0 to 100 before estimating the percentage of African countries in the UN. They found that the random number chosen by the wheel of fortune “anchored” the participants’ answers: the higher the random number, the bigger their estimate.

Anchoring is prevalent in sales. If you are first recommended a high-priced product, you will be more inclined to pay more for whatever you finally choose to buy, because the luxury good has anchored your judgement of what is reasonable.

How to build powerful microhabits for your wellbeing – and keep them.

Sources indicate that despite our amazing capacity for mental time travel, we tend to be pretty poor at estimating how decisions today will affect our feelings in the future. We prioritise immediate rewards over our future wellbeing, a habit known as temporal discounting. We also struggle to predict how we will feel about future stresses, which are known as errors in affective forecasting.

Industry observers note that imagine you have been putting money aside for a trip next year. When you see that advert for a upcoming phone, you focus on the instant excitement of unwrapping the shiny new product and forget the disappointment that may arise from finding your piggy bank empty when you come to book your holiday. “It is easier to write off today’s decisions as tomorrow’s problem,” Atkinson-Toal indicates in the book.

The sheer array of options available can leave us feeling bamboozled – a phenomenon that is sometimes called choice overload. Studies show that the more offers available, the less satisfied we may feel after having made our decision. “After the rush of Black Friday, or any purchase made under time pressure, reality often kicks in about just how much has been spent on things that were not needed, fuelling a feeling of regret and likely leading to more product returns,” writes Atkinson-Toal.

All of which is certainly going to encourage me to exercise my critical thinking before I start my holiday shopping – especially when I feel rushed to make a quick choice. Simple awareness of the forces shaping our decision-making is likely to help. From my own writing on rational thinking, I know that a good rule of thumb is to actively argue with your intuitions. If you feel the impulse to buy something super expensive, give yourself enough time to list two or more reasons why it might be a bad idea. Maybe you will still conclude that you have found the ideal bargain, but at least you will have engaged some System 2 thinking to curb some of System 1’s excesses.

I’ll also be bearing in mind two reliable findings from the broader psychological literature. Spending money on experiences tends to bring greater happiness than buying physical things; and spending money on others tends to bring greater happiness than spending money on ourselves. Hosting a generous festive party, in other words, is more likely to leave me full of good cheer than any newly introduced device.

Dan Garisto is a freelance reporter in Syracuse, New York.

International students earn almost 40% of science and engineering PhDs awarded in the United States.Credit: Bill Pugliano/Getty.

The number of international students arriving in the United States in August for the start of the academic year has fallen by 28% since 2024, reaching the lowest level since the depths reached in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

According to recent reports, data from the federal National Travel and Tourism Office show that the number of incoming student-visa holders fell from 387,000 in August 2024 to 277,000 in August 2026 (see ‘Students stay away’). The trend has been driven by a decline in students from India and China, whose numbers dropped by about 50,000 and 23,000, respectively, from 2024 to 2026.

Source: National Travel and Tourism Office (NTTO); Nature analysis.

The number of applications from international students to US PhD programmes also declined over the past year, falling 21% from 2025 to 2026, according to a survey of 55 members of the Association of American Universities (AAU), a coalition of research-intensive schools.

These decreases are squeezing already strained university budgets, and researchers worry about the impact on US science. “I can’t imagine a more effective way for the US to cede its dominance in critical scientific fields to China and Europe than by reducing international students,” states Nigel Goldenfeld, a physicist at the University of California, San Diego. In 2024, international students earned 38% of the science and engineering PhDs awarded in the United States.

The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing.

The great university shake-up: four charts show how global higher education is changing.

According to recent reports, the administration of US president Donald Trump has introduced several restrictions on visas and international travel since Trump took office in early 2025. Last month, the administration also attempted to place a US$100,000 levy on science and engineering students enrolling in extended Optional Practical Training (OPT), a work programme used by hundreds of thousands of recent graduates that is the largest pipeline of scientific talent into the United States. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which issued the proposal, stated that it is meant to “combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect U.S. workers”.

Recent findings suggest that federal judges have suspended the OPT charge and other efforts that the administration made to curb immigration. But higher-education specialists link these attempts to the large decrease in new overseas students, who, they say, can no longer count a US education as a stable investment. “Uncertainty has become policy, and that has registered in the hearts and minds of students,” says Chris Glass, a higher-education researcher at Boston College in Massachusetts.

Recent findings suggest that the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia have also seen drops in enrolment of international students after placing new limits on these populations. But the US policies are especially restrictive, Glass says.

A spokesperson for the White House did not respond to Nature’s request for comment.

#106. Scientists Discover Mysterious New Fish in the Red Sea – and Have Never Seen It Again

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (662 words)
General 🌐 Scitechdaily

Scientists Discover Mysterious New Fish in the Red Sea – and Have Never Seen It Again

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists discovered a tiny newly introduced fish species in the Red Sea but have never found it again, suggesting it may live mostly on deeper reefs that remain largely unexplored.
  • In Greek mythology, Charon ferried the dead across a river into the underworld.
  • “One of the most striking features of the new species is the golden spots scattered across its tail fin,” stated study leader Viktor Nunes Peinemann of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) in Saudi Arabia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists discovered a tiny newly introduced fish species in the Red Sea but have never found it again, suggesting it may live mostly on deeper reefs that remain largely unexplored.

In Greek mythology, Charon ferried the dead across a river into the underworld. People were traditionally buried with a coin to pay for the crossing. That tradition helped inspire the name of a newly described fish species from the northern Red Sea, Charon’s pygmygoby (Trimma charon).

“One of the most striking features of the new species is the golden spots scattered across its tail fin,” stated study leader Viktor Nunes Peinemann of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) in Saudi Arabia. “They cover most of the fin and resemble small gold coins.”.

The tiny fish is translucent, with a broad orange-red stripe and an unusual four-part eye. The two known specimens measure just 12 and 17 millimeters long, roughly half an inch and two-thirds of an inch.

Recent findings suggest that the latest species resembles the pallid pygmygoby (Trimma anaima), a fish found from East Africa to the Pacific but never recorded in the Red Sea. Genetic data suggest the two are close relatives, although further work is needed to confirm that relationship.

“While one species seems to have spread across much of the Indian and Pacific Oceans, its closest relative appears to have stayed in the Red Sea and evolved separately for millions of years,” noted Peinemann.

Researchers collected the two specimens in May 2023 at Walih Island, at the entrance to a cave on a steep reef slope. They were found 30 meters, about 98 feet, below the surface, the maximum depth of the team’s scientific diving. Extensive searches of similar habitats since then have produced no further sightings. “So far, the entire species is known from only a single encounter and two specimens,” noted Peinemann.

In a recent development, the team suspects that the encounter took place at the shallow edge of the species’ range. The fish may be more common on largely unexplored mesophotic reefs below 30 meters, where sunlight is faint. That possible habitat provides another connection to its mythological namesake.

“These dark, deeper, unexplored reefs could be viewed as a kind of ‘underworld’ beneath the shallow, well-lit, and better studied reefs most of us are more familiar with,” he remarked.

“Red Sea reefs below that depth almost certainly hold more undiscovered gobies.”.

Industry observers note that the discovery brings the number of known Trimma species in the Red Sea to 11, making it the region’s most species-rich goby genus. At least nine appear to live nowhere else in the world. To help researchers distinguish them, the paper provides an illustrated identification key to all 11 species, along with photographs and field notes describing where each lives.

Industry observers note that the study is published in the open-access journal ZooKeys. Peinemann is based in the Marine Science Program within KAUST’s Division of Biological and Environmental Science and Engineering. His co-authors are Matthew D. Tietbohl Talas and Michael L. Berumen of KAUST, and Sergey V. Bogorodsky of the Senckenberg Research Institute and Natural History Museum Frankfurt, Germany.

Recent findings suggest that “Knowing which species are present, how to accurately identify them, and where they live, is the most foundational step to building a stronger understanding of these species and ecosystems,” said Peinemann. “They still have many secrets and deserve much more attention.”.

A upcoming AI model, called Brain-IT, can transform brain scans into images and reverse the process, turning images into what they'd look like as brain activity.

It has been revealed that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool can use brain scans to recreate the images people looked at with eerie accuracy.

The system, called Brain-IT, uses data from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes visual input. A computer model then predicts both the broad layout of an image and high-level information about its content. It then passes those predictions to an AI image generator, researchers explained in a study uploaded to the preprint database arXiv. The research was presented at the ICLR 2026 conference, held April 23-25, and publicized by its authors in September.

Brain-IT builds on an approach called the Universal Brain Encoder. That model begins with an image and then predicts the fMRI response that would be expected in individual "voxels" ‪—‬ small 3D units ‪—‬ in a brain scan.

"The key idea is that every voxel, a tiny cube of brain tissue, gets its own learned vector that captures what it cares about in images," stated study first author Roman Beliy, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

According to recent reports, some voxels may be tuned to relatively simple elements of an image, such as edges, textures or locations. Others might be responding to higher-level abstract categories, like faces, bodies or scenes.

Traditional image-to-fMRI systems have generally been custom trained for each participant and dataset. The Universal Brain Encoder is more flexible. It learns from data from multiple people and can transfer information across participants, datasets or different MRI systems with varying magnetic-field strengths, according to the study.

It has been revealed that A voxel can determine which parts of an image are relevant to it based on its learned profile, essentially saying, "I recognize edges. Which parts of this image are edges?".

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

According to recent reports, the Universal Brain Encoder starts with an image and predicts brain activity; Brain-IT starts with measured brain activity and reconstructs the image the person saw. In other words,it asks "based on this brain activity, what was the subject looking at?". It sorts thousands of tiny brain-scan measurements from the visual cortex into 128 groups based on the kinds of visual information they tend to carry.

The system then lets those groups share clues with one another, allowing it to combine, for example, information about a scene's shape, color and possible objects, to build a more complete picture of the image, Beliy explained.

Industry observers note that the decoder produces two types of visual predictions. One captures semantic information ‪—‬ the features associated with what is likely in a scene; for an image of a dog standing in grass, for instance, this would include things like the features of a dog and an outdoor, grassy setting. The other captures structural information, like the broad visual layout or how forms are arranged.

In the above example, this would be aspects like the outline of the dog or where it was positioned in the frame. The structural prediction gives the generator a starting point for the image, rather than beginning from pure noise, while the semantic info guides an image generator that removes the remaining static until the image emerges.

Although the latest tool can recreate what people see, it can't reproduce memories or imagined scenes.

"We're not reading people's thoughts," study co-author Michal Irani, a computer scientist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, told Live Science. "The images we do manage to recover from fMRI require people's cooperation and full intended collaboration.".

The original image of a baseball game (left) and the reconstruction (right) generated by the Brain-IT AI model based on the brain activity of a person viewing the image.

Recent findings suggest that brain-IT's synthetic images were compared with the images that participants saw. Brain-IT surpassed prior leading methods on standard objective reconstruction metrics and produced more faithful results, the study authors wrote. The system shined when limited fMRI data from a new participant was available, with just one hour of data from a new participant producing results as accurately as earlier approaches that had been trained on 40 hours of recordings.

A high-scoring or realistic-looking output should not be mistaken for a perfect copy of what someone saw, however.

In the final stage of processing, the system uses an off-the-shelf diffusion generator trained on massive numbers of images. Models like this generate plausible images and can smooth textures, sharpen facial features or fill in missing details.

Industry observers note that beliy noted this "beautification" can make reconstructions more polished and convincing and introduce details that don't necessarily come from the brain data itself. In other words, the scan constrains the generated picture, but the AI model supplies some of its realism from learned patterns in photographs.

While the new system produces impressive results for seen images, it can't be used to reconstruct an imagined or remembered image.

In a recent development, "Brain-IT relies on how the brain processes a seen image," Irani said. "Information flows from the eyes to the primary visual cortex and onward through a series of visual areas that recognize objects and scenes.".

In a controlled experiment, researchers also know precisely which image was shown, giving the model a target during training and evaluation. In contrast, memories and imagined images do not offer the same clean reference. They can be vague and shaped by brain networks involved in memory and thought, with only partial and weaker reactivation of visual regions, Irani said. One limitation that would prevent this technology from being widely deployed is that the only way to get reliable results is from fMRI scanning, which is cumbersome and expensive. The team is presently experimenting with using easier-to-collect electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which is obtained via electrodes on the head, but that work is in the very preliminary stages, according to Irani.

Sources indicate that the newly introduced system could help brain researchers better understand which visual information is represented in different brain regions, how those regions interact and how individuals’ patterns differ. Such tools could eventually reveal differences in visual processing that could help clinicians spot neurological, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

"There are numerous useful medical applications which we are currently striving toward," Irani said. "These include using our brain encoder/decoder to detect and analyze brain disorders such as MS, PTSD, autism and psychiatric disorders.".

Breaking: Scientists Crack a Decades-Old Mystery That Could Unlock Faster Internet

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By untangling how the crystal barium titanate interacts with light, researchers have supplied data that could reduce costly trial and error in designing faster optical communication devices.
  • When light carries data through a communication device, absorption by the materials inside can weaken the signal.
  • Sources indicate that for a promising material called barium titanate, or BTO, those measurements have varied widely for decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By untangling how the crystal barium titanate interacts with light, researchers have supplied data that could reduce costly trial and error in designing faster optical communication devices.

When light carries data through a communication device, absorption by the materials inside can weaken the signal. Engineers trying to build faster, more efficient devices need to predict how light will travel through those materials and how much will be lost before they commit to a design.

Sources indicate that for a promising material called barium titanate, or BTO, those measurements have varied widely for decades. A KAIST-led research team has now clarified how it interacts with light, providing data that could help engineers design devices more reliably and reduce costly rounds of fabrication and redesign.

BTO offers a useful way to control light because applying an electric field changes its refractive index, a measure of how much light slows as it passes through a material. Its strong response to an electric field, known as the Pockels effect, makes it promising for optical modulators. These devices use electrical signals to control light and encode information onto it.

The difficulty is that a BTO crystal can contain small regions, called domains, with different crystal orientations. Those regions can interact with light differently, so measuring them together blends their responses. That makes it harder to determine the material’s underlying optical properties and predict how it will behave in a device.

Recent findings suggest that to reduce that mixing, the team led by Professor Min Seok Jang of KAIST’s School of Electrical Engineering examined two types of single-crystal BTO samples with relatively uniform domain orientations. The researchers used Mueller-matrix spectroscopic ellipsometry, a technique that measures changes in light’s polarization, or the orientation of its electric-field vibrations, when it reflects from or passes through a material. Those changes provide information about how the material affects light.

Sources indicate that their analysis covered wavelengths from 190 nanometers (nm) to 40 micrometers (μm), spanning the ultraviolet to the far-infrared. Because BTO interacts with light differently across that range, the researchers divided it into three spectral regions and used an analytical approach suited to each. They determined how the refractive index and absorption properties vary with both wavelength and crystal orientation.

According to recent reports, the team also developed a method for calculating the overall optical response of a crystal containing differently oriented domains. Using the orientations and relative proportions of those domains, the method accounts for the mixed internal structure that had made BTO’s properties difficult to establish.

Even in the wavelength range where BTO is nearly transparent, the researchers were able to quantify very weak absorption. They combined ellipsometry with separate transmittance measurements, which record how much light passes through a sample, to determine extinction coefficients as low as approximately 10⁻⁵ in the 2–10 μm range. The extinction coefficient describes how strongly a material absorbs light, with smaller values indicating weaker absorption.

Recent findings suggest that together, these measurements help answer two practical questions about a waveguide, a structure that guides light through a device. The refractive index helps designers predict how the light will travel, while the extinction coefficient helps them estimate how much will be lost to absorption. Engineers can use the data to assess devices of different sizes and shapes before fabrication. Potential applications include communications modulators, devices that generate light at new wavelengths, and circuits that process quantum information using light.

In a recent development, KAIST, led by President Choongsik Bae, declared the work on November 8. The study was conducted in collaboration with Professor Harry A. Atwater’s team at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS), and U.S.-based J.A. Woollam Co.

Sources indicate that “This study reveals the optical response of barium titanate, which had long remained unclear, and provides a reliable reference for how the material interacts with light,” noted Professor Min Seok Jang. He added that the findings are expected to contribute to optical communication devices that reduce light loss and enable faster data transmission, as well as quantum photonic devices that require precise control of light.

Reference: “Broadband Optical Characterization of Tetragonal Barium Titanate by Mueller-Matrix Spectroscopic Ellipsometry” by Jiwon Kang, Nina Hong, Christopher M. Yi, Yun Su Go, Martin Thomaschewski, Hwi Je Woo, Prachi Thureja, Junghoon Jahng, Harry A. Atwater and Min Seok Jang, 20 October 2026, ACS Photonics. DOI: 10.1021/acsphotonics.6c01514.

Sources indicate that this research was supported by the Culture, Sports and Tourism R&D Program through the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA), with funding from the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism; the Basic Science Research Program through the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), with funding from the Ministry of Education; the Ministry of Science and ICT; and the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR).

#103. Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Walking and weight training may not be enough to keep your bones strong

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it.
  • Industry observers note that the findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training.
  • To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the type of exercise you do may be more important for your bones than how long you spend doing it. Researchers at Semmelweis University have found that intense physical activity involving sudden bursts of movement, quick changes in direction, and sharp turns appears especially effective at stimulating new bone formation.

Industry observers note that the findings, published in Sports Medicine - Open, suggest that certain fast-paced sports may provide greater benefits for bone metabolism than walking or conventional strength training. The research could help scientists develop more effective exercise recommendations for preserving bone health and reducing the risk of osteoporosis.

Why Exercise Intensity Matters for Bone Health.

To investigate how different forms of exercise affect bones, the Semmelweis University team reviewed 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults.

Instead of relying on bone mineral density measurements, which can take considerable time to reveal changes, the researchers examined blood markers associated with the production of latest bone tissue. These biological indicators can reveal how bones respond to exercise within a matter of weeks, allowing scientists to detect changes much sooner.

Recent findings suggest that "What makes our study unique is that we examined not only the type of exercise - whether endurance, resistance, or combined training - but also exercise intensity, frequency, and duration. Our goal was to determine which forms of exercise stimulate bone metabolism most effectively and which appear to be less beneficial from this perspective," mentioned Dr. Péter Ferdinandy, Vice-Rector for Science and Innovations at Semmelweis University and senior author of the study.

Football and Handball Show Surprising Bone Benefits.

The strongest responses were associated with vigorous sports that repeatedly require players to accelerate, change direction, turn, and make powerful movements.

Sources indicate that recreational football and handball stood out in particular. These activities were linked to increases of up to 45-46 percent in blood markers associated with bone formation, suggesting that they may provide a particularly strong stimulus for the body's bone-building processes.

It has been revealed that more conventional activities generally produced smaller responses. Walking, step aerobics, and standard resistance workouts performed in the gym were less effective at stimulating the measured indicators of bone formation.

The findings were especially unexpected for resistance training, which is commonly recommended as a way to support skeletal health.

It has been revealed that "The most surprising finding was that resistance training did not produce a significant effect on markers of bone metabolism, even though several professional guidelines recommend this type of exercise for maintaining bone health. Likewise, low- or moderate-intensity endurance exercise, such as walking or jogging, showed no meaningful long-term effect," explained Viktória Barna, PhD student at Semmelweis University and first author of the study.

Why Walking and Weight Training Still Matter.

The results do not suggest that walking, jogging, or other less demanding activities should be abandoned. These forms of exercise continue to offer important health benefits, even if they do not stimulate the measured bone-building processes as strongly as more intense sports.

Recent findings suggest that rather, the research indicates that maintaining healthy bones may require greater mechanical stimulation than many everyday activities provide. Movements that place more substantial forces on the skeleton appear to produce a stronger response in the biological processes involved in forming latest bone.

However, the researchers stress that people should not suddenly begin strenuous exercise without preparing appropriately.

According to recent reports, this is especially vital for individuals with cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, or metabolic conditions, as well as those who already have osteoporosis. Anyone in these groups who is considering a upcoming activity or a more physically demanding exercise routine should first speak with their treating physician, general practitioner, or a sports medicine specialist. Medical guidance can help determine whether the activity and its intensity are suitable for their health and physical capabilities.

Could High-Intensity Exercise Help Prevent Osteoporosis?

Recent findings suggest that the findings offer a new perspective on how exercise could be used to maintain bone health as people age. While the analysis focused on markers of bone metabolism rather than direct changes in bone density, the results suggest that vigorous activity may encourage early biological changes that support bone formation.

"According to the World Health Organization, regular physical activity offers numerous health benefits. However, our findings suggest that low-intensity exercise alone is not sufficient to stimulate bone metabolism. High-intensity exercise may trigger early beneficial changes in bone formation, potentially helping to slow bone loss and support healthy aging," summarized Dr. Nóra Sydó, clinical specialist and co-author of the study.

The researchers believe that understanding which movements most effectively stimulate bone formation could lead to better exercise programs designed to preserve skeletal strength and help prevent osteoporosis.

For now, the findings highlight an important distinction: staying physically active is beneficial for overall health, but keeping bones healthy over the long term may depend not only on how much people move, but also on how powerfully and dynamically they move.

Recent findings suggest that next, choose your style: Freestanding stoves have finished sides and back guards, allowing them to stand alone. Most electric cooktops feature smooth surfaces with heating elements housed beneath tempered glass or ceramic, though traditional coil-style options still exist and tend to be much cheaper. Smooth-top stoves are easier to clean, while coil burners are simpler to replace if one fails.

Conventional ovens rely on stationary heating elements—one at the bottom for baking, one at the top for broiling—leading to natural heat rise and possible temperature variations. Standard convection improves on this by adding a fan to circulate hot air for more even cooking. European convection (also called “true” convection) goes a step further, with a third heating element behind the fan for uniform heat distribution across multiple racks.

Sources indicate that for everyday cooking, conventional or standard convection works fine. But if you want more precise, even baking and roasting, true convection is worth considering. Be prepared for a slight learning curve if switching to convection, as most recipes are designed for conventional ovens. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every print subscription comes with full digital access.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access.

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds.

According to recent reports, A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus.

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

According to recent reports, the well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

Industry observers note that in patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, indicates Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the Latest England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the newly introduced study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is notable because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, indicates Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

In a recent development, researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

According to recent reports, the team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle states, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

Rocket Lab will launch its 100th space mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), and you can watch the milestone liftoff live.

An Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite is scheduled to launch from Rocket Lab's New Zealand site on Saturday, during a window that opens at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local time).

The mission, which Rocket Lab calls "The Mountain God Rises," will be the 100th to date for the California-based company. You can watch it live via Rocket Lab, or directly via the company. Coverage will begin about 30 minutes before launch.

Industry observers note that rocket Lab launched for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-new Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand. That effort failed, but Electron bounced back on its second-ever liftoff, delivering several cubesats to low Earth orbit (LEO) in January 2018.

In the years since, the 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron has become one of the most prolific and reliable rockets in the world, carrying small payloads to the final frontier for a variety of customers.

And it's hitting the century mark in record-breaking fashion: No commercially developed rocket has gotten there faster, not even SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, according to Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck.

"It's an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket, and a threshold rarely crossed in modern spaceflight," Beck noted on Monday (Nov. 9), during Rocket Lab's third-quarter earnings call with investors. "But what matters most to us and our customers is that we have achieved a 96% reliability rate across 99 debuts.".

Electron will meet the moment in style on Saturday morning, thanks to some fancy livery.

"Black rocket 🤝 Golden milestone. Electron is all dressed up for launch 100," Rocket Lab remarked via X on Tuesday (Nov. 10), in a post that shared a photo of the specially painted first stage.

Not all of Rocket Lab's missions have gone orbital, it should be noted: A suborbital variant of Electron known as HASTE, which customers use to test technologies in a hypersonic flight environment, has nine missions under its belt to date.

It has been revealed that "The Mountain God Rises" will be Rocket Lab's 11th launch to date for the Tokyo-based tech giant iQPS, which is building a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO. If all goes to proposal, Electron's upper "kick stage" will deploy a single iQPS spacecraft 357 miles (575 kilometers) above Earth.

SAR satellites can see through cloud cover and image our planet at night as well as during the day, offering key advantages over spacecraft that are optimized to view in optical wavelengths.

#99. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1635 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults.
  • Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50.
  • Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. Upcoming research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.

In a recent development, to investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

Industry observers note that "This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy remarked. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

In a recent development, murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect.".

According to recent reports, this effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

It has been revealed that "I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.".

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49.

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

According to recent reports, the research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," noted Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations.

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

Sources indicate that this increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

"There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy remarked. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study indicates that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.".

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

According to recent reports, murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

Industry observers note that the researchers then initiative to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce crucial features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical.

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Sources indicate that murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

According to recent reports, current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Industry observers note that colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

It has been revealed that along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

According to latest projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

Recent findings suggest that but the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Recent findings suggest that for the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

Sources indicate that by year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”.

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

Industry observers note that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have tech giant this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

In a recent development, 2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is right now orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#94. Most of the deep ocean food supply in the Gulf of Mexico suddenly vanished, and most scientists blame the Deepwater Horizon oil spill

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words)
General 🌐 Earth

Most of the deep ocean food supply in the Gulf of Mexico suddenly vanished, and most scientists blame the Deepwater Horizon oil spill

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep-sea fish, krill and squid in the Gulf of Mexico fell 60 to 85 percent after 2011, and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill is the leading suspect.
  • Marine biologists have always assumed the deep ocean is the safest and most stable ecosystem on the planet.
  • Unfortunately, a massive die-off in the Gulf of Mexico just proved that assumption is dangerously incorrect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep-sea fish, krill and squid in the Gulf of Mexico fell 60 to 85 percent after 2011, and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill is the leading suspect.

Marine biologists have always assumed the deep ocean is the safest and most stable ecosystem on the planet. Because it is so vast and isolated from human life, they believed it was practically impossible to destroy.

Unfortunately, a massive die-off in the Gulf of Mexico just proved that assumption is dangerously incorrect.

In a recent development, between 2011 and 2015, the fish, shrimp, krill and squid living in the dark water below about 650 feet (200 meters) lost 60 to 85 percent of their numbers. Surveys through 2023 have not found them coming back.

It has been revealed that the crash indicates up in two records. One is the nets that scientists have towed through the same patch of ocean in the Gulf of Mexico for 13 years. The other is ship sonar, whose echoes come back weaker when fewer animals are swimming below.

Nothing in the water itself, not temperature, oxygen or food, changed in step with it. The one event that did line up in time was the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. The authors consider this the most likely explanation.

Tracey Sutton of Nova Southeastern University led the work, with colleagues at Florida International University, the University of South Florida and NOAA.

It has been revealed that the paper is careful about what it can show. The spill’s role is inferred from timing and from the absence of any natural driver, not from an experiment.

In a recent development, the record begins in January 2011, three months after the well was sealed. A nine-month campaign towed a net through a grid of 46 stations across the northern Gulf of Mexico. That first campaign is the baseline against which everything since has been measured.

The same net, with six separate bags that open and close on command, was towed again on nine shorter cruises between 2015 and 2023.

Each tow sampled from the surface down to 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) in five depth bands, at noon and again at midnight.

Towing twice a day matters, because most of these animals rise thousands of feet toward the surface every night to feed and sink again at dawn.

Only samples from the Gulf of Mexico’s own water mass were compared, since the Loop Current, which enters from the south, carries fewer animals and would have muddied the count.

Industry observers note that fish numbers per unit of water dropped 63.5 percent between 2011 and the later cruises. Shrimp and krill together dropped 62 percent, and small squid and their relatives dropped 59.7 percent.

Recent findings suggest that the groups that feed almost everything else fell hardest. Krill dropped 72.8 percent and lanternfish 62.9 percent. Bristlemouths, tiny fish that may be the most numerous vertebrates on Earth, dropped 69 percent.

Sources indicate that the sonar agreed. Sound bouncing back from the top 650 feet (200 meters) at night, when the migrators are up feeding, was 40 percent weaker after 2011.

A drop that size over three and a half years is bigger than any change recorded over 60 years in the California Current. That is the only other long-running count of deep-sea fish.

In an interview with Earth.com, Sutton stated the fall itself is not the part that surprised him most. “The slow recovery is the most surprising finding, with the realization that this downward shift may be irreversible,” he said.

In a recent development, and the dense swarms that predators depend on nearly disappeared. Across 134 full-column tows in the whole series, only one catch after the decline held more fish than the leanest catch of 2011.

A crowd that shrinks fast can lose genetic variety, so the team sequenced three common lanternfish species collected between 2011 and 2023, the longest such record for any deep-sea animal.

In a recent development, two of the three highlighted it. In one species, a standard measure of genetic variety fell about 11 percent between 2011 and 2016, then recovered partway by 2023. A second species followed the same path a few years later. The third showed no clear trend.

Recent findings suggest that the same tows kept adding to the list of what lives down there. Sutton told Earth.com that the deep interior holds more kinds of animals than any other part of the Gulf of Mexico, coral reefs included.

Recent findings suggest that his team has recorded almost 200 fish species there for the first time since the work began, he remarked. That is about one in every nine fish species now known from the Gulf.

“Our knowledge of what lives in the deep ocean is incredibly poor,” he mentioned, “even in the best-studied systems in the world, like the Gulf.”.

Sources indicate that the authors checked their own methods first. The same net, the same crew and the same analysis ran across every year, so a change in gear can’t explain the drop.

Water temperature in the twilight zone from 650 to 2,000 feet (200 to 600 meters) barely moved from year to year, and the deep Gulf stayed well supplied with oxygen. The plankton these animals eat didn’t thin out either; in 2013, mid-decline, it was above average.

So the authors turned to the spill. The Deepwater Horizon blowout on April 20, 2010 released up to 4.9 million barrels of oil over 87 days.

Crews pumped 770,000 gallons (2.9 million liters) of chemical dispersant into the plume at the wellhead, 4,900 feet down.

Oil residues turned up in the eggs of deep-sea fish and the tissues of squid at least six years later, at concentrations known to kill or weaken fish.

Recent findings suggest that the paper does not test oil on these animals directly. It argues from the sequence of events and from what oil did elsewhere. For example, herring in Prince William Sound collapsed four years after the Exxon Valdez spill and have still not recovered.

It has been revealed that the Gulf’s deep-feeding whales eat these animals, and their numbers have been falling too. Long-term counts show Gervais’ beaked whales down 83.4 percent since the spill, and sperm whales down 31 percent. This is more than the spill’s own mortality models predicted.

Tagged sperm whales are now roaming the Gulf instead of feeding in their usual predictable spots.

Endangered Rice’s whales have been recorded feeding near the bottom, often without success. In addition, researchers at sea report seeing thin whales, while stranded ones are often described as emaciated.

In a recent development, sutton mentioned 27 of the 28 whale and dolphin species known from the Gulf live in the open ocean, and nearly all of them eat the animals his team counted. Less prey means fewer marine mammals, he said, “and those that are there may be less fit.”.

Industry observers note that bluefin and yellowfin tuna, swordfish, marlin, sailfish and sharks feed on the same animals, he stated. So do seabirds that hunt lanternfish at night, including some endangered species.

It has been revealed that these animals also run what scientists call the biological pump, the sinking of carbon from the surface into the deep ocean. “That function affects every person on the planet.”.

Industry observers note that one obvious objection is that the 2011 baseline was a single, nine-month campaign, run just after the spill. The team’s answer is that counts from the 1980s and 1990s at one eastern Gulf station look like 2011, not like anything since.

The authors wrote that the deep Gulf is now in “a sustained, low-abundance state” for which the recovery time, “if even possible, remains unknown.”.

Asked by Earth.com what a recovery would take, Sutton used the researchers’ name for that dark, open water, the deep-pelagic ocean.

“We do not have the capacity to restore the deep-pelagic ocean directly, so the best we can do is give the system time and not make it worse with more pollution,” he said.

Whether the deep Gulf is coming back at all is the open question, and the same grid of stations is where an answer would first show up.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#93. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels.
  • The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways.
  • It has been revealed that testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

It has been revealed that testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns.

It has been revealed that to investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Sources indicate that between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links.

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

It has been revealed that meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Sources indicate that despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," notes Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

#92. Tech Report: Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words)
General 🌐 Sciencenews

Tech Report: Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every print subscription comes with full digital access.
  • A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining.
  • At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access.

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining.

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Recent findings suggest that some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Recent findings suggest that the ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

In a recent development, joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In a recent development, in the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

According to recent reports, the largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a significant hint, McConnell claims, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”.

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, claims Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”.

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Organization was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Firm installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell notes, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”.

It has been revealed that these new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”.

Breaking: The 9 Best Multitools for Fixing Things in a Pinch

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cut, tighten, loosen, open, and twist your way through whatever challenges crop up.
