  • For situations where you don’t have your full tool kit by your side, jump into action like a real-life MacGyver using a multitool.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cut, tighten, loosen, open, and twist your way through whatever challenges crop up.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

For situations where you don’t have your full tool kit by your side, jump into action like a real-life MacGyver using a multitool. These handy pocket-size companions have come a long way from the Swiss Army Knives of yesteryear, boasting major improvements not just in overall design, but in the quality of tools, materials, and the total number of features offered. Modern-day multitools are designed to be twisted, wrenched, and squeezed with just about the same force that any regular item in your toolbox endures.

Industry observers note that A good multitool is typically made of all-stainless steel or equally durable metal with as many as 30 tools integrated into the frame. That remarked, the majority of them still fit comfortably in a pocket and weigh less than a half pound.

There are dozens of multitool manufacturers, so we got our hands on models from established, popular brands like Victorinox, Gerber, Leatherman, SOG, and more to find out which stood out from the pack. Following our tests and in-depth research, these are the multitools we pick up for fixing nearly anything in a pinch.

It’s hard to nail down one aspect of the Arc that I like best, because it does just about everything well. The opening and closing mechanism is responsive and every tool is accessible from the outside. Plus, the 20 listed functions all work well, as opposed to those on some other multitools that feel like afterthoughts for the sake of an eye-popping marketing claim. This effectiveness across the board is precisely why it is our new best overall pick.

Recent findings suggest that in comparison to our former best overall pick, the Victorinox Spirit X, the Arc shines the brightest when looking at its blade. Unlike the Spirit X, which is made entirely of stainless steel, the knife on the Arc is made of MagnaCut. That means it’s more resistant to corrosion and rust and retains its edge longer.

In a recent development, beyond this, the blade is simply wider, longer, and based on a pretty basic touch test, feels a lot sharper. In my hands, it made it easier to poke through boxes sealed with duct tape and slice off a chunk of an apple.

It has been revealed that the Arc also comes with a larger set of scissors, a thicker saw, and a larger file. Furthermore, it’s equipped with a hip clip that slides directly onto your pants while the Spirit X requires a holster that must be looped through your belt to carry it on your person outside of a pocket.

RoverTac’s 12-in-1 initially caught our eye because it has a good number of useful tools—and it’s affordable, too. While it might be bulky and heavy, we have to admit it’s a decent value. We don’t expect it to hold up to intense use, but in a “save your butt” kind of capacity, it’s certainly holds up to light use.

The long-nosed pliers, wire cutter, and wire stripper all worked reasonably well, as did the can and bottle openers and various screwdrivers. RoverTac claims the tool includes a saw blade, but it’s more like a serrated knife, which worked—just not very well.

The plain knife blade is sharper than it looks and easily cut through rope and twine during our tests. The 12-in-1 comes with a sewn nylon sheath to attach to your belt. Don’t expect this to be the pride of your tool collection, but when you need it most, it will be there.

While no multitool can replace a set of full-size hand tools, the Gerber Gear Center-Drive multitool is by far the closest that we’ve tested. The foldable center-axis provides a lot more length in comparison to the average multitool screwdriver, which gives you extra reach for tight spaces.

The blade on the Center-Drive is also the longest of any that we’ve tested. It feels large enough to take on real cutting responsibility like thick rope or small branches. The high-carbon steel also ensures long-term durability so you don’t have to worry about constantly sharpening the blade between uses.

Recent findings suggest that the Center-Drive is bulkier than other options on this list, but the included nylon sheath is designed to slip onto your belt. Another plus is that there’s a full bit set included.

Fresh out of the box, the Swiss Tool Spirit X impressed us with its design and finish. The tools are packed into the frame very closely, like scientific instrumentation. All the tools—save one—deploy from the outside of the frame, so you can access them without much hassle. The company claims 24 tools in this multitool, but we counted 23, including one that’s simply a hook for a lanyard.

According to recent reports, while the needle-nose pliers, wire cutters, scissors, three standard screwdrivers, and can opener work well, it was the less common tools that really impressed us. This is the first multi we’ve seen with a metal saw, which is on the edge of the file. It cut through mild steel hardware surprisingly well, and the file did a nice job cleaning up the edges when we were done.

Industry observers note that the Phillips screwdriver shank flares out at the end so that all four points on the head are the same size, making for very solid engagement. The Spirit X’s bottle opener is made from wide stainless steel stock, which keeps it flat on the bottle cap so it doesn’t slip or cut into the cap. The combination reamer-punch efficiently opens up holes in wood, leather, and soft metals, and it can drill holes through 3⁄4-inch pine board.

An all-around great pick, this multitool will get the job done, no matter what that job happens to be.

Full Victorinox Swiss Tool Spirit X Multitool Review.

According to recent reports, the next iteration in one of Leatherman’s most popular lines comes with a weighty price tag. But it’s justified, since we had a hard time finding fault with the Wave Alpha.

Recent findings suggest that the multitool comes with a standard knife blade, a saw, a file, and a pair of scissors. The file worked well smoothing out nails, and the saw comfortably powered through small branches.

However, we were most pleasantly impressed with the scissors. They’re much larger than any other pair of scissors we've seen on a multitool (“the largest cutting surface ever on a pliers-based Leatherman,” according to the brand). Because of their size and the spring that pushes the handle back up after every snip, we were able to hold the bottom still in hand and easily use our thumb to press down on the blade to cut. This simplified cutting through large pieces of paper, even for those of us who are lefties (since nearly no scissors are designed for cutting with our dominant hand).

According to recent reports, the classic pocket knife is made of MagnaCut steel, which is corrosion-resistant and has great edge retention. During testing, we focused on everyday items like twine, paper, cardboard, and zip ties and opening sealed packages. We never needed more than one stern pull of the blade to get through any of them.

The central tool of the Wave Alpha is the plier-wire cutter, which we found easy to use thanks to the biting grip of the ridges and the ergonomic handle.

According to recent reports, though Leatherman lists 16 tools, we counted closer to 12. For instance, the file is designated as two separate tools, with the traditional flat side counting as one and the diamond-coated edge counting as another. That’s a fairly common embellishment with multitool descriptions.

Full Leatherman Wave Alpha Multitool Review.

With its svelte, minimalist frame featuring three main tools, this Gerber cuts down on the unnecessary junk and keeps its tools simple and effective.

It has been revealed that as a pocket knife–based multitool, it features a full 3-inch, locking plain blade. Although it isn’t the sharpest right out of the box, it cut cleanly through paper, plastic, rope, twine, and steak, and was adequate for some light whittling.

Recent findings suggest that the side opposite the blade features a hex bit driver and scissors. The driver has a reversible bit in a magnetic holder—we love this because you get legit flat and Phillips screwdrivers that just plain work.

The scissors are a bit larger than those found on other models and were easy to control when cutting out intricate shapes from paper to medium cardboard. Between the scissors and the driver is a sharp, narrow awl. We weren't able to use this to drill holes in wood and plastic, but it works well, as intended, to poke holes through leather and canvas.

It has been revealed that rounding out the eight functions is a nice bottle opener that pivots off the end of the tool frame. It doubles as a pry bar (the bottle opener flipped over) and a “hammer” (the wide base of the bottle opener). Is it less a hammer and more just a flat surface for hitting things? Sure. But when you need to finish tapping in a tent stake or small nail, it’ll do.

The plier-based Leatherman Signal comes with several standard items, including a stainless steel blade and a serrated saw. However, it impressed us most with its several outdoor-specific functions.

Sources indicate that these include a detachable ferro rod that, in combination with the serrated saw, creates sparks for your campfire. The ferro rod also doubles as an emergency whistle. During testing, I was particularly pleased with the carabiner on the bottom of the multitool. While not a major feature, being able to clip it onto my hiking backpack and forget about it made it so much easier to carry with me than other options.

It has been revealed that perhaps the only major downside is the hammer tool. It functions more like a blunt, flat end you can use in a pinch.

Everyday life doesn’t always require a saw, hammer, or bulky pliers. The Leatherman Micra is a keychain tool, and it doesn’t pretend to be anything else. The Micra hosts a number of items that are still quite handy when small and, importantly, are often the most useful in day-to-day life.

Industry observers note that the multitool is built around a pair of scissors, which are the perfect size for cutting tags and snipping loose threads. Tools on the body include tweezers, a nail file and cleaner, a small screwdriver, and a bottle opener, among others.

While carrying the Leatherman Micra around, I was genuinely astonished at how often I used it. I frequently pulled it out for small tasks like picking something out from under my nails, plucking a small hair out of place, or tightening the screws on my sunglasses’ hinges.

According to recent reports, the Micra works so well because it knows what it is. The convenience and portability make it hard to go anywhere without it.

In a recent development, with its wide frame and large plier jaws, the Dual-Force is a beast of a multitool. You can open the pliers and slip the pivot to spread the dual-position jaws extra wide to grab large fasteners or objects. The jaws feature three separate gripping areas: two for large or small round objects and one for gripping flat things. We appreciated their versatility for holding well in a variety of situations.

Sources indicate that one of our favorite things about the Dual-Force is that all the other tools are accessible when the pliers are closed. This multitool also features a bit holder with two Phillips and one plain screwdriver bit. We regard these among the most useful multitool screwdrivers available, although they are sometimes difficult to use in tight spaces.

The Dual-Force is rounded out with a large knife, a saw blade, and a three-sided file. The knife blade is reasonably sharp out of the box, and we easily cut through thick rope with it. We used the saw blade to cut both green and dried-out sticks and branches with relative ease. We were able to use the file on both wood and metal, although it was better suited for the metal.

While the number of tools and functionalities on your multitool isn’t the only measure of how helpful it’ll be, it does give you a sense of its versatility. The multitools we recommend have anywhere from five to 20 or more different functions.

Note that, in their descriptions, manufacturers often count different capabilities of a specific tool individually to arrive at a higher number of “tools.” Pliers, for example, may be counted three or four times if they can function as needle-nose pliers, regular pliers, wire cutters, and wire strippers.

Sources indicate that it’s key to pay attention to the quality of each tool and, of course, how often you’ll use them. For instance, a multitool with a screwdriver attachment is great, but if that multitool’s grip doesn’t give you the leverage to twist off seized screws or only comes with one screwdriver bit, it’s far less effective in practice.

In a recent development, we recommend starting your search by listing three or four tools you use most. Then, opt for a multitool that performs well at those functions. A multitool that has a few tools you use frequently will end up being more valuable to you than one packed to the brim with tools you don’t use much at all.

Sources indicate that one of the key reasons to own a multitool is for its portability and convenience compared with carrying a full set of tools. So, if you can’t fit it in a pocket or in the center console of your car, it’s probably too significant. That mentioned, size isn’t everything. Each item on a multitool needs enough space from the others to work effectively, and you need to make sure you have a good grip for leverage.

The weight of a multitool only becomes a problem if it is too heavy to comfortably clip onto a belt or slip into a pocket. The majority of the tools on our list are made of stainless steel, which is durable yet relatively lightweight.

According to recent reports, can a Multitool Replace a Tool Kit? In short, no. Multitools are useful in a pinch or when you just need them for a quick fix, but they cannot replace a full tool kit. The biggest utility of a multitool is its convenience. It can function well enough for small repairs or to get by when you’ve got nothing else nearby.

According to recent reports, we designed our tests to utilize every tool and function of each model. We carved white pine boards and maple branches. We opened bottles, cans, and shipping packaging. We disassembled and reassembled an old British carburetor, an electrical junction box, and a standard three-prong outlet.

Sources indicate that we cut rope, twine, lamp wire, 14-gauge indoor branch circuit wire, maple saplings, branches, paper, and plastic. We also stripped the wires we cut and crimped electrical connectors. With the pliers, we gripped, squeezed, twisted, and turned various bits of hardware. Finally, we filed wood, metal, and even our own fingernails.

Sources indicate that during these tests, we paid close attention to the performance of the tool in the given task, the ease of use, how each multitool ergonomically fit in our hand as we worked, and how we expect each tool to last over a long period of time. After all that was noted and done, we noted our impressions to compile our final list.

It has been revealed that for testing across the board, we evaluated each tool in common situations. For instance, the saw isn’t likely going to cut through 2x4s, so we opted for small branches, twine, and cardboard boxes.

#90. The true power of humans and AI working together as a team is being heavily underestimated right now

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words)
AI & Tech 🌐 Earth

The true power of humans and AI working together as a team is being heavily underestimated right now

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A reanalysis of 74 human-AI studies finds people and AI did best together when AI explanations came with feedback that let humans learn.
  • In a recent development, A person with a good AI assistant should beat either one working alone.
  • A latest recount of those same experiments says they left out something that people need in order to get good at anything – finding out whether they were right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A reanalysis of 74 human-AI studies finds people and AI did best together when AI explanations came with feedback that let humans learn.

In a recent development, A person with a good AI assistant should beat either one working alone. Two years ago a tally of 74 experiments said otherwise: on average, the human-AI pair did worse than whichever partner was better by itself.

A latest recount of those same experiments says they left out something that people need in order to get good at anything – finding out whether they were right.

Only 10 of the 74 studies ever told participants the correct answer after a decision. In the few that did, and that also let the AI explain itself, the pair tended to come out ahead.

In a recent development, julian Berger and Stefan Herzog of the Center for Adaptive Rationality at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin led the reanalysis. Colleagues at the University of Copenhagen and elsewhere in Europe joined them.

According to recent reports, they didn’t run latest experiments. They went back through every study in the 2024 review and coded what each one had let its participants learn.

“Learning effects in human-machine interaction remain virtually unexplored,” Berger remarked.

The 2024 review, published in Nature Human Behaviour, pooled studies in which people worked with an AI system on tasks such as sorting images, predicting house prices, or writing code.

Across 370 experimental conditions, the human-AI pair scored below the stronger partner on average.

Sources indicate that the pair came out ahead only when the human was already better than the AI. When the AI was the stronger one, the pair did worse than the AI by itself. Neither the AI’s stated confidence nor its explanations changed that.

Berger’s team found that the typical study was a single session, with no practice trials, a median of 30 decisions, and no word on whether any of them was correct.

Industry observers note that only 10 studies, 14 percent of the 74, included a condition with outcome feedback. Just three of those looked at whether people’s use of the AI changed over the trials, and none varied feedback on purpose.

Feedback matters because it is how a person learns when to trust an AI assistant and when to overrule it. Without it, a participant who sees the AI’s answer has no way of telling whether the AI, or they themselves, tend to be right.

According to recent reports, the team re-ran the comparison, splitting the 370 conditions by whether people got feedback. With feedback, the pair’s edge over the better partner was slightly positive. Without it, slightly negative.

By the team’s statistics there was an 84 percent probability the gap ran that way, which isn’t enough to be sure of. The team saw a clearer result once it sorted the conditions by AI explanations too.

In the 24 conditions where people got both an explanation of the AI’s reasoning and feedback on the outcome, the pair tended to outperform the better partner alone.

It has been revealed that in the 148 conditions with explanations but no feedback, the pair did clearly worse. Without explanations, feedback made no reliable difference either way.

The authors’ reading is that an explanation helps mainly when a person can check it against results and learn how far to trust it.

Recent findings suggest that because no study varied feedback within an experiment, the team could only compare studies with it against studies without it. Other features of those studies could explain the differences.

In a recent development, in 12 further models that added each of the original review’s other factors, the direction held. Still, they wrote, experiments that switch feedback on and off are needed before anyone can call it a cause.

Most studies also reported only average performance across all trials, which hides any improvement late in a session.

In the three studies with trial-by-trial data, people learned to go along with an AI that was outperforming them when the task gave them something to learn from.

The authors wrote that their estimate may, therefore, understate how much learning helps.

Whether any of this carries over to chatbots is open. Herzog said a conversation with a chatbot could make tailored feedback and explanations easier to deliver.

“But for that to happen, people also need to find out what is actually correct; a chatbot’s answers can be wrong and do not constitute independent feedback,” he said.

In a recent development, he added a second worry. “At the same time, latest risks arise from cognitive ‘offloading’ – that is, delegating mental work to AI. In the medium and long term, this could jeopardize learning success or even lead to loss of skills.”.

The team called for experiments that vary feedback and the task itself, and for sharing trial-level data so that learning can be measured directly.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

How the 'Dune' director turned a little-known short story into one of the best sci-fi movies of the 21st century.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In "Star Trek", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication.

According to recent reports, but in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun.

It has been revealed that the film's journey to the massive screen began when a screenwriter best known for his work on horror franchises such as "Final Destination", "A Nightmare on Elm Street" and "The Thing" read a short story in an online magazine. Eric Heisserer was so impressed by Ted Chiang's "Understand" that he bought himself a collection of the author's short stories. One in particular, the Nebula Award-winning "Story of Your Life", piqued his interest.

"It had a very profound emotional effect on me," he reminisced to Deadline. "I was in tears, and I was both heartbroken and uplifted. My head was just full of big ideas. I had to walk around the block a couple of times afterward and just hug my friends. The next day, I was like, 'Oh god, I want to give this to other people.'".

So when 21 Laps (the production company that later went on to make "Stranger Things") invited Heisserer to discuss possible future projects, the writer mentioned "Story of Your Life". The producers were also smitten.

"I was so excited, but I had that dread that a lot of producers get, which is, 'Are the rights available?'" 21 Laps' Dan Levine told the Hollywood Gold podcast. "You read something that blows you away, and then you find there aren't the rights, and there's no chance, you have to move on. So we were trying to track down this Ted Chiang, and he had no agent. He had a day job. He was impossible to find, so we started the hunt for Ted Chiang.".

In a recent development, an up-and-coming Canadian director named Denis Villeneuve had also found his way on to 21 Laps' radar after his 2010 French-language drama "Incendies" earned rave reviews and an Academy Award nomination. He told the producers that he'd always wanted to direct a science fiction film — a hint of things to come? — and they showed him "Story of Your Life".

Industry observers note that he was also drawn to the story, while the now-located Chiang was suitably impressed by the director's work on "Incendies" to make a deal for the rights. And with Amy Adams also interested in playing the lead role of linguist Dr Louise Banks, the film that would eventually become "Arrival" was ready to proceed — or, at least, it would be once Villeneuve had completed his first three Hollywood movies, "Prisoners" (2013), "Enemy" (2013) and "Sicario" (2015).

In a recent development, with 12 alien spaceships arriving simultaneously around the globe, "Arrival"'s poster-friendly elevator pitch could almost have been borrowed from "Independence Day". Indeed, the question of whether these whisper-quiet, chocolate button-shaped craft belong to the "Day the Earth Stood Still" / "Close Encounters" friendly extraterrestrial camp, or have the invasion of planet Earth on their minds is a mystery the world's governments are desperate to solve.

Sources indicate that "Denis didn't really see this as an alien invasion movie — more an alien arrival movie," producer Aaron Ryder told SFX magazine. "What would be the protocols that were in place? How would they be implemented? How would people react? What would the government be doing? What would the news organisations be saying? That was the tone and the texture, which is established right up front.".

Sources indicate that these Hollywood blockbuster components were not part of "Story of Your Life". But even though Heisserer's script was not a direct translation of Chiang's tale, he retained the most important bits — namely Dr Banks' efforts to establish a means of communication with seven-legged extraterrestrial heptapods, and the profound effect their language has on her perception of time.

Designed by Carlos Huante, the heptapods themselves are like giant elongated hands, alien visitors light years away from the "Star Trek" tradition of actors with a few ridges glued to their foreheads. Like the evil 456 in "Torchwood: Children of Earth", they're enclosed in gaseous chambers and make sounds imperceptible to the human ear.

This, however, is where "Arrival" gets really interesting. Working alongside physicist colleague Dr Ian Donnelly (Jeremy Renner), Banks gradually exchanges foundational vocabulary with two heptapods they name Abbott and Costello. They discover that the alien visitors use a sophisticated written language of circular "logograms", squirted into their atmosphere as if it were sentient squid ink.

In a recent development, "The idea in the short story is of circular language that has no beginning and no end," Villeneuve explained in an interview with IndieWire. "We were looking for no relation to any human language. I had to figure out how to produce logograms from my aliens while avoiding being long and boring. The sounds were an expression of their emotions, with more intellect coming from the signs. This beautiful species uses written language as their first means of expression instead of movement or gesture. They produce words out of their bodies.".

According to recent reports, but Banks and Donnelly's research project has a purpose. With the world's military on high alert — and, ironically, struggling to communicate — they need to work out how to ask the aliens a fundamental question: Why are you here?

According to recent reports, the heptapods' answer — "offer weapon" — is tantalizingly ambiguous. Are they planning to attack? Or is, as Banks suggests, 'weapon' simply being used as a synonym for 'tool'?

Recent findings suggest that aside from a bomb planted on the heptapod ship by a rogue US soldier, "Arrival" is mostly free from the big-budget explosions that are part-and-parcel of most alien visitation movies. Instead, the film's denouement delivers a twist — the crux of Chiang's story — that rivals "The Sixth Sense", "Fight Club" and "The Prestige" in its audacious sleight of hand.

It has been revealed that it turns out the "weapon" in question is actually the heptapod language, which, thanks to their non-linear perception of time, gives speakers a unique perspective on the past, present, and future. Therefore, those scenes we assumed to be flashbacks to the life and tragic death of Louise's daughter, Hannah, are actually flashforwards, as her increased understanding of heptapod-speak gives her memories of a life she hasn't yet lived.

Villeneuve put on multiple test screenings to ensure the big reveals hit properly.

"I wanted to screen it with people who knew nothing about the project," he mentioned. "What we discovered is when someone in the audience felt too lost — if intellectually they were not engaged — the ending was less powerful from an emotional point of view. So we tried to give as few clues as possible, but enough clues to be able to stay engaged and follow the story.".

Those subtle hints become obvious on second and third viewings, whether it's a lingering shot of a wedding ring absent in the movie's "present" or a conversation about the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (the notion that the structure of a language can influence the way its speakers think). The absence of young Hannah's father also takes on tragic new meaning when we realize it's Ian, who'll leave after Louise tells him about their daughter's sad fate.

"We were walking on this tightrope of trying to play things so it could play both ways, because of the reveal at the end," Adams recalled in a Vanity Fair conversation with Villeneuve. "I had to do so much work to understand how I play a character so that the first time you watch it you think that it's one thing, and the second time you watch it you can see it from a totally different perspective.".

In a recent development, while Adams didn't get the Oscar nomination her performance deserved, everything else paid off, with the film making over $200 million worldwide from its reported $47 million budget. (The film did win an Academy Award for sound editing, while receiving further nods for best picture, director, and adapted screenplay.).

Villeneuve has famously gone on to become Hollywood's go-to guy for intelligent sci-fi, thanks to "Blade Runner 2049" and the smash-hit "Dune" saga, and will next be given the opportunity to resurrect James Bond.

Normally we'd take this opportunity to say no one could have foreseen Villeneuve's subsequent ascendancy but — in a story involving heptapods and some clever people at 21 Laps — who can be so sure?

In a recent development, "Arrival" is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US, and Netflix in the UK.. It's also available on Blu-ray via Amazon.

Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. #88. Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crows can make visual decisions twice as promptly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen.
  • Sources indicate that the findings, published in the journal Science, offer newly introduced insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions.
  • Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crows can make visual decisions twice as promptly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

Sources indicate that the findings, published in the journal Science, offer newly introduced insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.

It has been revealed that to test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.".

The results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds.

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an important role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

The recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

These signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes.

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," indicates Andreas Nieder.

Sources indicate that unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as rapidly as primates.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

#87. Tech Report: Staying social may keep an older mind sharp, but not every kind of activity counts

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1250 words)
General 🌐 Earth

Tech Report: Staying social may keep an older mind sharp, but not every kind of activity counts

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, among social activities older adults join, volunteering and sports clubs were linked to better memory in 24 countries.
  • Sources indicate that older adults who volunteer or belong to a sports club tend to do better on memory and thinking tests than people who join nothing.
  • According to recent reports, the benefit didn’t show up evenly, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, among social activities older adults join, volunteering and sports clubs were linked to better memory in 24 countries. Church groups were not.

Sources indicate that older adults who volunteer or belong to a sports club tend to do better on memory and thinking tests than people who join nothing. The gap grows with each extra kind of social activity they take on.

According to recent reports, the benefit didn’t show up evenly, though. Volunteering and sports clubs were linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline in all five national surveys studied. Church groups and political groups were not consistently linked to any gain.

Behind the pattern are the records of nearly 58,000 people in 24 countries, followed for about six years. The authors describe it as the first analysis to pool five national aging surveys to understand the impact of social connection.

It has been revealed that jiahong Sun of Guangdong Medical University and Bo Xi of Shandong University led the work with first author Yuedong Wang. It’s an observational study, so it can show that joiners scored higher, not that joining caused the higher scores.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview with Earth.com, Sun noted the practical message is about variety and sticking with it. “A practical step would be to take part in a few sustainable activities, ideally including three or more types of social engagement,” he said.

Social activities, he suggested, might include volunteering, joining a sports club, attending a training course or spending meaningful time caring for children..

The findings of earlier studies on the effect of social engagement disagreed with each other.

Sources indicate that the Rush Memory and Aging Project linked higher social engagement to a five-year delay in the onset of cognitive impairment. A Dutch study of about 2,000 people found no link.

The authors suspected small samples, under 3,000 people, and inconsistent ways of measuring social life.

In a recent development, so Wang’s team pooled five long-running surveys of people in middle age and beyond. Three of them are the Health and Retirement Study in the United States, the English Longitudinal Study of Aging, and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study.

The Mexican Health and Aging Study and the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe complete the set.

The European survey alone supplied almost half of the 57,793 participants. Median ages ran from 57 in the Chinese survey to 73 in the American one.

Each survey asked people whether they had taken part in social groups over the past month or the past year.

Memory was tested by having people recall a short list of words, right away and again later. Thinking was tested with tasks like counting backward from 100 by sevens or naming as many animals as possible in one minute.

Because the tests differed, the researchers converted every score onto one common scale, so a result from Mexico could be compared with one from England.

On that scale, people who took part in at least one social activity scored higher than people who took part in none, in all five surveys.

Sources indicate that each added kind of activity came with a higher score. People who kept up three or more scored more than twice as far above the inactive group as people with just one activity did.

Industry observers note that the three-or-more group’s advantage also grew over time. Their scores improved a little faster each year than the inactive group’s did, and that extra yearly gain revealed up on the memory test.

On the thinking tasks, the yearly difference was too small to separate from chance.

It has been revealed that what the study measured was test scores, not dementia diagnoses. The authors described the trend as a dose-response pattern: more kinds of social contact, higher scores.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him about which activities helped, Sun pointed to two that demonstrated the same link everywhere and several that didn’t.

In a recent development, volunteering and sports club membership were linked to better cognitive scores in all five surveys. Attending training courses and caring for children were linked to faster yearly gains.

Political groups, community groups, church groups, and religious groups revealed no consistent link across the surveys.

“This does not mean that these activities are harmful or ineffective; their associations may depend on the social and cultural context in which they occur,” Sun remarked.

Industry observers note that why would an active social life protect thinking? The authors offered three possibilities. Activities that demand attention may keep brain connections in use. This idea is often summed up as “use it or lose it.”.

It has been revealed that social contact may add to the mental reserve that education builds up over a lifetime. And meaningful activity may lower chronic stress, which harms the brain region that handles memory.

According to recent reports, the association was not the same for everyone. Sun remarked it appeared stronger among women, adults aged 60 or older, people with at least a high school education, and people without depressive symptoms.

It was also stronger among people who lived alone, were of normal weight, or lived in rural areas.

Two more groups that made the list puzzled the authors: current smokers and people who drank alcohol.

One possibility they raised is that smokers and drinkers may do their socializing in organized groups, the kind that keep a mind busy. They called that reading speculative and the whole set of subgroup results exploratory.

For people over 60, the authors’ explanation is plainer. After retirement, people have more free time for groups.

Recent findings suggest that people were asked about their social activities once, at the start. The analysis assumed those habits held for the next six years., but this was not checked.

The thinking tests also differed from country to country, so a score in China and a score in England don’t measure exactly the same skill.

And people who were already sharper may have been the ones who joined clubs in the first place, which would make the clubs look better than they are.

The analysis adjusted for age, education, depression, loneliness, and several other factors, but the authors wrote that other differences between joiners and non-joiners could still explain part of the gap.

Dementia is the stake behind all of this. In 2019, about 57 million people were living with it, and the authors cited projections of nearly 153 million by 2050.

With no effective treatment available, they wrote, finding risk factors that people can change is a public health priority.

Recent findings suggest that the study counted how many kinds of activity a person did. It didn’t ask whether they enjoyed them, led them, or how often they went.

“Our next steps are to examine not only the number of social activities, but also their quality, purpose, level of personal involvement and emotional experience,” Sun told Earth.com.

He added that future research should also test whether programs that get older adults into sustained social activity actually improve their cognitive health.

Until a study like that runs, the evidence is a pattern across six years and 24 countries. Whether joining is what makes the difference, or whether sharper people are the ones joining, remains an unanswered question.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health.

#86. A strange red speck captured by Webb looked like a candidate for the earliest galaxy ever seen, but now it seems to be moving like a brown dwarf

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words)
General 🌐 Earth

A strange red speck captured by Webb looked like a candidate for the earliest galaxy ever seen, but now it seems to be moving like a brown dwarf

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that capotauro, a candidate early galaxy, moved 0.13 arcseconds in 3.5 years.
  • In December 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope photographed a strip of sky for the CEERS survey and recorded a compact red point that, according to the latest analysis, is a brown dwarf inside the Milky Way.
  • Astronomers later named the point Capotauro and calculated that its light might have left a galaxy about 100 million years after the Big Bang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that capotauro, a candidate early galaxy, moved 0.13 arcseconds in 3.5 years. Astronomers now say it is a cold brown dwarf in the Milky Way.

In December 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope photographed a strip of sky for the CEERS survey and recorded a compact red point that, according to the latest analysis, is a brown dwarf inside the Milky Way.

Astronomers later named the point Capotauro and calculated that its light might have left a galaxy about 100 million years after the Big Bang.

Webb returned to the same field in June 2026, and the point was no longer in the same place.

A team led from the University of Edinburgh’s Institute for Astronomy (IFA) says that rules out a distant galaxy, although the object’s distance of roughly 2,400 light-years remains an estimate.

CEERS, the Cosmic Evolution Early Release Science survey, covered a field in a region called the Extended Groth Strip.

Giovanni Gandolfi and his colleagues picked out the object, catalogued as U-100588. They named it Capotauro after the old name of Corno alle Scale, a mountain in the Italian Apennines.

In a recent development, capotauro appeared only in the reddest filters of Webb’s NIRCam camera and vanished at shorter wavelengths. Astronomers call such an object a dropout, because it drops out of the bluer images.

According to recent reports, distant galaxies can behave this way, since hydrogen in the early universe absorbs their shorter wavelengths. Among the extragalactic options, Gandolfi’s team favored a redshift of about 32.

According to recent reports, redshift is a measurement of how far its light has been stretched by cosmic expansion. The confirmed record at the time stood near redshift 14, held by a galaxy seen 280 million years after the Significant Bang.

According to recent reports, that team also listed a very cold brown dwarf or a free-floating planet as possibilities, and it mentioned the observations could not settle the question. The doubt was raised early, and an impostor closer to home stayed on the table.

It has been revealed that two Webb programs, MINERVA and SPAM, covered the same field in mid-to-late June 2026. Their medium-band images gave the Edinburgh group, with first author Fengyuan Liu, a second epoch about 3.5 years after the discovery data.

Galaxies at such distances do not show measurable motion across the sky over a few years, while objects in the Milky Way can.

It has been revealed that liu’s team measured Capotauro’s position in four images, F410M and F444W from December 2022 and F430M and F460M from June 2026. It had moved by 132 milliarcseconds, give or take 20, which is about 0.13 arcseconds.

Recent findings suggest that for scale, that angle equals the width of a US quarter seen from about 24 miles (38 kilometers). The detection reached more than 6 sigma, a statistical level that leaves very little room for chance.

A shift that small can be faked by misaligned images, so the team built a local reference frame. It used 68 isolated, compact sources within 3 arcminutes of Capotauro, most of them galaxies, and solved for the alignment of all four images together.

The team then tested the noise under the object. The researchers planted artificial moving sources at 75 blank positions near Capotauro, ran 1,200 trials, and checked how far the noise pushed each recovered position.

The paper states that the data “completely exclude” any extragalactic source. That covers a galaxy and a black hole-powered nucleus, and also a proposal by Ferrara and colleagues that the light came from a giant supernova at redshift 15.

Sources indicate that the latest images also highlighted no significant change in brightness over 3.5 years, which counts against a supernova. Liu’s group found one more problem in the record.

It reports that its own brightness values differ from the earlier ones by as much as 58 percent, and it suggests the earlier measurement may have been too high because its aperture was oversized.

The team compared the object’s brightness across filters with templates of known cold brown dwarfs. The best match was spectral type Y1, with a temperature near 350 Kelvin, or about 170 degrees Fahrenheit (77 degrees Celsius).

It has been revealed that NASA describes Y dwarfs as the coldest class of brown dwarfs, objects that never gathered enough mass to shine as ordinary stars. Webb has found brown dwarfs only about twice the mass of Jupiter in a young star-forming cluster.

Sources indicate that most known Y dwarfs lie within 30 parsecs, about 98 light-years. One of the coldest, WISE 0855, sits just 7.5 light-years from the Sun.

Recent findings suggest that capotauro’s estimated distance is 730 parsecs, with an uncertainty of 110, or about 2,400 light-years. The authors call it “one of the most distant Y dwarfs found to date.”.

Combined with its motion, that distance gives a sideways speed of about 82 miles (132 kilometers) per second. Such a speed may mark an old object from the Milky Way’s thick disk, the authors wrote.

Maruša Bradač and her colleagues found two candidates beyond redshift 30 near the Bullet cluster, and spectra and motion measurements pointed to cold brown dwarfs instead.

Kevin Hainline’s group had reached similar photometric fits for Capotauro in a study of cold dwarfs in deep Webb fields, placing it about 1,600 light-years away.

Liu’s team explains why the confusion lands at that redshift. Water, methane and ammonia in a Y dwarf’s atmosphere can erase almost all its light through the F356W filter.

The brightness then climbs sharply near 4 to 5 microns. Read as a hydrogen break in a galaxy, that rise gives a redshift of about 30 to 32.

The authors recommend that future searches include cold brown dwarf templates and compare images from different years.

It has been revealed that the 2,400 light-year figure is not a direct geometric measurement. Webb’s images could not pin down Capotauro’s parallax, the small annual shift that reveals distance, and the team derived the figure by scaling template brightness.

The template library stops at type Y1. Capotauro could therefore be colder and closer than the estimate, which would also lower its calculated speed.

Recent findings suggest that A third set of Webb images, timed for parallax, could fix the distance. The object is so faint that detailed spectroscopy would be “inherently impractical,” the authors wrote.

In the June 2026 images, Capotauro was still a red point, about 0.13 arcseconds from where Webb recorded it in December 2022.

According to recent reports, the study has been accepted by the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society and posted online as an advance article, before copyediting and typesetting. A preprint is also on arXiv.

#85. A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words)
AI & Tech 🌐 Sciencedaily

A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A promising latest approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence.
  • These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology.
  • In a recent development, researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A promising latest approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence. At the center of the breakthrough is a special class of materials known as multiferroics, which combine electrical and magnetic properties that can be controlled together using extremely small voltages.

These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology. However, a major obstacle has prevented their use in conventional computer chips. When multiferroics are made thin enough to fit inside these devices, they typically lose the electrical and magnetic behavior that makes them valuable. Scientists call this problem the "dead layer" effect.

In a recent development, researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces extremely thin films of bismuth ferrite, a widely studied multiferroic material, without sacrificing its essential properties. Even more remarkably, the process gives the material new magnetic characteristics that could make it especially useful for future electronics.

According to recent reports, "We've established that we can get rid of the dead layer," noted Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. "We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want -- down to a few angstroms -- and it's still ferroelectric, and it's still magnetic.".

The findings were published in the journal Nature Materials.

Why Multiferroics Could Transform Computer Chips.

What makes multiferroics so attractive for computing is the unusual connection between their electrical and magnetic properties. Their atomic structure is made up of repeating units in which positive and negative charges are positioned on opposite sides, creating a property known as electrical polarization.

In a recent development, applying a small voltage can reverse this polarization, effectively switching the positions of the positive and negative charges. This provides a potential way to store digital information as binary values (ones and zeros) using very little electricity.

Because the material's magnetic behavior is linked to its electrical polarization, the stored information can also be retrieved magnetically. This combination could enable computer memory and logic components that require significantly less energy than existing technologies.

The challenge has been making these materials small enough for practical devices. Modern computer chips require exceptionally thin layers, but multiferroics traditionally stop functioning properly when reduced to such dimensions.

Two separate effects cause this breakdown. First, the material's atomic structure becomes distorted, disrupting the arrangement and chemical environment necessary for its properties to function. Second, internal electric fields interfere with the material's polarization until it can no longer be maintained. Together, these effects destroy both its ferroelectric and magnetic behavior, creating the troublesome dead layer.

How Brown Engineers Eliminated the Dead Layer.

To solve the problem, the Brown University team developed a new method for producing thin films of bismuth ferrite.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers deposited the material onto a foundation made of dysprosium scandate, a compound derived from rare earth elements. This underlying material has a crystal structure with slightly smaller dimensions than bismuth ferrite, creating a mismatch between their atomic arrangements.

That mismatch places the bismuth ferrite under compression, helping preserve the atomic structure required for its electrical and magnetic properties to remain intact.

The team also incorporated a second metallic layer designed to counteract unwanted electric fields. By preventing those fields from disrupting the material's electrical polarization, the additional layer addresses the other major cause of the dead layer effect.

Together, these changes allow the bismuth ferrite film to retain its multiferroic properties even when reduced to just a few angstroms in thickness.

It has been revealed that but the researchers discovered something else. Rather than simply preserving the material's original capabilities, their approach actually improved its magnetic behavior.

The engineered layers caused the bismuth ferrite to exhibit altermagnetism, an unusual form of magnetism that combines useful characteristics of two more familiar magnetic states: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.

This discovery could be particularly crucial for developing faster and more compact computer components.

It has been revealed that "Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out," Caretta said. "The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds -- they can be fast, densely integrated and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout.".

According to recent reports, in other words, altermagnets offer a potentially valuable combination of speed, compactness, and readable signals. These characteristics could help engineers build computer components that operate efficiently without the interference problems associated with conventional magnetic materials.

The ability to create this magnetic behavior in an exceptionally thin multiferroic film makes the discovery especially promising for future chip designs.

A Latest Path Toward Energy-Efficient AI Computing.

As artificial intelligence continues to drive demand for computing power, developing hardware that consumes less electricity has become an increasingly notable goal.

It has been revealed that caretta believes the fresh findings could help bring multiferroic materials closer to practical use in low-power memory and computing devices. Although the technology still needs further development before it can be incorporated into commercial chips, the research demonstrates that a long-standing materials limitation can be overcome.

Sources indicate that it also indicates that carefully engineering a material's atomic environment can do more than preserve its existing properties. Under the right conditions, it can produce useful behavior that was not present in the original material.

"We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials," Caretta remarked. "The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that's useful -- and sometimes even better than what nature gives us.".

According to recent reports, the research received funding from the U.S. Army Research Office (W911NF-21-2-0162), the National Science Foundation (DMR-2039380, OIA-2327352) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-AC02-05CH11231).

#82. Which science-fiction novels have been best at predicting the future?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1690 words)
General 🌐 Newscientist

Which science-fiction novels have been best at predicting the future?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Newscientist

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Check your subscription status, update your details and more.
  • Industry observers note that newly introduced Scientist has always been interested in science fiction and its attempts to imagine the future.
  • In a recent development, it’s true that some of the sci-fi he was reading then was rapidly overtaken by events and, in the process of that, rendered redundant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check your subscription status, update your details and more.

Industry observers note that newly introduced Scientist has always been interested in science fiction and its attempts to imagine the future. In 1958, when the magazine was 2 years old, it published an article by Ian S. Menzies in which he wrote: “Like every other form of literature, s. f. ranges from excellent to awful. But the best of science fiction today is far superior to much other fiction.” Elsewhere in the feature, Menzies talked about the risks of the “rapid catching up of reality with fiction”.

In a recent development, it’s true that some of the sci-fi he was reading then was rapidly overtaken by events and, in the process of that, rendered redundant. What Menzies couldn’t know was that other works from that same period would still be regarded as prescient, notable or relevant, or even all three, decades later.

According to recent reports, so, which sci-fi stories, published over the seven decades of New Scientist’s history, have proved to be both prophetic and enduringly pertinent as the world has changed around them? Here are some of my personal picks.

Industry observers note that the Death of Grass by John Christopher (1956) is an English period piece, with all the particular social politics of its era on display (sexism included). Yet somehow it manages to foreshadow a host of modern-day crises, from pandemics and the fragility of food supply lines to the befouling and stripping of the land by substantial agriculture.

According to recent reports, the book opens with the news that a virus is killing grasses; eventually that comes to include all cereal crops. Abruptly, the country’s food reserves are gone, and no more food is coming. The novel’s main characters are mostly middle-class professionals who do a few things “right” early on. They are quick to acquire guns and flee London; also, quick to gun down anyone who tries to stop them. They make their way in convoy through a brown land, heading towards a Cumbrian valley where one of their group has a relative. The valley is gated; one way in, one way out. They think they could be safe there.

First they have to survive their journey, though, and England, within hours, is lawless. I finished the book wishing that I could buy a remote valley and build a wall across the bottom of it.

Industry observers note that the Moon Is a Harsh Mistress by Robert A. Heinlein (1966) is the story, set in 2075, of a group of lunar residents who plot to overthrow their overlords on Earth. It’s a great premise rendered quite dull in execution; much of the book reads like the minutes from a local council meeting. In addition, the sexual politics of the colony are filtered through male 1960s sensibilities, adding cringeworthy moments.

Sources indicate that the reason this remains a classic is that one of the characters in the book, Mike, is an AI. Not just some 60s idea of what an AI might be, but our idea of an AI. On the very first page, our narrator Mannie (who speaks a futuristic version of English) writes: “Mike was a fair dinkum thinkum, sharpest computer you’ll ever meet… Not that Mike would necessarily give right answer; he wasn’t completely honest.” Remind you of anything?

Ursula K. Le Guin’s astonishing novel The Dispossessed (1974) remains daisy fresh. Le Guin, as her fans will know, could do it all: character, politics, ideas, exquisite writing… and, in this case, spaceships too.

Industry observers note that our hero, Shevek, is a brilliant physicist and also a good man (what a wonderful creation he is!) trying to do right in a future where the human colonies have gone different ways – one into anarchy, for example, another into the rule of an elite – as they struggle with climate change, moral exhaustion, repression, inequality… and much else that we struggle with today. If you’ve never read this one, I highly recommend it.

I’m going to cheat for the 80s and pick two books, because I can’t choose between Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale (1985) and William Gibson’s Neuromancer (1984).

Recent findings suggest that in Atwood’s masterwork, the US has been captured by a radical right-wing group and is now called the Republic of Gilead. Women’s rights have been scrapped. Our hero, named Offred by the latest regime, is assigned as a handmaid to a family of loyalists. Her job is to produce a baby for the commander who is her new master. She is, in short, a womb with arms and legs, and nothing more, to Gilead.

I don’t think I need to draw any lines for you, straight or otherwise, from this book written 40 years ago to current events.

Atwood aside, I didn’t want to leave out Neuromancer because its vision of our digital future is so weirdly prescient. Gibson, famously, was no computer expert and wrote the book on a typewriter. Yet he foresaw what cyberspace would actually be like.

Case, our chief protagonist, is a former hacker trying to make ends meet in Japan after his ability to access cyberspace has been taken from him. Then a woman called Molly approaches him, asking him to get involved in a heist. Cue a high-stakes drama in and out of cyberspace. The book is a bit dense to start with, but it’s well worth sticking with.

Is Neuromancer’s cyberpunk dystopia still thrilling in 2025?

Industry observers note that octavia E. Butler’s Parable of the Sower (1993) is a barnstormer of a novel that remains as relevant today as when it was first published. Our hero, Lauren Olamina, is a young woman living in a gated community in a United States that is rapidly falling apart.

Climate change is escalating and the streets are full of desperate people forced into savagery simply to survive. Lauren’s community is hanging on, but soon the chaos is going to come through that gate.

Industry observers note that lauren, still a teenager, develops her own religion and names it Earthseed. Its divine purpose is for humans to colonise the stars. Such a bold vision is preposterous amidst the horror of the world Lauren is forced to make her way through, and yet it sustains her.

According to recent reports, N.K. Jemisin on the prescience and brilliance of Parable of the Sower.

The book is a hymn (I think) to the power of taking full responsibility for your life and facing up to the fact that everything changes. Let us hope, as with The Death of Grass, that this version of the future remains in some parts fictional.

Butler wrote a follow-up, Parable of the Talents, in which Lauren sees her dreams begin to come true. A third book in the series remained unfinished when Butler died.

Industry observers note that one does need some time to pass before being able to decide if a book has truly got the future right. However, I am reasonably confident that The Three-Body Problem by Cixin Liu (2008) is going to prove to be so.

3 Body Problem review: Cixin Liu’s masterpiece arrives on Netflix.

The story is a brilliant one. Aliens are heading for Earth, and they’re not friendly, but it’s going to take them hundreds of years to arrive. Can the scientists of Earth band together and push science forward so hard that humans will survive the coming invasion? Yes, Liu wrote a book all about physics, but made it gripping!

Sources indicate that so, in the case of the book, the science push is all about aliens. But it doesn’t take a significant leap of the imagination to suggest that there might be some key real world parallels here. This is the first of a trilogy. The two follow-up novels are also fantastic.

I’m going to take a chance on two very different novels from recent times that might, in the future, be viewed as accurate visions.

First, Station Eleven (2014) by Emily St. John Mandel, which essentially predicted the covid-19 pandemic. Except in Mandel’s pandemic, the world was left in ruins.

According to recent reports, we follow a travelling group of actors and musicians as they journey between communities in this future world. The book explores the idea that “survival is insufficient”; that humanity needs art, culture and history to truly live. Its ideas still feel extremely relevant 12 years later.

Sources indicate that second, Kim Stanley Robinson’s chronicle of the near future, The Ministry for the Future (2020). Clear-eyed, but essentially optimistic, it describes humanity’s efforts to deal with climate change in the decades to come.

This is a very untraditional book in structure, and although you could say the main character is Mary Murphy, the head of the titular ministry, parts of the book are devoted to (fictional) witness accounts of future events. It’s not an easy read, but then it’s not an easy subject, and this is a massively ambitious work.

Despite the horrors contained in the book, we may end up wishing, in the future, that it had been more prescient, rather than less.

So those are my picks. You may have better ones. In terms of Ian S. Menzies’s central argument seven long decades ago, I think that what he stated still holds true. Science fiction continues to range from excellent to awful. But the best of sci-fi today is still far superior to much other fiction. It’s where the major ideas are, simple as that.

Industry observers note that did Emily get it right? Come and join the discussion about the sci-fi novels that have best predicted the future.

Emily H. Wilson is author of the Sumerians series and is working on her first sci-fi novel. She is a former editor of Latest Scientist, and is now the magazine’s science-fiction columnist.

#81. A tourist’s vacation photo of a yellow flower helped botanists catalog a completely new species

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (866 words)
General 🌐 Earth

A tourist’s vacation photo of a yellow flower helped botanists catalog a completely new species

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh yellow-flowered plant species discovered through an iNaturalist photo in Portugal's Algarve faces threats from invasive trees and habitat loss.
  • A yellow toadflax that grows almost only in the hills of Monchique, in Portugal’s Algarve region, has been described as a latest species, Linaria alfercensis.
  • It has been revealed that botanists first noticed it in a photo that a visitor to the area posted on iNaturalist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh yellow-flowered plant species discovered through an iNaturalist photo in Portugal's Algarve faces threats from invasive trees and habitat loss.

A yellow toadflax that grows almost only in the hills of Monchique, in Portugal’s Algarve region, has been described as a latest species, Linaria alfercensis.

It has been revealed that botanists first noticed it in a photo that a visitor to the area posted on iNaturalist. The citizen science platform lets people share pictures of wild plants and animals.

João Farminhão of the University of Coimbra’s Centre for Functional Ecology (CFE) described the species in August 2026 with four colleagues from Portugal and Spain. Its flowers “did not match any described taxon in corolla colour pattern,” the team wrote.

Industry observers note that the iNaturalist record came from Castelo de Alferce, in the municipality of Monchique. The plant clearly belonged to a group of toadflaxes called Linaria subsection Versicolores.

This observation prompted dedicated fieldwork in the Monchique Igneous Complex in 2024 and 2025.

In a recent development, on April 4, 2024, André Carapeto of the Portuguese Botanical Society collected the plant that became the holotype, the reference specimen for the species. He found it at an elevation of 1,027 feet (313 meters).

The holotype is kept in the herbarium of the University of Coimbra, with a duplicate at the Royal Botanical Garden in Madrid.

Sources indicate that the plant had been collected before without being recognized. Herbarium specimens gathered in 1995 and 1996 near Picota and in the Odelouca valley belong to the upcoming species.

The name honors the civil parish of Alferce, where the species was first recognized.

Sources indicate that the flower is deep yellow, with two orange to brownish-red stripes along the throat that split at the tip. The palate, the bulge that closes the mouth of the flower, is orange and often spotted with brownish red.

According to recent reports, flowers usually measure 0.8 to 0.9 inch (21 to 24 millimeters) long, including the spur. The erect flowering stems usually reach 6.7 to 15 inches (17 to 38 centimeters).

Recent findings suggest that the plant flowers and sets fruit from March to May. Its seeds are black to blackish gray and measure 0.02 to 0.03 inch (0.4 to 0.8 millimeter).

Its closest relatives are Linaria algarviana, which has violet-purple flowers, and Linaria bimaculata, whose throat stripes are rounded at the tip. Together, the three form a group of toadflaxes found only in the Algarve.

Its fruit capsules are longer than those of these two relatives, usually measuring 0.13 to 0.15 inch (3.4 to 3.8 millimeters).

It has been revealed that farminhão and Carapeto raised Linaria bimaculata to species rank in a 2024 study of Algarve toadflaxes, drawing on 78 iNaturalist records. Many of those records had first been uploaded under another species name.

It has been revealed that the Iberian branch of Linaria subsection Versicolores includes at least ten species. Toadflaxes belong to the tribe Antirrhineae of the plantain family, Plantaginaceae.

The new species grows mostly on soils derived from nepheline syenite, an igneous rock that makes up most of the Monchique Igneous Complex.

It occurs on the southern slopes of Serra da Picota, along the Odelouca river basin and near Marmelete. It favors annual meadows on gravel and sandy soils in clearings and on the edges of rocky heathland, often among boulders.

Industry observers note that the researchers combined DNA analysis, using a method called genotyping-by-sequencing, with a near-complete review of herbarium specimens. They also compared where these toadflaxes grow with geological maps.

According to recent reports, records from iNaturalist entered the analysis only if they were classified as reliable after a check of their photos. Most also had a location accurate to within about 490 feet (150 meters).

Sandstone, coarse sand, igneous rocks and windblown sand plains act as soil “islands” for these plants, while limestone, fine sands, shales and graywackes appear to work as barriers.

Together with shifts in flower color and shape, this pattern points to a role for geographic isolation and inferred soil specialization in the group’s diversification.

The authors propose a preliminary listing as Endangered under criterion B of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The listing reflects the species’ small geographic range, declining habitat quality and few locations.

The species’ extent of occurrence covers about 34.6 square miles (89.6 square kilometers). It is known from four locations, and its area of occupancy is about 17 square miles (44 square kilometers).

Each locality holds fewer than 50 flowering plants, although the total population cannot be reliably estimated.

The main threat is believed to be the invasive silver wattle, Acacia dealbata, whose spread has intensified after recurrent wildfires. Native to southeastern Australia, it is legally listed as an invasive species in Portugal.

Recent findings suggest that the species has also lost habitat to eucalyptus plantations in the past. Forestry work, including road widening and timber storage, threatens plants along road verges, as does tourist development on the Picota slopes near Covão da Águia.

The study was published in the journal Plant Ecology and Evolution.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

Sources indicate that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

According to recent reports, all that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

In a recent development, antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

Sources indicate that during that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off.".

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a major deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating.".

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an crucial question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

Industry observers note that the Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.
