#27. Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women with higher blood levels of two common "forever chemicals" may face an increased risk of developing a particularly aggressive form of breast cancer, according to latest research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S.
  • In a recent development, the study identified a connection between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer and two widely encountered chemicals: perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS).
  • Both substances belong to a large family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women with higher blood levels of two common "forever chemicals" may face an increased risk of developing a particularly aggressive form of breast cancer, according to latest research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).

In a recent development, the study identified a connection between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer and two widely encountered chemicals: perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS). Women with greater concentrations of these substances in their blood were more likely to develop this type of cancer. However, researchers found no clear link between either chemical and breast cancer risk overall.

Both substances belong to a large family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS. These chemicals have been used in numerous everyday consumer products and are often described as "forever chemicals" because they resist breaking down in the environment. They can also accumulate in the human body and remain there for years.

"Women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health," said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. "This NIH study links two forever chemicals to a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer and demands further investigation. Under President Trump's leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks, and give women the information they need to protect their health.".

Why This Aggressive Breast Cancer Is Concerning.

ER-negative breast cancer differs from more common forms of the disease because its tumor cells lack the receptors that allow estrogen to stimulate cancer growth. These cancers are often more aggressive and generally have poorer outcomes than tumors that respond to estrogen.

Recent findings suggest that despite their severity, researchers still have relatively little information about what makes someone more likely to develop ER-negative breast cancer. The new findings suggest that exposure to certain persistent environmental chemicals could be one contributing factor.

"Our findings, which we confirmed using a meta-analysis of prior research, indicate that certain legacy PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, are associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer, a more aggressive tumor type with few known risk factors," explained NIH Stadtman Investigator Alexandra White, Ph.D., who led the study.

The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

Higher Forever Chemical Levels Linked to Greater Cancer Risk.

To investigate the possible connection, NIH scientists and their collaborators examined blood samples that had been collected years before participants received a cancer diagnosis. The researchers measured concentrations of 17 different PFAS chemicals, allowing them to compare earlier exposure levels with subsequent breast cancer outcomes.

The results revealed substantial differences for two chemicals. Women in the highest PFOA exposure group had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer than women in the lowest group. The association was even stronger for PFOS, with the highest exposure group showing a 93% higher rate, nearly twice that of the lowest group.

These percentages represent relative differences between groups rather than the absolute probability that an individual woman will develop breast cancer. The findings also establish an association, not proof that the chemicals directly cause the disease.

The analysis used data from the Sister Study, a major research project conducted by NIH's National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS). Between 2003 and 2009, the study enrolled 50,884 women ages 35-74 from across the United States and Puerto Rico.

Industry observers note that all participants were free of breast cancer when they enrolled, although each had a full or half-sister who had already been diagnosed with the disease. For the PFAS investigation, researchers analyzed information from 1,609 women who subsequently developed breast cancer and a comparison group of 2,269 women.

Could Reducing PFAS Exposure Lower Cancer Risk?

Although PFAS can remain in the environment and the body for long periods, researchers emphasize that exposure is not necessarily unavoidable. The findings could eventually help identify fresh ways to reduce the risk of aggressive breast cancer.

"These findings matter for women's health broadly," said first author, Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., who previously worked as an NIH research fellow and is now a researcher at DLH, a scientific research organization. "Although PFAS are persistent in the environment and in our bodies, exposure to them is still potentially modifiable, meaning people can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open upcoming avenues for prevention.".

Recent findings suggest that the researchers are also interested in understanding how these chemicals might influence cancer development. Because the strongest associations appeared in tumors that lack estrogen receptors, the findings suggest that PFAS could act through biological processes unrelated to hormonal signaling.

Industry observers note that potential explanations include changes in gene activity or alterations in the immune system. However, the study did not directly investigate these mechanisms, so their involvement remains uncertain.

Newer Forever Chemicals Raise Unanswered Questions.

According to recent reports, although PFOA and PFOS have largely been phased out and replaced with other PFAS compounds, measurable amounts of both substances are still present in most people's bodies. Their persistence means that exposure to these older chemicals remains a potential public health concern.

Industry observers note that the researchers say additional investigations should focus on populations with greater PFAS exposure, as well as groups that experience higher rates of ER-negative breast cancer. Such research could help clarify the strength of the observed associations and identify whether certain populations face greater risks.

Scientists also need to determine whether the newer chemicals introduced as replacements for PFOA and PFOS carry similar health concerns.

"More research is needed, particularly evaluating the risk of breast cancer associated with newer replacement PFAS chemicals," White said.

The findings add to growing questions about the long-term health effects of forever chemicals and highlight the importance of understanding how environmental exposures may contribute to aggressive forms of breast cancer.

The research received support from NIEHS grants Z01ES044005; Z1AES103332; and R01ES032831.

#26. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3 min read (638 words)
General 🌐 Sciencenews

The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Sciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every print subscription comes with full digital access.
  • Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds.
  • The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access.

Like parrots, Infernogallus could deftly strip the flesh from large seeds.

The ‘hell chicken’ Infernogallus (foreground) dines on Cretaceous fruits, sharing its habitat with a Tyrannosaurus rex (background).

Illustrated by Danielle Dufault, © Danielle Dufault, 2025.

Sources indicate that more than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

Recent findings suggest that in 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in Upcoming York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

When the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

Recent findings suggest that this chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

It has been revealed that these fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston states. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”.

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston indicates.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”.

#25. The 7 Best Smokeless Fire Pits We Tested (and Yes, They Produced Hardly Any Smoke)

📅 16 Mar 2021 • ⏱️ 17 min read (3448 words)
General 🌐 Popularmechanics

The 7 Best Smokeless Fire Pits We Tested (and Yes, They Produced Hardly Any Smoke)

📅 16 Mar 2021 | ⏱️ 17 min read | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • From set-it-and-forget-it backyard centerpieces to grab-and-go options for weekend camping trips, we tried well-regarded options from Solo Stove, Breeo, Blue Sky, and more.
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that engineered to contain flames and burn fuel more completely, smokeless fire pits deliver ambient warmth with a lot less smoke in your eyes than a traditional campfire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From set-it-and-forget-it backyard centerpieces to grab-and-go options for weekend camping trips, we tried well-regarded options from Solo Stove, Breeo, Blue Sky, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that engineered to contain flames and burn fuel more completely, smokeless fire pits deliver ambient warmth with a lot less smoke in your eyes than a traditional campfire. They achieve this through two points of combustion: The first happens at the bottom, where airflow feeds burning wood; the second occurs at the top, where the fire’s smoke and gas output are burned off. And while no smokeless fire pit is 100 percent smokeless, if you use best practices (like burning dry wood) they come pretty darn close.

We tested smokeless fire pits in our New York and Pennsylvania backyards, building fires rather than judging them on specs alone. Along with smoke output, we considered size, which affects wood capacity and where the heat actually lands, as well as how easy each pit was to empty of ash and store once done, among other factors. We also used them repeatedly over time to see how their finishes held up, because a brand-new pit can look very different after several fires.

Sources indicate that solo Stove is the brand most people associate with smokeless fire pits (though Breeo was the first game in town). The latest joiner in Solo Stove’s lineup is the Summit, an upgraded take on the ever-popular Bonfire. Its 23-pound weight makes it just as easy to lift and store off-season, and there’s even less setup required. All-in-all, it’s the best smokeless fire pit for most people who want to enjoy a backyard fire pit that can be stored off-season.

Because the Summit is four to five inches shorter than the Bonfire, it does a better job of keeping your feet warm, one of the major gripes our Test Editor Brad Ford had of the earlier model. He claims that while it holds less firewood, it undoubtedly produces a higher flame that extends well above the rim.

It has been revealed that another improvement he points out is the Summit’s integrated stand, which he notes is sturdier and allows for better airflow than that of the Bonfire’s detached stand. There’s also a deeper ash pan, which is particularly helpful because the Summit burns through wood fast and needs frequent reloading. In terms of price, the 19.5-inch Summit is $100 more than a Bonfire of the same size, an extra cost that’s well worth the investment.

Full Solo Stove Summit Smokeless Fire Pit Review.

Industry observers note that after trying out the Breeo X Series 24 for several months, test editor Brad Ford loved it. According to Ford, “One of the coolest details of the X Series 24 is its Corten finish. (It is also available in a stainless-steel finish.) Corten is a structural steel alloy you often see used for bridges or power line towers. It’s designed to oxidize, or rust, creating a natural finish that protects the steel rather than continuing to degrade it. This eliminates the frustration I’ve had with some stainless-steel fire pits that discolor after a couple uses.”.

It has been revealed that beyond this, Ford also liked, “that Breeo intended for their smokeless fire pits to be used for cooking from the get-go, which means they’ve got accessories for the X 24 that work very well. And most of their cooking accessories are compatible with all their fire pits. Top this all off with the fact that the X 24 is made right in Lancaster PA, USA, unlike most other popular brands.”.

The Breeo X 24 weighs more than twice as much as the other models we’ve tested, so it’s not exactly portable—but it is long-lasting.

As the largest pick of the lot, the X Series was easy to load with wood and start a fire. We fit 18- to 20-inch logs into it, laying them across the raised X in the bottom of the pit. This patented design keeps the logs high, allowing air to flow in and feed the fire from the bottom.

Cleanup required scooping ash out, as the unit is too heavy to dump out easily—Breeo sells a shovel designed to ease this process. The brand also offers several accessories for cooking over the fire, which make the X Series as much a grill as it is a fire pit.

This hefty, all-black fire pit is a great-value addition to an outdoor setup. Its wide diameter gives you plenty of room to build a substantial fire, and the shape and airflow make for a good, largely smokeless burn. It takes both wood and pellets right out of the box, no adapter or switch-up required. And the lift-out ash catch has two handles, making it one of the easiest models to empty. (You still have to reach into the drum to lift it out, though, so wear gloves.).

Sources indicate that the black coating is practical, too: Unlike stainless steel, it doesn’t show every fire mark. Once in place, it blends nicely with patio furniture, particularly setups with black metal legs. While it does scratch more easily than others we tested, you can touch it up with high-heat spray paint, just like you would a grill.

Industry observers note that some things to bear in mind: At 35 pounds, it’s heavier than many of the models we tested, so you’re unlikely to move it around much once it’s situated. The price doesn’t include a cover, which you’ll definitely want if it’s going to live outside for the season.

In a recent development, because the ash catch sits inside the main body, with no separate base beneath it, we’d also place this one on a fireproof mat to be extra safe. And this may be petty, but the branding is the most prominent of any pit we tested: you’ll be looking at the words “Blue Sky” on the base every time you sit down.

In a recent development, if you want to bring the campfire with you wherever you go, the Packfire portable fire pit is an ideal choice. It packs down into a backpack, so you can carry it on your shoulders and set it up wherever your adventures take you. In fact, its innovative design won it a spot in our 2026 Home Awards.

Industry observers note that the fire pit is composed of three sections: the base, which serves as a stand and ash pan; the body, which, when fully set up, surrounds the base; and the ring, which holds the body in place. Cleanup is easy: Simply lift the ring and body off the base, pour the ashes out, and break everything back down for travel.

In a recent development, it’s worth noting that even though it’s built for travel, the fire pit is still a bit cumbersome to carry around. While our Director of Product Content, Will Egensteiner was testing the Packfire, he mentioned its 27.5 weight was a factor. “As I heaved it onto my back to put it away, I almost tipped over. And I’m not a small guy.”.

The substance of this fire pit starts with the box: One of the largest and heaviest we had to maneuver into location for testing (only the Breeo was heavier), moving it really requires two people or a dolly. Some of that initial box weight comes from the generous bag of wood pellets packed inside, but the pit itself, at 45 pounds with nothing in it, is hardly lightweight.

Assembly is a little less impressive. Attaching the legs required a drill, as, while an Allen key and screws were included, some of the holes weren’t perfectly aligned, making the process more fiddly than it should have been. It does, however, come with spare screws.

Recent findings suggest that once assembled, though, this thing is a very good-looking workhorse. The large bag of wood pellets kept going for about 35 minutes before burning down to embers; produced virtually no smoke; and the heat output was surprisingly high.

Simply by flipping the inside container, you can also fire up 14-inch logs inside. The exterior frame stayed remarkably cool and, given it’s black, didn’t discolor the way the stainless steel ones did. While the inside picked up some black streaks from the flames, they looked more like evidence of a real fire than damage, which we actually liked.

The ash disposal is a true highlight. You don’t have to lift, twist, or tip the pit to empty it: An ash pan slides out from the side, shovel-style, so you can dump the refuse without moving the fire pit at all. It also comes with a perfectly fitted cover, which is particularly useful given how difficult this one would be to haul away when not in use.

This seriously smart, compact fire pit is made for small spaces and taking on the road. It’s lightweight, straightforward to assemble, and comes with six pieces: a pit and ash can that sit on top of one another; two pieces that twist together to form a fire poker (a little tight to sync up, but ultimately quite a useful piece); and a spark screen with a screw-in knob to lift it (also a very nice extra).

Truly, the whole kit is quite remarkable, given the price. The ash catch is also cleverly designed to fit inside the fire pit for storage, so there’s nothing extra to haul around when not in use. The black finish looks sharp and has the added benefit of hiding burn marks better than lighter finishes. (The downside is, it scratches easily.).

Recent findings suggest that the whole thing packs into a carrying bag with a shoulder strap and drawstring closure. It’s also lighter than any other model we tested, making it an excellent choice for beach parties, camping trips, or anywhere you need to carry your fire pit more than a few feet.

There is one important caveat: Because the pit is so compact, you’ll mostly be limited to twigs, which burn promptly. Use wood pellets instead, for a longer, more consistent fire. The carrying bag also feels flimsy, like it could break down quickly with repeat use, but, for the price, that may not matter.

Recent findings suggest that this one looks like a saucer and comes with just three pieces: a main body that locks securely into the ash holder base and a wind guard that twists onto the rim. It’s also one of the roomier pits we tested, with a wider, more-open design that accommodates both more and larger pieces of wood than many others. The manufacturer claims it handles logs up to one pound. We’d have preferred a measurement in inches, but went with 16 inches, which it handled better than the Tiki. You can also add a griddle attachment to turn it into a cooker.

This one really does produce a roaring fire that can warm four people comfortably. The wide, funnel-like shape seems to encourage a bigger, more expansive flame; sitting around it felt more like a bonfire than simply burning wood in a container. After 25 minutes, we still had a substantial fire going. Its lower stature kept our feet warm too.

The biggest downside is ash removal. The pan in the base is relatively shallow, and the wide fire pit is awkward to twist and lift off for cleaning. You’ll want long arms—or a second person—to do it comfortably. The stainless-steel finish also turned a light bronze after just one use. A cover costs extra.

It has been revealed that before lighting a single fire, we evaluated the things that can make or break a smokeless fire pit before you ever use them. We assessed the packaging and how well each pit was protected in transit, weighed every model, and evaluated assembly. We read the instructions, noting whether they were clear, complete, and actually useful.

We considered whether it could be disassembled for storage, and what came in the box versus what required an additional purchase. While We had plenty of outdoor space to work with, safety always came first: we set every pit on heavy-duty pavers and kept a fire extinguisher close at hand.

It has been revealed that then we lit them up. We used comparable loads of seasoned firewood to assess how easily each pit started, how much smoke it produced, how evenly it burned, and how much heat it put out. We paid attention to flame height and consistency, too, and whether the fire actually warmed people sitting around it—not just looked good from a distance. We measured logs to see exactly what each pit could accommodate and tested wood pellets where models supported them.

Industry observers note that finally, we evaluated the less glamorous but equally important details: how easy each pit was to tend, how much ash accumulated, how easily that ash could be removed, and what it took to clean and put each model away. And because a fire pit can be beautiful at 7 p.m. and a pain in the ass at 10 p.m., we tested for both.

Sources indicate that whether you want a smokeless fire pit to heat your outdoor space or be more of an ambient seasonal moment is an vital consideration. For long nights by the fire with family and friends, you’ll likely want to invest in a larger model that measures 24 inches in diameter. In testing, models that size and up exuded warmth for several feet, and could easily warm four to six people.

They could also handle 14- to 16-inch-long logs. The trade-off: Models this size are a lot heavier and harder to move. If you’re looking for more of a warming accent, narrower fire pits work wonders. You can also maximize some models’ output by adding a heat deflector that sits above the flames and pushes heat out laterally, instead of letting it escape upward.

Ideally, the smokeless fire pit should work right out of the box, with limited-to-no setup, besides setting the pit on a base. It should also break down easily. If you’ll be storing it between fires or seasons, a model that’s easy to disassemble, carry, and put away is key.

The shallower and wider the smokeless fire pit, the easier it is to make a fire from scratch. You simply have more base room to work with to set up your paper, kindling, and wood, and less depth to maneuver to light your fire once ready. No matter your choice, you’ll definitely want a lighter with a long metal wand and a safety catch. None of the models we tested included one.

Recent findings suggest that burning pellets instead of wood was the closest we got to a truly smokeless fire during our testing. Made of compressed wood waste like sawdust, chips, and shavings, pellets are easy to light, always bone dry, and produce a hotter, more consistent flame than logs. There are trade-offs, though: They lack the classic crackle and pop of a wood-burning fire and that wonderful smell.

Recent findings suggest that bags of the stuff also typically cost more than a handful of logs at the hardware store, yet burn about the same length of time. But, if you’re allergic to smoke, don’t want your sweaters to smell of it, have wet wood drying out, or want a reliable and even fire every single time, pellets are an excellent way to go. Some fire pits work with them right out of the box; others need an adapter.

Recent findings suggest that every smokeless pit burns wood. Many smokeless fire pits can also use wood pellets right out of the box. Some, like Solo Stove, need an adapter, so the tiny pellets don’t drop right through the pit’s air holes into the ashcan below. Some portable options may only be wide or deep enough to handle twigs (pellets may be a better option for those).

Pro tip: Wet or green wood will always be slow to burn and emit a lot of smoke; use a moisture meter to suss out whether your logs are dry enough to light up before putting a match to them.

In a recent development, if you blueprint to use your fire pit regularly, easy ash removal should be a deciding factor. The last thing you want to have to do is pick up and tip a heavy steel drum over a trashcan in order to empty it of ash. Instead, look for a removable ash pan or tray that allows you to lift the ash out cleanly once the pit has fully cooled (usually 12 to 24 hours after a fire has ended). Otherwise, you’ll need a shovel to scoop out the ash.

It has been revealed that if you don’t have space to leave your fire pit outside all year, think about who will move it and how often. Even a small pit designed for camping trips can weigh as much as 20 pounds. Fortunately, these options usually come with a carrying bag, so you can sling them over your shoulder. Meanwhile, larger models can top 45 pounds (the 24-inch Breeo weighs just over 60 pounds), which matters when you have to move it under cover or into the garage at the end of the season. Units that come apart make this easier; having a dolly or hand truck on hand helps, too.

Material affects how long your latest pit will look the way it does on arrival. While stainless steel looks shiny and modern from the start, heat from the flames will discolor it, and potentially quite promptly, as some testing highlighted. (You can restore its original shine with a stainless-steel cleaner such as Bar Keepers Friend, but that’s extra work.) Corten-steel usually costs more but forms a protective rust-colored patina that looks attractively weathered over time. Painted or powder-coated steel usually costs less, but can scratch and chip with repeat use.

Recent findings suggest that whatever finish you choose, keeping your smokeless fire pit empty of ash and covered when it’s not in use will help extend its life. Rainwater sitting in a fire pit full of ash can create a corrosive, alkaline slurry that accelerates rust and can damage the metal. Some models come with a cover as part of their bundle; others charge extra for it. Our reviews note whether a cover is included in every pick.

Smokeless fire pits can be a lot more than a place to warm your hands on chilly nights. In some cases, you can turn them into an outdoor kitchen. Brands like Breeo, Solo Stove, and Cuisinart have grill grates, griddles, pizza ovens, or roasting sticks that let you cook over an open fire. Other add-ons also make a difference, like a cover, if you proposal to leave it outside when not in use; a spark screen, particularly if you have toddlers and pets around (though, warning: they can also get hot to the touch); and fire pokers or ashtray lifters, so you don’t get your hands dirty. Definitely check the accessory lineup before you buy your pit; they’re often model-specific. A pair of fire-resistant gloves is always a good investment.

While product photos often depict smokeless fire pits sitting on wood decks or backyards, it’s worth noting that their bases can get hot enough to scorch or discolor lawns, wood decks, composite, and asphalt. Ideally, yours should sit on brick, concrete, stone, or sand. But in the absence of that, a dedicated base (sometimes included, other times sold separately) helps raise the unit off the ground. For an even safer setup, consider adding a fireproof mat underneath. You should also keep a bucket of water or a fire extinguisher nearby and check for local burn bans before lighting. For more on fire pit safety, check out our story.

#24. Tech Report: A Global Rebound for Mangroves

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words)
General 🌐 Nasa

Tech Report: A Global Rebound for Mangroves

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Nasa

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After decades of decline, this ecologically significant type of forest is making a comeback.
  • Scientists began using satellites to map mangrove forests in the 1970s after the launch of the first Landsat satellite.
  • A global rebound began around 2010, the scientists found, led by the expansion of mangrove forests in Asia, Australia, and South America.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After decades of decline, this ecologically significant type of forest is making a comeback.

Scientists began using satellites to map mangrove forests in the 1970s after the launch of the first Landsat satellite. For decades, the story they told about mangroves was dominated by loss and decline. Research published in Science suggests that the tide has turned.

A global rebound began around 2010, the scientists found, led by the expansion of mangrove forests in Asia, Australia, and South America. The researchers analyzed Landsat imagery collected between 1984 and 2023, looking for signs of changes in the extent and density of mangrove canopy.

Sources indicate that they tallied losses of nearly 3,000 square kilometers (1,200 square miles) between 1984 and 2010, followed by an unexpected increase of nearly 2,000 square kilometers (770 square miles) of mangroves after 2010. They also found that many of today's mangrove forests have denser, more closed canopies than they did in 2010, a sign of healthier, less degraded forests, particularly in South America.

It has been revealed that "Other research groups have mapped and analyzed long-term changes in select regions, but these are the first global mangrove maps that cover such a long period," said Zhen Zhang, an environmental scientist at Tulane University. "About two-thirds of the expansion was due to mangroves colonizing upcoming areas and the other third due to restoration and regrowth in degraded areas," he added.

One of the most notable reversals occurred in Southeast Asia—especially Burma (Myanmar). The country lost mangroves rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s due to the expansion of agriculture, aquaculture, and firewood harvesting in coastal areas, but the trend reversed around 2010, when mangrove area began expanding in many places. The authors attribute the turnaround to increased awareness and restoration efforts after the devastating Indian Ocean tsunami in 2004, strengthened legal protections for forests, and high rates of sedimentation that opened up fresh mudflats for colonization.

It has been revealed that the pair of Landsat images above highlights expansion of mangrove forests in Palaw Township in Burma's Myeik District—an area that has seen both significant regeneration of degraded mangrove forests and the spread of trees into upcoming areas since 2010. In this region, much of the regeneration appears to be occurring in abandoned rice fields (brown) south of the village of Kyauktaung. People on nearby Pyin Bukyi Island, meanwhile, have experimented with conservation projects and tree planting efforts to support mangroves. Despite the gains, deforestation remains a common challenge in Burma, which lost 28.6 percent of its mangrove area between the 1980s and 2010. Since then, the country's mangrove area has grown about 10 percent.

Sources indicate that mangrove trees are relatively small—averaging about 13 meters (43 feet)—but mighty from an ecological perspective, with mangrove ecosystems storing up to four times as much carbon as taller inland tropical forests. The trees play an important role in protecting coastal communities from erosion and storm surges, and their distinctive stilt-like roots provide habitat and vital nursery grounds for fish, shrimp, crabs, and other marine life.

In several areas, such as around the mouth of the Amazon River and in northern Australia, extensive deposition of sediment has created new mudflats that mangroves have successfully colonized, contributing to steady increases in each of these regions since the 1990s. At the northern and southern edges of their range, including the southeastern U.S., warming temperatures and fewer freezes have also allowed mangroves to push into areas that were previously too cold, Zhang explained.

Recent findings suggest that there are some areas, however, where losses have outweighed gains. Substantial mangrove losses in the Niger Delta, for instance, have reduced the total mangrove area in West and Central Africa since 2010. North America and southern Africa, meanwhile, have seen widespread degradation after tropical cyclones devastated broad swaths of mangroves. "The global successes we've seen with mangroves during the past decade should not be seen as grounds for complacency," cautioned Zhang. "This underscores that conservation and slowing deforestation can lead to huge positive impacts when coupled with natural expansion and regeneration.".

#23. Some cancer cells survive chemotherapy by turning into giants

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words)
General 🌐 Earth

Some cancer cells survive chemotherapy by turning into giants

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cancer cells that survive chemo swell into giant senescent cells that summon immune repair, and drugs that block their IAP proteins kill them.
  • Chemotherapy can kill a cancer cell, but some survivors enter an unusual state.
  • Recent findings suggest that then they start pumping out the chemical signals a wound uses to call in the immune system’s repair crew.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cancer cells that survive chemo swell into giant senescent cells that summon immune repair, and drugs that block their IAP proteins kill them.

Chemotherapy can kill a cancer cell, but some survivors enter an unusual state. After a near-lethal dose, they stop dividing and swell to many times their normal size.

Recent findings suggest that then they start pumping out the chemical signals a wound uses to call in the immune system’s repair crew. These surviving cells may help tumors return.

A team in Dublin has identified a mechanism that keeps them alive after the damage, along with experimental drugs that kill them in laboratory tests.

Seamus Martin, the Smurfit Professor of Medical Genetics at Trinity College Dublin, led the work from his lab with postdoctoral fellow Gokhan Gunay at the university’s Smurfit Institute of Genetics.

Collaborators at the University of Cologne and the Olivia Newton-John Cancer Research Institute in Melbourne took part.

Nearly all of it was done in human cancer cells grown in the lab, with some experiments in mice, and none of it involved patients.

In an interview with Earth.com, Martin was asked what surprised him most. He pointed to the cells themselves.

“These are really bizarre-looking cells,” he stated.

“They are truly gigantic when compared with normal cells (approx. 10X normal size) and this is highly unusual behavior for cells, even cancer cells.”.

The team gave cervical, bowel and lung cancer cells a three-hour pulse of cisplatin or etoposide, two common chemotherapy drugs that work by damaging DNA.

The dose killed about 40% of the cells within two days. The rest stopped dividing and were still alive a week later, flattened and enormous.

Industry observers note that biologists call this state senescence, and cells in it are often nicknamed zombie cells. They stop dividing but remain alive, secreting a stream of inflammatory proteins.

In a tumor, those signals can attract immune cells that promote new blood vessel growth and help create conditions that support tumor growth.

Martin’s lab studies the machinery that makes cells self-destruct, and the team wanted to know why these cells hadn’t.

The chemotherapy had switched on the cells’ own self-destruct receptors.

Two of them, known as Fas and DR5, rose sharply on the surface of the damaged cells, in every cell type tested and in mouse tumors treated with cisplatin.

Inside the cells, those receptors had assembled the protein complex that normally triggers death. It was fully assembled, and something was holding it back.

In a recent development, one of the restraints turned out to be a family of proteins called inhibitors of apoptosis, or IAPs. The senescent cells were making more of one of them than untreated cells do.

“IAPs act as the antidote to the killing effects of Death Receptors that enable the senescent cells to survive,” Martin told Earth.com.

“However, this now leaves the senescent cells in a state of addiction to the IAPs for their continued survival, which now makes them extremely vulnerable to IAP antagonists.”.

Drugs that destroy IAPs already exist, and several have entered clinical trials. The team tested two of them, BV6 and birinapant, which wiped out the IAP proteins inside cells within eight hours.

Given alongside chemotherapy, the drugs killed more cancer cells outright and left far fewer survivors to enter the zombie state.

Given afterward, to cells that had already turned senescent, they killed those cells at doses that did little to normal cells.

Cells engineered to lack the self-destruct receptors, or the enzyme they activate, were largely protected from the drugs, which is how the team knew the receptors were doing the killing.

A widely studied senolytic drug, navitoclax, kills senescent cells by a different route, and it worked just as well without those receptors.

The team also went the other way. Mice bred without caspase-8, the enzyme the receptors activate, built up senescent cells in the lining of the small intestine and showed more inflammatory signaling in the liver.

In cells, deleting the same enzyme let more survivors enter senescence and kept them alive longer.

Old mice told a similar story. In lung, kidney and heart tissue from 24-month-old animals, the two death receptors were higher than in three-month-olds.

According to recent reports, there was one living test of the drugs. Mice with an inherited retinal disease, which produces leaky latest blood vessels and senescent cells in the retina, got injections of BV6 into the eye.

Their lesions shrank, and the count of senescent cells in the retina fell.

Professor Martin described the strategy as a one-two punch.

The first punch is a standard DNA-damaging drug such as cisplatin, and the second, delivered days later, is a drug that kills the senescent cells the first punch created.

In the paper, the team suggested giving an IAP-blocking drug 5 to 7 days after each round of chemotherapy.

Given ahead of chemotherapy instead, it would push more cells toward death in the first place.

It has been revealed that the timing is the hard part, Martin noted. The second punch has to land while the tumor is vulnerable, and he said several trials of IAP-blocking drugs have been run or are under way.

The one-two punch has not been tested against a tumor in an animal in this study.

The chemotherapy-plus-drug experiments were in dishes, and the tumor experiments in mice measured the receptors rather than survival.

The one animal test of the drugs’ zombie-killing power was in a diseased eye, not a cancer.

Whether a human tumor’s survivors depend on IAPs the way these lab cells did is the open question.

Answering it means the trial the team proposes: chemotherapy paired with an IAP-blocking drug, timed to the days when the giant cells appear.

Martin said getting that timing right may decide whether the second punch connects.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

Latest Update: A latest treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago.
  • Industry observers note that as a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps.
  • According to recent reports, to help solve this problem, Thomas A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that fossils provide an extraordinary window into Earth's distant past, revealing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that existed millions of years ago. Yet the fossil record tells only part of the story. Fossilization is exceptionally rare, meaning that just a tiny fraction of the organisms that once lived on Earth have been preserved. Even when fossils survive, scientists can only discover them if the rock layers containing them are accessible today.

Industry observers note that as a result, our picture of prehistoric life is filled with major gaps. Some geological periods and parts of the world have produced abundant fossils, giving scientists a detailed understanding of the life that existed there. Other periods and regions remain largely unexplored. Because fossil excavations require considerable time and resources, knowing where to search could make a major difference in uncovering fresh evidence of ancient life.

According to recent reports, to help solve this problem, Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History (SNSB) and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna have developed a latest tool for guiding fossil research. The two paleontologists analyzed the geographic distribution of fossil discoveries from animals that inhabited shallow marine environments over the past 540 million years. For the first time, they also mapped the regions of the world where fossil information is missing, providing a clearer picture of where future discoveries may be possible.

Mapping 540 Million Years of Ancient Marine Life.

To build their map, the researchers examined records from the Paleobiology Database (PBDB), the world's leading freely accessible repository of fossil information. The database contains a substantial portion of the paleontological findings published by scientists around the world.

Using these records, the team reconstructed where fossils from ancient shallow marine environments have been documented throughout Earth's history. They also examined how fossil research has developed over decades and centuries, measuring how frequently investigations in different regions have produced newly introduced scientific information.

The researchers then compared these findings with geological information from the Macrostat database. This allowed them to assess not only where fossils have already been discovered, but also where suitable rock formations could provide opportunities to fill notable gaps in the fossil record.

Where Earth's Missing Fossils May Be Hiding.

In a recent development, the analysis revealed a surprising imbalance in our understanding of prehistoric life. The Early Mesozoic (approx. 252 to 66 million years ago) and the Palaeozoic (approx. 539 to 252 million years ago) have already been studied extensively. According to the researchers, additional fossil discoveries from these periods are unlikely to produce a substantial increase in scientific knowledge in the near future.

According to recent reports, the greatest opportunities for expanding the fossil record may instead lie in more recent geological history. Although scientists have already collected extensive evidence from the Cenozoic Era (beginning 66 million years ago), the analysis suggests that its shallow marine deposits still contain significant untapped potential for fossil discoveries.

It has been revealed that to help researchers investigate this period, the team identified locations around the world where previously unknown fossil species are especially likely to be found. Crucially, these are also places where the appropriate geological layers are exposed or otherwise accessible, making actual discoveries possible.

A Treasure Map for Future Fossil Discoveries.

Recent findings suggest that by highlighting regions where important evidence may still be waiting, the latest approach could help paleontologists plan more productive expeditions and make better use of limited research resources. Rather than concentrating on areas that have already been explored extensively, scientists can focus on locations with the greatest potential to reveal something new about Earth's prehistoric ecosystems.

"The fact that many regions of the Earth remain unexplored offers hope for valuable latest discoveries," says SNSB paleobiologist Neubauer.

Industry observers note that "But precisely because expanding the fossil record is quite challenging and progresses only slowly, our work can help researchers worldwide to focus their research specifically on these still largely unexplored areas. We provide a valuable guide for planning future projects and excavation campaigns. The same applies to the examination of existing museum collections awaiting scientific analysis. Through sensible prioritization, we can fill gaps in the fossil record strategically.".

#20. Tech Report: Nov. 13, 1971: Mariner 9 orbits Mars

Tech Report: Nov. 13, 1971: Mariner 9 orbits Mars

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read | Source: Astronomy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On May 30, 1971, Mariner 9 debuted, setting off on its mission to Mars.
  • In a recent development, with Mariner 8, Mariner 9 was one half of the Mars 71 mission.
  • When Mariner 9 arrived at Mars, it encountered a global dust storm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On May 30, 1971, Mariner 9 debuted, setting off on its mission to Mars. On Nov. 13, 167 days later, it entered orbit around Mars, making it the first spacecraft to orbit another planet.

In a recent development, with Mariner 8, Mariner 9 was one half of the Mars 71 mission. But when Mariner 8 debuted on May 9, it failed to achieve orbit and tumbled out of the sky after five minutes, crashing into the Atlantic Ocean. As a result, Mariner 9 inherited all of 8’s goals in addition to its own, giving it an extensive list of objectives: surface mapping, atmospheric monitoring and analysis, surface data collection, and returning around 3,000 photographs.

When Mariner 9 arrived at Mars, it encountered a global dust storm. Because it had been designed for longevity, the orbiter was able to wait out the storm and begin its mission afterwards. (Soviet spacecraft Mars 2 and Mars 3 did not fare as well.) Over the course of about a year, Mariner 9 returned 7,329 photos and mapped 85% of the martian surface. It also revealed a dynamic and active world – including shield volcanoes, dry river valleys, ice at the martian poles – and gave researchers close-up views of the surfaces of Phobos and Deimos.

#16. Tech Report: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Tech Report: Scientists discover a hidden danger of viral infections that vaccines may prevent

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection.
  • Industry observers note that scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses.
  • Most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vaccines may do more than protect people from the immediate effects of a viral infection. Newly introduced research suggests they could also help prevent lasting damage to the immune system that remains even after the virus has disappeared.

Industry observers note that scientists at Pompeu Fabra University discovered that mice recovering from an acute viral infection experienced prolonged problems with their immune defenses. Although the animals had successfully fought off the virus, their immune systems remained impaired, making it harder to respond to latest threats. Remarkably, mice vaccinated before infection did not develop these problems, suggesting that vaccination may provide an additional layer of protection beyond preventing illness.

Most people think of common viral infections, such as colds or stomach viruses, as temporary illnesses. A virus enters the body, multiplies, causes symptoms, and is eventually brought under control by the immune system. Once symptoms disappear, recovery is generally considered complete. The immune response also creates protection against future encounters with the same virus.

But what if the immune system continues to experience harmful effects long after the infection appears to be over?

Viral Infections Can Leave Lasting Immune Damage.

Researchers from Pompeu Fabra University's Infection Biology Laboratory investigated this possibility in a study published in Cell Death & Disease.

In a recent development, using mice with acute viral infections, the team examined what happened to their immune systems after the animals had recovered. They found that eliminating the virus did not necessarily restore normal immune function. Instead, the infection left behind changes that persisted well beyond the initial illness.

According to Andreas Meyerhans, an ICREA research professor at UPF, who led the research, "there is a general perception that an acute viral infection is a relatively minor and transient event: once the virus is controlled and the symptoms have resolved, the body has fully recovered and is back to normal. But this view may underestimate consequences that are not immediately visible and can persist long after the infection itself has resolved.".

The researchers traced these lingering effects to significant changes in the spleen, an organ that plays an important role in coordinating immune defenses. As the immune system fought to eliminate the virus, the spleen developed fibrosis, a condition involving the buildup of scar-like tissue. The arrangement and positioning of immune cells within the organ also became disrupted.

These structural changes interfered with the interactions between immune cells that are necessary to activate T cells. These specialized cells are essential to adaptive immunity because they help recognize and destroy infected cells.

As a result, the mice remained less capable of launching effective immune responses when exposed to fresh challenges. Even though the original infection had been brought under control, their immune defenses continued to function poorly.

It has been revealed that "The infection can be controlled, but that does not necessarily mean that the host has fully recovered," claims Dr. Paula Cebollada Rica, first author of the study. "Our findings show that the immune-related consequences of an acute viral infection can persist beyond the period in which the virus is detectable, leaving the animals in an immunocompromised state.".

Vaccination Prevented Lasting Immune System Damage.

Recent findings suggest that after identifying these long-term effects, the scientists investigated whether they could be avoided. They focused on vaccination, which prepares the immune system to recognize and fight a pathogen before an infection occurs.

The results revealed a striking difference between vaccinated and unvaccinated animals. Mice that received vaccination before infection did not develop the spleen damage or immune dysfunction seen in the other group.

Their spleens maintained their normal structure, and their T cells continued to function at levels comparable to those of mice that had never been infected.

Sources indicate that this finding suggests that vaccination can protect the immune system itself from some of the harmful consequences of fighting a viral infection. In the mouse model, vaccination not only protected against the disease caused by the virus but also preserved the animals' ability to respond to future immune challenges.

Recent findings suggest that "Vaccinated animals did not experience T-cell dysfunction or splenic alterations after recovering from an acute viral infection. This means that vaccination not only prevented the disease resulting from the acute infection but also preserved the immune system's ability to cope with new challenges," Cebollada Rica explains.

A Hidden Benefit of Vaccines With Public Health Implications.

Industry observers note that the findings broaden the potential benefits of vaccination by highlighting a form of protection that may not be immediately apparent. Beyond reducing the immediate effects of an infection, vaccines may also help prevent persistent changes that weaken immune defenses.

Although these results were obtained in mice and do not establish that the same effects occur in humans, they raise important questions about how viral infections influence long-term immune health and how vaccination might help protect it.

The research also comes at a time when vaccination policies and infectious disease prevention efforts are increasingly influenced by political decisions. The researchers emphasize the importance of scientific evidence in understanding the full consequences of infections, particularly when policy choices can undermine coordinated efforts to prevent infectious diseases.

Understanding the broader benefits of vaccination could therefore influence not only medical care but also how public health officials explain the value of vaccines to the public.

"The benefits of vaccination highlighted by this research are important not only for healthcare, but also for how we communicate the value of vaccination to the population at large," Meyerhans states. "It is important that people are aware of the broader protection that vaccination can provide and continue to trust in vaccines as one of the most effective tools to prevent diseases. Put simply, vaccines provide strong health benefits at a relatively low cost to society.".

#13. Breaking: REVIEW: Spectrum Optics SkyPilot 127

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1360 words)
General 🌐 Astronomy

Breaking: REVIEW: Spectrum Optics SkyPilot 127

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Astronomy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the smart telescope revolution has grown rapidly over the past few years.
  • Industry observers note that that’s where the SkyPilot 127 from Spectrum Optics ($999) takes a different approach.
  • At first glance, the SP127 looks like a conventional catadioptric with a standard finder on a motorized alt-azimuth mount.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the smart telescope revolution has grown rapidly over the past few years. Most of these scopes focus primarily on electronic imaging, though, and while amateur astronomers may marvel at the images, they also still enjoy the simple pleasure of looking directly through a telescope.

Industry observers note that that’s where the SkyPilot 127 from Spectrum Optics ($999) takes a different approach. Rather than replacing direct observing with a screen-based experience, the SP127 combines a traditional 5-inch (127 millimeters) f/15 Maksutov-Cassegrain telescope with a smart guidance and imaging system.

At first glance, the SP127 looks like a conventional catadioptric with a standard finder on a motorized alt-azimuth mount. But looks can be deceiving.

The secret lies in that “finder.” On closer inspection, it is not a finder at all, but a 2.1-inch (53 mm) f/4 ED refractor outfitted with a digital camera. This second optical tube is the heart of the SP127’s electronically assisted system, serving as both guide scope and imager. The guide scope determines the telescope’s position through plate solving, slews to selected targets, maintains tracking, and captures images. Spectrum Optics also includes the same intelligent camera and 53 mm refractor in its separately sold SPi53 Smart Telescope system.

The camera is built around a Sony IMX662 CMOS color sensor with 2.9-micrometer pixels and a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels. It includes 64 gigabytes of onboard storage.

According to recent reports, the MirroSky app, available for iOS and Android, is central to the SP127’s operation. It controls target selection, image capture, live stacking, and display, while the guide scope and camera work together to find objects and produce live-stacked images.

Meanwhile, the Maksutov is dedicated primarily to visual observing. The optical tube weighs approximately 6.5 pounds (2.95 kilograms) and measures 14.6 inches (370 mm) long. A Vixen-style dovetail makes it easy to remove the optical tube from the mount. Total weight for the assembled SP127 is about 26 pounds (11.8 kg).

In addition to the guide scope/imager, the SP127 comes with a 25 mm Plössl eyepiece, a 90° 1¼” star diagonal, a screw-on visual back, an adjustable tripod with steel legs 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) in diameter, cables, an AC adapter, and a Bahtinov focusing mask for the guide scope. The camera’s nosepiece is also internally threaded to accept standard 1¼” filters.

Sources indicate that in its standard configuration, the included camera photographs through the 53 mm refractor rather than the Maksutov. Although the camera is removable, Spectrum Optics recommends a separate camera for imaging through the Maksutov because its long focal length and narrow field are not well-suited to the included camera’s plate-solving system. That doesn’t mean you have to invest in more equipment, though; I took some very nice shots of the Moon simply by holding my iPhone to the Mak’s 25 mm eyepiece.

The SP127’s hybrid arrangement works well in practice. After the user selects a target in the app, the guide scope directs the mount to the correct location, then tracks the sky. The observer can view the target visually through the Maksutov while the guide scope stacks and displays images via the app. A word of caution, however: Be careful not to shake the instrument when looking through the eyepiece. Even a slight motion will blur the image being photographed.

Like most Maksutov-Cassegrain systems, the SP127 excels at medium and high magnifications. Its 1,900 mm focal length is especially well-suited for observing the Moon, planets, planetary nebulae, and double stars.

Spectrum Optics MirroSky SkyPilot SP127 Primary Optical Tube: 5-inch 127mm Maksutov-Cassegrain Focal Length: 1900mm Length: 14.6 inches (370 mm) Focal Ratio: f/15 Guide Scope Optical Tube: 53mm ED refractor with Sony IMX662 CMOS camera Focal Length: 200mm Focal Ratio: f/4 Assembled Weight: 26 lbs. (11.8 kg) Mount Payload: 9 lbs. (4 kg) Connectivity: built-in Wi-Fi, 2.4 and 5 GHz Camera Storage: 64GB onboard storage Tripod: Full-size adjustable steel-leg tripod Eyepiece: 25mm Plössl Price: $999.99 Contact: Spectrum Optics 2175 S Grand Ave Santa Ana, CA 92705 1-888-879-5143 spectrumoi.com.

Industry observers note that for this review, I arranged to receive a sample SP127 directly from Spectrum Optics. It arrived securely packed and in perfect condition.

Industry observers note that setup was easy, thanks to the well-illustrated paper manual that came with the scope. After I aligned the guide scope with the Maksutov during the day, as the instructions suggested, the scope was ready to go. I had everything together in under half an hour.

Recent findings suggest that control is handled entirely through the MirroSky app. To initialize the scope to the sky, the system uses onboard sensors combined with date, time, and location information supplied by the connected smart device. The camera includes dual-band Wi‑Fi capability supporting both 2.4 and 5 gigahertz connections. During use, the app’s interface was straightforward and easy to navigate. Target acquisition was quick and accurate. Chosen objects were always centered in the field of view. The app also provides guided tours and a database containing more than 100,000 stars, solar system members, and deep-sky sights.

Sources indicate that tracking performance was accurate for visual observations and short-exposure imaging. Since the SP127 uses an alt-azimuth mount, field rotation may become evident around the edges with longer exposures.

The SP127 can be powered by eight user-supplied AA batteries in the mount, a suitable external 12-volt power source, or the included AC adapter.

I found that the Maksutov performed very well. Lunar views were well-defined, with crater walls, rilles, and other surface features standing out crisply. I was especially impressed when, in moments of steady seeing, the SP127 detected a few of the craterlets on the floor of Plato. It passed another tough test by resolving Schröter’s Valley, a sinuous rille near craters Aristarchus and Herodotus.

It has been revealed that planetary performance also proved impressive. Multiple cloud bands as well as the Great Red Spot were clearly visible on Jupiter, and shadows cast by Galilean moons could also be seen on the planet’s cloud tops.

Double stars were another strong point, thanks to the long focal length. The Trapezium in the Orion Nebula, for instance, was striking. The included eyepiece did well, but the view really sparkled when I swapped in my own eyepieces with shorter focal lengths.

Recent findings suggest that throughout it all, I was very impressed with the crispness of the images, showing the high quality of the Maksutov’s optics. Like most catadioptric telescopes, the SP127 focuses by moving the primary mirror. This takes tight manufacturing tolerances to maintain a precise focus without tilting the mirror. I found that alignment stayed spot-on after swapping eyepieces and refocusing the view.

Sources indicate that I was equally impressed with the imaging results using the 53 mm guide scope. The app allows you to customize settings, including gain, exposure length, number of frames to capture, and dark frames. After I experimented with the settings, the Orion Nebula appeared in vivid color after only two minutes of exposure, even as it was setting in my light-polluted sky. The Pleiades also recorded beautifully, although not all members squeezed into the guide scope’s approximately 1.6° by 0.9° field. The Horsehead Nebula, the Whirlpool Galaxy, the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, and more displayed details exceeding what you might expect from such a small aperture, especially after post-processing using apps like PixInsight, GIMP, and Photoshop.

Industry observers note that the SkyPilot 127 is one of the most original entries in today’s smart telescope market. For observers who still enjoy looking through an eyepiece but appreciate the convenience of app-driven targeting and imaging, the SP127 offers something genuinely special. In a small but growing group of smart telescopes that combine traditional eyepiece observing with integrated electronic imaging, the SP127’s hybrid design makes it an appealing bridge between conventional astronomy and the smart telescope revolution.

#11. Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1208 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A major latest study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks.
  • The independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago.
  • An estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A major latest study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks. However, the findings also point to a possible increase in risk over a longer period, making the decision more complicated than it initially appears.

The independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago. The annual conference brings together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, emerging evidence, and advances in clinical care.

An estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes. Statins are widely prescribed to lower cholesterol and reduce these risks, including in people who have never experienced a cardiovascular event. This preventive approach remains a central part of the American Heart Association's 2026 joint guideline on dyslipidemia.

Do Older Adults Need to Keep Taking Statins?

Although statins are an established treatment for reducing cardiovascular risk, questions remain about how much benefit they provide when people reach their 70s and beyond, particularly if they have never had a heart attack or stroke.

In a recent development, "While the Association's recent joint guideline recommends lifestyle and potentially medication for people with high LDL-C at younger ages to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, recent studies question the health benefits of continuing statins in the later decades of life," stated study author Rita F. Redberg, M.D., M.Sc., FAHA, professor of cardiology and the Araxe Vilensky Endowed Chair in Cardiology at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. "A few previous studies assessed the safety of discontinuing statins for primary prevention at age 70 and later, and they found no difference in mortality. One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins. Whether it is safe to discontinue statins to prevent a first CVD event in the elderly remained unclear and the question we explored in our study.".

It has been revealed that to investigate, researchers enrolled nearly 1,900 adults aged 70 and older who were taking statins specifically to prevent a first cardiovascular event. Every participant also had at least two chronic medical conditions, such as a history of cancer or lung disease.

Industry observers note that participants were divided into two groups. One group stopped taking statins, while the other continued their prescribed treatment. Researchers tracked their health for approximately two years, with additional follow-up extending as long as four years. They examined rates of heart attack, stroke, and death, along with changes in quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and muscle wasting (known as sarcopenia).

What Happened When Older Adults Stopped Statins?

According to recent reports, the initial findings were largely reassuring. After approximately two years, participants who stopped taking statins did not experience a statistically significant increase in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths compared with those who remained on the medications.

Stopping treatment also did not produce measurable improvements in the other outcomes researchers examined. Quality of life, muscle discomfort, falls, and muscle wasting were similar in both groups.

Industry observers note that there was, however, a small difference in cardiovascular outcomes. Over the first two years, the results indicated approximately one additional cardiovascular event for every 40 people who discontinued statins compared with those who continued treatment.

According to recent reports, the longer follow-up revealed a more concerning pattern. Over a period of up to four years, 12.7% of participants who stopped statins experienced a heart attack, stroke, or death, compared with 9.2% of those who kept taking the medications.

Longer Follow-Up Reveals a Potential Risk.

Redberg explained that the higher rate of serious outcomes during the four-year follow-up represents a new finding in research on statin discontinuation among older adults. She suggested that the difference may have emerged because this trial included more participants and tracked them for a longer period than earlier studies.

These results complicate the question of whether older adults should continue cholesterol treatment indefinitely. While the findings suggest that stopping statins may be a reasonable option for many people in this age group, they also indicate that remaining on treatment could offer some protection over time.

"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," she said. "There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event.".

It has been revealed that the trial involved 1,880 participants aged 70 and older (average age of 77; 53% men, and 47% women), all of whom had at least two chronic health conditions. Individuals with established cardiovascular disease or a previous cardiovascular event were not eligible to participate.

It has been revealed that researchers conducted the study between November 2021 and April 2026 across 24 medical centers in Switzerland, France, and the Netherlands. Of the participants, 938 were assigned to discontinue statins, while 942 were assigned to continue taking their medications.

According to recent reports, throughout the trial and subsequent follow-up, researchers recorded heart attacks, acute ischemic strokes, and deaths from any cause. Participants also completed surveys assessing their overall quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and sarcopenia.

One limitation was that some participants did not remain in their originally assigned groups. Some people instructed to stop statins eventually resumed treatment, while others assigned to continue taking statins stopped using them. Altogether, approximately 14% of participants switched from their assigned treatment approach during the study.

Recent findings suggest that to determine whether these changes affected the findings, the researchers performed several additional statistical analyses. The results remained unchanged.

Taken together, the findings suggest that discontinuing statins may be an option for many adults over 70 who have not previously experienced cardiovascular disease, especially when considering outcomes over the first two years. However, the higher rate of heart attacks, strokes, and deaths during longer follow-up underscores why stopping treatment should be an individualized decision made with a healthcare professional rather than a general recommendation for all older adults.
